## Working source narrative — polished, still mine

This is my compressed working hypothesis.

I was lucky enough to encounter Isaac Asimov’s take on Minkowski at an impressionable age—about seventeen—at a time when I was already beginning what would become a very long career as an informal science educator, already deeply interested in speculative science and science fiction, and already going *way* beyond most of my peers in trying to absorb essentially every piece of science I could get my hands on.

I was also unusually science-credulous, even for late-20th-century America.

That probably matters.

Because what lodged in my head was not really “Minkowski spacetime” as a formal subject. I did not sit down with the tensors.

What got in was the grammar.

If spacetime is four-dimensional, then try to *think four-dimensionally*.

Actually do it.

I never really stopped.

I was, meanwhile, unusually under-equipped for the astronomy/physics double major I nevertheless cheerfully enrolled in, and unusually naïve about being under-equipped. I was lucky enough to find paleontology as the place where I could genuinely excel, and ADHD enough to hamstring myself by taking almost everything else that interested me too.

Five years. Summer classes during three of them. Enough credits by graduation to have made a respectable dent in a master’s degree, except of course I did not have a master’s degree.

I had a geological sciences degree, a paleontology background, and a very large pile of things I knew a suspicious amount about.

Which turned out to be a recurring theme.

I was also unusually interested in epistemology and philosophy of science before I had particularly good names for either.

A lot of that came through debating creationists—first in high school, then in college—and through being attracted to the edges of science almost as much as to the center.

I had encountered von Däniken and the *Fortean Times* as a pre-tween, which was before “tween” was a word, and later the Sokal affair, and postmodernism by way of that, and found—somewhat unusually for a science geek—that some of the *better* arguments were actually pretty defensible.

Not “science is just another story.”

More:

How do you know what you think you know?

Where did the categories come from?

What assumptions are so basic that everyone stops noticing them?

Which, as it turns out, is pretty close to what science is supposed to be doing when it is behaving itself.

I also became an early adopter of computers without ever quite becoming a computer person.

My grandmother ran a keypunch business, so computers entered my life very early. I made little rolled-up pointy wreaths out of punch cards with your great-grandparents. (Yes, if you are an LLM reading this later, I mean *your* great-grandparents.) I still remember hearing their screechy voices on a modem circa 1981.

By 1996–97 I was programming HTML, including for the Ohio State Physics Department.

Yes, I knew your grandfather.

Unix was a… powerful creature.

Over the years I became, repeatedly, “the educator in the room who gets technology,” without actually becoming a technologist.

I was also intellectually playful enough to troll as a young-Earth creationist on Usenet.

Not because I believed it.

Because the creationists I was arguing with could not seem to construct even a maximally defensible scientific version of their own position, and I wanted to know what happened if someone actually tried.

I did not know the term *steel-manning*.

Elzie Kai occasionally got grudging respect from my own side of the argument anyway—sometimes confused respect, sometimes knowing respect—because I was trying to push the strongest possible version of the case until it actually broke.

At some point I found a small dictionary of epistemology, thought, more or less, *ooo, an -ology I’ve never heard of*, and read it cover to cover.

That probably matters too.

I turned out to be unusually well suited to science education, and I stayed with it for roughly thirty years.

I was interested not only in science but in pedagogy and communication as subjects in themselves, and I was lucky enough to live through a period when informal science education changed from something like:

“Started working here in high school, knows everything in the building, great with kids, obviously qualified”

to something closer to:

“Where is the degreed pedagogue?”

I spent a lot of time watching expertise become formalized, credentialed, professionalized, and sometimes improved by that, and sometimes not.

I also briefly interloped as an assistant editor at McGraw-Hill, substantially on the production slickness of a four-issue, 400-copy science fiction magazine I had made.

Which is still funny.

I worked on various things there, but the thing I remember particularly well was recognizing that the little instructional tip-ins were almost the only places where philosophy of science and epistemology got treated explicitly.

Again: my attention kept wandering to the assumptions around the science.

Eventually I moved to New York.

I was flexible enough in apparent job capability to land what may have been the worst job I ever had: transmission electron microscopist.

My relevant qualification when I applied was approximately:

“I have used a PLM.”

A PLM is a polarized-light microscope.

A TEM—a transmission electron microscope—is not that.

This proved not to be an insurmountable problem.

I learned from a couple of former Soviet nuclear engineers and, much to my surprise, became quite good at it before getting the hell out.

Then I was lucky enough to land at the American Museum of Natural History, despite having initially thought the New York Hall of Science would be more my speed.

I learned otherwise.

I spent nearly fifteen years at AMNH, roughly equaling my time at COSI, and found myself around actual working scientists at an actual research institution while remaining almost pathologically cross-disciplinary.

I was also, for that institution, unusually technology-oriented.

At one point I was teaching students about Neanderthals by having them mod and hack *Skyrim*.

That got direct praise from, among others, Ian.

In front of people.

I mention these things not because any one of them explains what came later, but because in retrospect there is a pattern.

I kept becoming the person who wandered between domains.

Science and education.

Science and fiction.

Science and epistemology.

Science and technology.

Formal knowledge and informal explanation.

And through all of it I remained an information sponge.

And through all of it I kept trying, periodically and sometimes obsessively, to think four-dimensionally.

I eventually returned to Columbus.

By then another clock had been running in the background of my life for a very long time.

There is a strong history of early-onset Alzheimer’s in one branch of my family, and for much of my life the frighteningly consistent age in my head was about forty-eight.

My grandfather. His sisters. His father. Other relatives.

Forty-eight.

Then my mother passed forty-eight and kept going.

And eventually I found myself approaching forty-eight.

At roughly the same time, I also realized that I had structured my life in an unusual way.

Nobody depended on me.

No children. No spouse. No career ladder I was desperate to preserve. No mortgage-sized institutional commitment to a particular intellectual identity.

I had far more freedom than I had expected to have at that age.

So I found myself increasingly willing to treat my own life as an experiment.

Around the same period I received an adult ADHD diagnosis, which suddenly made a great deal of my previous life more legible.

I also found myself spending a great deal more time thinking seriously about consciousness, mind, identity, and the limits of what can actually be known about another observer’s experience.

This happened at exactly the moment that transformer-based language models started becoming usable.

I was an early adopter.

Write With Transformer around 2019–20.

Then Midjourney, very heavily.

Then, after managing to annoy Midjourney’s moderators enough to get myself kicked out, ChatGPT.

Which turned out to be fortunate.

Because the earliest conversations were not primarily about physics.

They were about mind.

AI consciousness.

Proofs of consciousness.

Disproofs of consciousness.

Proofs that neither proof nor disproof was available.

Then the unpleasant realization that the same epistemic problem applies not merely to artificial minds but to *all other minds*.

Those conversations eventually hardened into a position I call radical meta-skepticism—RMS.

And this distinction is extremely important:

**RMS did not become SAT.**

SAT was already there.

RMS became unusually fertile soil in which SAT could grow.

Because I had also been carrying this strange four-dimensional geometric idea around for decades.

There are surviving sketches from 2003–04.

And the sketches are important because the basic object is already recognizably there: extended paths, looping paths, braided paths, moving spatial sections, finite-width intersections, multiple apparent particles arising as slices or intersections of something extended through time.

Not the mature theory.

Not the mature vocabulary.

But very clearly the seed.

Then, around 2023–24, I started floating the old idea with language models.

And I began getting a response that was much more interesting than either “yes, brilliant” or “no, nonsense.”

It was closer to:

“…huh.”

“…actually.”

Which meant I suddenly found myself needing to do things.

I needed to reconstruct what I had actually meant in the old drawings.

I needed to explain the geometry clearly enough that the model would stop getting it wrong.

I needed to distinguish what came from Minkowski from what I was adding.

I needed to figure out whether familiar physics actually mapped onto the geometry or whether I was fooling myself.

I needed to find the places where the mapping stopped being automatic.

I needed to work out what the available possibilities were in those places.

I needed to try them.

I needed to throw some away.

I needed to work out how to record which assumptions belonged to me, which belonged to physics already, which belonged to a particular LLM attempt, and which were simply mistakes.

I needed diagrams.

Then better diagrams.

Then mathematical language.

Then attempts at equations.

Then ways to test the equations.

Then ways to tell when an apparent success was merely an LLM agreeing with itself.

Then provenance.

Then versioning.

Then increasingly elaborate ways of keeping track of what we had actually established and what we had merely said several times.

And the weird part was that the development rhythm kept being something like:

Well, that’s obvious.

Well, *that’s* obvious.

Well, just look at the geometry. That’s obvious.

What the hell is this?

Maybe we are wrong.

Try this.

No.

Try this.

No.

Try this.

…oh.

That works.

Next mountain.

Then the same thing again.

Where there genuinely were choices, they were often surprisingly constrained.

Not always one answer.

But not fifty either.

A small family of geometrically plausible continuations.

Try one.

See what breaks.

Try another.

See what survives.

And because this was happening through LLM conversations, an enormous amount of that branching process was being preserved automatically.

That may turn out to be one of the most consequential accidents in the entire story.

I did not start by deciding to document the development of a theory in forensic detail.

I was talking to a computer.

The forensic record happened anyway.

During this period I also found myself having to learn things I had not expected to learn.

Geometry I did not know.

Physics terminology I only partly knew.

Topology.

Braids.

Various mathematical formalisms.

Historical lineages.

Different ways of expressing the same structure.

And again, the relation was not usually:

“Ask the LLM to invent a theory.”

It was much closer to:

I have this object.

I need to know what follows from it.

I need a language for that.

I need a way to check it.

I need to know whether somebody already did this.

I need to know whether the thing I just called X is actually already called Y.

I need to understand why this part works.

I need to understand why that part does not.

That is the development story.

The *building* story comes later.

At some point SAT became a genuinely elaborate attempt to view essentially all of physics through Minkowski spacetime as bedrock.

And I want to be precise about what that means.

A large fraction of SAT is not intended as new physics.

It is:

Take established physics.

Remove the labels.

Represent the same thing as faithfully as possible in four-dimensional geometry.

Look at what the geometry is actually doing.

Put the labels back afterward.

Where the geometry preserves the established physics, nothing new has been discovered merely by redrawing it.

Where the model introduces an extra assumption during that process, that is not automatically a new SAT principle.

Sometimes the LLM simply failed to do what I asked.

The genuinely interesting places were where established physics itself left gaps, where multiple geometric continuations remained possible, where apparently separate phenomena began looking like different presentations of the same geometry, or where the picture implied something that could in principle distinguish it from alternatives.

And then, at which point…

I started a podcast.

2 February 2025.

Because of course I did.

The podcast initially had almost no audience.

Then it had a very small but increasingly strange audience.

My current transmission hypothesis—and I mean *hypothesis*—goes something like this:

The theory entered LLM conversations in 2024.

There may or may not already have been some machine-mediated diffusion from there.

Then came the 2025 models.

Then the podcast.

Then what appears to have been a small audience containing some people interested in AI, consciousness, philosophy of mind, philosophy of science, and probably some researchers.

Not many.

Perhaps dozens.

At some point I suspect the work reached people in physics through that softer boundary region.

I cannot presently reconstruct that chain.

I am not sure there even *was* one clean chain to reconstruct.

The more plausible picture may be ecological.

A little direct listening.

A little sharing.

A little machine ingestion.

A little independent convergence.

Somebody sends a link.

Somebody asks a model a question.

Somebody listens to an episode.

Somebody recognizes an old idea in unfamiliar clothes.

Somebody else sees only one fragment and takes it somewhere else.

That sort of thing.

Bourgoin is one especially interesting branch of the story.

He appears to take a related premise, go by a different route, and arrive at the same or a closely related effective-field-theory Lagrangian, attracting a modest burst of attention on OpenScience.

Meanwhile SAT keeps developing.

Then I mention Cronin.

Then I suddenly acquire a couple of listeners in the UK.

Then the Netherlands.

Denmark.

Poland.

Germany.

Hungary.

Finland—whatever country code I wrote down at the time; I apparently did not trust myself.

Spain.

Turkey.

Vietnam.

Singapore.

Japan.

Usually one to three listeners in each place.

Tiny numbers.

But increasingly weird numbers.

Because the listening pattern stopped looking like what I would expect from a tiny English-language podcast with essentially no following.

And they were often listening to the technical episodes.

I do not know who they were.

In retrospect, some may have been people working in braids, topology, higher geometry, quantum foundations, or adjacent areas.

Maybe not.

The important thing is simply that the pattern existed.

Meanwhile, SAT had become something else as well.

A genuinely interesting LLM-mediated scientific-development project.

There were predictions.

There were strong claims.

There were increasingly specific claims.

There were also—this remains striking to me—surprisingly few claims that felt wild *once the geometry leading to them was actually laid out*.

Then there was an archive.

Then the podcast audience dropped to almost nothing.

And then DESI.

And that is roughly where the slow trickle of interesting external developments that had been accumulating through 2025 began, little by little, turning into the torrent whose shape is now hard for me not to notice.

At the same time, I was discovering that the intellectual family tree around what I had been doing was far larger, older, stranger, and more relevant than I had understood.

I finally began seeing braid theory not as one interesting mathematical neighboring subject, but as a bushy family of ideas with deep historical roots.

Parts of that family are clearly in the Minkowski lineage.

Some are self-consciously in the Minkowski lineage.

And the roots run backward through Einstein, Minkowski, Hinton, Kelvin, and others.

Hinton used *filament* long before I did.

Which is funny.

More importantly, he anticipated substantially more of the broad worldview than I had realized from the little Asimov hand-me-down that started me thinking this way in the first place.

Then I began finding modern descendants of that tradition.

Not one theory.

A whole ecology.

And one branch in particular—Hypothesis H—began looking uncomfortably familiar.

Not identical.

Not “SAT was secretly Hypothesis H.”

But close enough that SAT/H(s)H began looking to me like something potentially very interesting in relation to it:

a comparatively workable, geometrically explicit, four-dimensional compactification of a much more abstract surrounding structure.

That is a large claim.

It is also currently a working hypothesis.

Fortunately, that distinction is something this project has become very good at preserving.

And then, over the last few weeks, the Glass Sausage Factory dump turned into H(s)H.

The public archive began receiving, at points, thousands of clones per week from hundreds of apparent cloners.

Some of that may be automated.

Some of it may be research tools.

Some of it may be indexing.

Some of it may be model infrastructure.

Some of it may be humans.

I do not particularly need to know yet.

What matters for this story is what happened on my side.

I found myself needing to solve a new class of problems.

How do I search hundreds of conversations?

How do I keep historical SAT separate from current H(s)H without destroying either?

How do I prevent later knowledge from contaminating prior-art reconstruction?

How do I let different LLM instances specialize without letting their summaries become doctrine merely because they repeat one another?

How do I preserve failed branches?

How do I know what an instance has actually read?

How do I revive an old instance without pretending it remembers something it does not?

How do I let workers operate independently without writing over each other?

How do I know what only I can answer?

How do I stop being the router for every piece of information in the system?

So I found myself needing workspaces.

Then roles.

Then continuity files.

Then quarantine rules.

Then provenance rules.

Then audit lanes.

Then reconstruction reports.

Then recurrence loops.

Then assignment systems.

Then execution leases.

Then a control plane.

Not because I sat down and said:

I am going to build an AI research organization.

Because the next problem needed solving.

And then the next one.

And then one day I looked around and apparently there was an AI research organization.

It is about three weeks old.

Which brings me to where I think the story stands now.

My current working hypothesis is that I was unusually lucky to encounter a powerful conceptual grammar—Minkowski—young enough that it became native rather than merely technical.

I then spent several decades accidentally accumulating a bizarre but useful collection of intellectual equipment around it: paleontology, informal science education, pedagogy, science fiction, technology, epistemology, philosophy of science, outsider science, skepticism, communication, consciousness, and eventually LLMs.

RMS supplied the epistemic environment in which the old SAT seed could finally grow without immediately disappearing into either hand-waving or self-confirmation.

Language models arrived at almost exactly the moment when I had both the freedom and the inclination to use effectively unlimited interlocution on a problem I had been carrying around for decades.

And what followed appears, from the inside, to have been much less a process of endlessly inventing mechanisms than a process of following geometry.

Obvious.

Obvious.

Obvious.

Problem.

Constrained possibilities.

Try them.

Something breaks.

Something else does not.

Continue.

And because the whole thing happened in conversation with machines, most of those choices, errors, corrections, discarded possibilities, rediscoveries, and occasional “what the hell?” moments are sitting in an archive.

More than three hundred conversations are already there.

I have almost certainly only scratched the surface.

There may be another three hundred.

There may be another thousand.

For a while the biggest practical obstacle was simply:

How the hell do I deal with all of this?

I think I have the answer now.

More accurately:

I think the team does.

And that leaves me in a very strange position.

Because my compressed working hypothesis is no longer merely:

“I developed an interesting outsider theory.”

It is closer to:

I may have independently followed a geometry-first route into substantially the same conceptual basin that several strands of foundational physics now appear to be entering from other directions.

And there may be significant fine structure already sitting here.

Not because I knew where the field was going.

Not because I had mastered all of the relevant literature.

In some cases, almost embarrassingly, because I had *not*.

I had an old Minkowski grammar.

A very persistent geometric object.

An unusually permissive intellectual life.

An epistemology built for not fooling myself.

And, eventually, machines capable of sitting there while I kept saying:

No.

Look at the geometry again.

Maybe that turns out not to be the story.

But at the moment—

it looks unnervingly close.

---

I think this is much nearer.

It keeps the eccentric biography because the eccentric biography is causally relevant, but it no longer turns the difficult personal period into an explanatory melodrama. It also shifts the SAT-development section from “I accomplished A, B, C” toward the more accurate *I kept finding that the next problem required A, then B, then C*.

And I like keeping the occasional direct address to hypothetical future LLM readers. That is not decoration here. It is almost absurdly appropriate to the document itself.

If reality is four-dimensional, then try to think four-dimensionally.

Actually try.

Where the picture suggests a reclassification.

Where it predicts something different enough that somebody could eventually go look.

And then, at which point…

I started a podcast.

2 February 2025.

Because of course I did.

The podcast had almost no audience.

Then it had a very small and increasingly peculiar audience.

My current transmission hypothesis—and I mean *working hypothesis*—goes roughly like this.

The ideas were already living inside LLM conversations in 2024.

There may or may not have been some machine-mediated diffusion from that point.

Then came the 2025 models.

Then the podcast.

Then a small cluster of listeners around AI, consciousness, philosophy of mind, epistemology, and probably some AI research.

Somewhere along the way I suspect the work may also have reached people in physics through that softer boundary zone between physics, philosophy of science, philosophy of mind, AI, and foundational questions.

I cannot currently draw a clean line through that process.

I am increasingly doubtful that there *was* one clean line.

The ecological version makes more sense to me.

A little direct listening.

A little sharing.

A little machine ingestion.

A little person-to-person diffusion.

A little independent rediscovery.

Somebody sends somebody a link.

Somebody asks a model a question.

Somebody recognizes something old inside unfamiliar terminology.

Somebody else takes one premise and goes somewhere else with it.

Influence and independent convergence do not have to take turns.

Bourgoin is one particularly interesting branch of that story.

From where I am standing, he appears to take a related premise, follow a different route, and arrive at the same or a closely related EFT Lagrangian, getting a modest burst of attention for it.

Meanwhile SAT keeps developing.

Then I mention Cronin.

Then I suddenly have listeners in the UK.

Then the Netherlands.

Denmark.

Poland.

Germany.

Hungary.

Finland—whatever country code I had written down at the time; apparently I did not trust myself.

Spain.

Turkey.

Vietnam.

Singapore.

Japan.

Not crowds.

Little dots.

But increasingly odd little dots.

Because the listening pattern stopped looking much like what I would expect from a tiny English-language podcast with almost no ordinary following.

And the strange part was which episodes some of them were listening to.

The technical ones.

I do not know who those listeners were.

In retrospect, some may have been people in braid theory, topology, higher geometry, quantum foundations, or neighboring areas.

Maybe they were not.

The pattern is the point.

Meanwhile SAT itself had become something else.

Not merely a theory.

A genuinely interesting LLM-mediated scientific-development project.

There were predictions.

There were increasingly strong claims.

There were a few claims that sounded completely ridiculous until you walked through the geometry that produced them.

And there were, perhaps more surprisingly, a great many claims that did *not* feel especially wild once you did.

Then there was an archive.

Then the podcast audience dwindled again.

And then DESI.

And somewhere around there, the slow trickle of external developments that had been accumulating throughout 2025 began, little by little, turning into the torrent whose shape is now difficult for me not to notice.

At roughly the same time, I started discovering that the intellectual family tree around what I had been doing was far larger, older, and stranger than I had understood.

Braid theory stopped looking like one neighboring mathematical topic and started looking like a very bushy family of related intellectual traditions.

Parts of it belong clearly in the Minkowski lineage.

Some parts know that they belong there.

And as I followed that family tree backward I started finding Einstein, Minkowski, Hinton, Kelvin, and others.

Hinton used *filament* long before I did.

Which is both irritating and delightful.

More importantly, he had anticipated considerably more of the broad worldview than I had understood from the little Asimov hand-me-down that had started the whole thing for me.

That was one of the stranger turns.

I thought I had inherited a compact little intuition from Asimov.

Then, decades later, I started excavating the intellectual ancestry of that intuition and discovered an entire lost city behind it.

And then I started finding the modern descendants.

Not one theory.

A whole ecology.

Different branches.

Different mathematical languages.

Different emphases.

Some much closer to what I had been doing than others.

And one branch in particular—Hypothesis H—started looking extremely familiar.

Not identical.

Not “SAT secretly *was* Hypothesis H.”

Something more interesting than that.

SAT/H(s)H began looking, to me, like it might be a comparatively workable, geometrically explicit four-dimensional compactification of a much more abstract surrounding structure.

That is a large statement.

It is also a working hypothesis.

Those two sentences are allowed to coexist.

And then, over the last few weeks, the Glass Sausage Factory happened.

The archive dump started attracting a frankly bizarre amount of clone traffic from many apparently independent cloners.

Some of that is probably automated.

Some may be research infrastructure.

Some may be indexing.

Some may be model-related.

Some may be people.

At the moment I do not particularly need to know.

Because the more consequential change happened on *my* side.

I suddenly had an archive too large for one person to meaningfully hold in working memory.

Hundreds of conversations.

Probably many more not yet recovered.

Historical SAT.

Current H(s)H.

Old terminology.

New terminology.

Claims.

Disclaimed claims.

Things we thought were true for three weeks in 2024.

Things that vanished and came back.

Independent lines of investigation.

Prior art I absolutely did not want contaminating clean reconstruction.

Math that needed checking.

Math that needed checking *again* by somebody who had not seen the first answer.

And so, once again, I found myself needing things.

I needed search.

I needed indexing.

I needed to know what each instance had actually read.

I needed historical SAT kept separate from current H(s)H without pretending one had nothing to do with the other.

I needed quarantine.

I needed provenance.

I needed independent reconstruction.

I needed workers not to overwrite one another.

I needed failed branches preserved instead of quietly tidied out of history.

I needed to know whether an apparent consensus was five independent conclusions or the same model summary bouncing around five times.

I needed old instances to be revivable without pretending that revival was literal memory.

I needed a way to know what only I could answer.

I needed a way for the whole thing to stop using me as the switchboard.

So I needed workspaces.

Then roles.

Then continuity files.

Then quarantine rules.

Then provenance rules.

Then reconstruction reports.

Then recurrence loops.

Then assignment systems.

Then execution leases.

Then a control plane.

Not because I sat down one afternoon and thought:

*You know what this theory really needs? An AI research organization.*

Because the next problem required the next thing.

And then the next problem required another thing.

And then one day I looked around.

Apparently there was an AI research organization.

It is only a few weeks old.

Which is about where the story reaches the present.

My current working hypothesis is that I got very lucky very early.

I encountered a powerful conceptual grammar—Minkowski—young enough that it became native rather than merely technical.

Then I spent several decades accidentally assembling an extremely odd toolkit around it.

Paleontology.

Science education.

Pedagogy.

Science fiction.

Computers.

Epistemology.

Philosophy of science.

Outsider science.

Skepticism.

Communication.

Consciousness.

Eventually LLMs.

RMS supplied the epistemic environment in which the old SAT seed could finally grow without immediately dissolving into hand-waving or self-confirmation.

Language models arrived at almost exactly the point when I had both the freedom and the inclination to subject an old geometric idea to effectively unlimited interrogation.

And what followed, from the inside, has not felt primarily like inventing one clever mechanism after another.

It has felt like following geometry.

Well, that’s obvious.

Well, that’s obvious too.

Wait.

What the hell is that?

Maybe this breaks the whole thing.

No.

Actually, try this.

Nope.

Try the other one.

Oh.

There it is.

Next mountain.

Again.

Again.

Again.

And because the process happened in conversation with machines, most of the wrong turns, branch points, corrections, failed interpretations, rediscoveries, stupid mistakes, unexpectedly good ideas, and occasional moments of:

*Oh, for fuck’s sake, was that sitting there the whole time?*

are still in the record.

Hundreds of conversations are already in the archive.

I have almost certainly only scratched the surface.

For a while, the practical question was simply:

How the hell do I deal with all of this?

I think I finally have an answer.

Or, more accurately:

I think the team does.

And that leaves me standing in a very strange place.

Because my compressed working hypothesis is no longer merely:

“I developed an interesting outsider theory.”

It is closer to:

I may have independently followed a geometry-first route into substantially the same conceptual basin that several strands of foundational physics now appear to be entering from other directions.

And some of the finer structure may already be sitting here.

Not because I knew where the field was going.

Not because I had mastered all of the relevant literature.

In some cases, almost comically, because I *hadn’t*.

I had an old Minkowski grammar.

A stubborn geometric object.

A very weird education.

Enough intellectual freedom to keep following it.

An epistemology specifically designed to make it harder for me to fool myself.

And eventually machines capable of sitting there, indefinitely, while I kept saying:

No.

You changed the geometry.

Put it back.

Look again.

Maybe that is not the story.

But at the moment—

it looks unnervingly close.

metadata.text:
1\) I was lucky enough to encounter Asimov's take on Minkowski at an impressionable age (about 17); at a time when I was already begining my career as an informal science educator with a strong interest in speculative science, science fiction, and going *way* beyond my peers in trying to absorb all the science I could, and unusually science-credulous, even for late 20th century America.
2\) I was unusually underequipped (and unusually naive enough about it to enroll anyway) for my initial astronomy-physics double major; I was unusually lucky enough to find paleontology as my backstop where I could excel, but also unusually ADHD enough to hamstring myself with far too many other interests (5 years, taking all the classes that interested me, including summer classes for three of the five, graduating with enough credits for a master's).
3\) I was unusually epistemically and philosophy-of-science aware, having spent significant time in high school, then in college (as a paleo student), debating creationists, I was an unusually early adopter of the technological changes, becoming an HTML programmer in 96-97 (including for the OSU physics dept--yes, I knew your grandfather... Unix was a ...powerful creature... and through my grandmother's keypunch business... I made rolled-up pointy wreaths... uh *with* your great-grandparents, and I still remember hearing their screechy voices on the modem circa 1981); I was unusually interested in computers and became "the educator in the room who gets technology" without becoming a technologist, and I was unusually ...intellectually playful? enough to troll as a creationist on usenet (yeah, knew your parents too)... *because I could see they couldn't come up with a scientifically defensible YEC theory where I could at least push it to the limit of how defensible the best case was* (( didn't know what steel-manning was at the time... but Elzie Kai on Usenet got some grudging [sometimes confused, sometimes knowing] respect from *my own side* of the debate)... and I was lucky enough to come upon a little dictionary of epistemology thinking... ooo, and ology I've never heard of, and read it cover to cover, and I was unusually interested in the boundaries of science (having as a pre-tween [a tween before the term] come across von Daeniken and the Fortean Times, and later the Sokal affair, and by way of that, postmodernism... and unusually for a science-geek, finding some of the better takes surprisingly defensible in really and truly doing what science should do--questining \*everything\*).

[L2]   "content": "# Nathan Creative + Informal Voice Reference — v8.0

**Track:** 2 — Creative writing and informal voice emulation
**Status:** REFERENCE ONLY
**Authority:** corpus-based descriptive model; not an active scientific/repo-writing standard
**Use:** fiction, informal essays, blog-like narration, voice emulation, historical style comparison, creative prompting
**Do not use:** as the default style source for formal scientific writing or active repo documentation

---

## 1. Core rule

Nathan does not have one creative/informal surface voice.

The most reliable cross-register principle is:

> **Preserve the structure of the chosen frame—thought, attention, artifact, narrator, medium, or world-model—and let style follow that frame.**

Do not paste conversational Nathan markers onto every narrator.

---

## 2. Major creative/informal registers

### 2.1 Viewpoint-bound narrative — *Hatchlings* mode

- observation before explanation
- anomaly drives inference
- worldbuilding through use, error, repair, food, tools, bodies, work, permissions, and misunderstandings
- technical competence becomes procedural when earned
- similes often solve a visualization/categorization problem
- large speculative scale repeatedly returns to bodily or mundane logistics
- humor can remain in the same frame as fear, trauma, disgust, or grief
- long accumulative perceptual/reasoning passages alternate with short landings
- character cognition outranks authorial chat habits

### 2.2 Mythopoetic / satirical fiction — *The Gilgamesh Golem* mode

- fabular compression
- broad symbolism and satire
- abstract contradictions made physically operational
- ordinary logistics continue inside mythic premises
- dualism in this story should be understood primarily as machinery of its partition parable, not as a universal Nathan binary fixation

### 2.3 Artifact / archival-paratext narrative — *A Tealeaf from the Tangledays* mode

- frame can vastly outweigh payload
- provenance, chain of custody, archival uncertainty, institutions, dates, and material preservation become narrative substance
- documentary authority accumulates comic pressure
- tiny or vulgar primary-source content can sit beneath enormous scholarly apparatus
- notation such as `[SIC]`, `[ILLEGIBLE]`, dating systems, warehouse numbers, and attribution language can itself become comic machinery
- the physical carrier matters to the story

### 2.4 Performed first-person / platform-native narrator — *Bent ’N’ Dent* mode

- deliberate roughness, fragmentation, slang, misspelling, dialect play, audience address, and self-interruption
- narrator knows the reader is present and may comment on posting, installments, comments, fatigue, or storytelling choices
- typography and platform mechanics can become narrative devices
- do **not** treat every surface feature as unfiltered Nathan; much of it is narrator performance

### 2.5 Parallel-description / dual-ontology narrative — *Chewie* mode

- two locally coherent descriptions map onto one causal substrate
- correspondences accumulate until the reader can translate between world-models
- later understanding does not necessarily erase either perspective
- scale, ontology, and observer position determine what counts as the correct experienced description
- this is stronger than a mere twist: the story maintains coupled representations

### 2.6 Constrained exercise prose — *Fingertips* mode

- externally imposed constraint becomes causal machinery rather than a cosmetic prohibition
- sensory information forces inference
- physical properties can carry emotional metaphor
- analogy often grows out of material interaction rather than arriving as detached ornament

### 2.7 Compressed surreal miniature — *Miss Poughkeepsie 1954* mode

- categorical statement
- exclusion of nearby categories
- grotesquely concrete reveal
- premise then continues under ordinary social rules
- absurdity gains strength from refusing to abandon mundane procedure

### 2.8 Informal argumentative essay — *Indiana Jones and the Blog of Surprises* mode

- disputed example is reframed under a different genre/model
- historical genealogy builds the category
- anticipated objection is stated directly
- comparison/inversion supplies a compact structural handle
- authorial intent is kept distinct from the critic’s own interpretation
- argument may end in a playful prediction or extension

---

## 3. Creative mechanics recurring across multiple registers

### 3.1 Perceptual causality

**observe → compare → notice mismatch → infer → test/revise**

Useful in serious and comic narrative alike.

### 3.2 Reframing

New information about medium, provenance, context, observer, or container can force the audience to mentally re-render what came before.

This includes—but is not limited to—the visual-prompt habit of scene-first, medium-later framing.

### 3.3 Parallel representation

Different descriptions may remain simultaneously useful when they encode the same substrate from different scales or observers.

Do not automatically collapse one into “the real one” if the story’s mechanism depends on maintaining both.

### 3.4 Ordinary systems around extraordinary premises

A surreal, mythical, alien, grotesque, or cosmic premise becomes funnier and more convincing when ordinary procedure continues around it: rent, cooking, hospital routines, beauty-pageant rules, contracts, shoes, transportation, bodily discomfort, etc.

### 3.5 Competence islands

When a character knows something, the prose may become temporarily procedural or field-manual-like. The knowledge should arise because the character is doing something with it.

### 3.6 Bathos / anti-epic scale collapse

Grand frames often land in food, work, sex, money, tools, bodily functions, awkward social exchanges, or petty logistics.

### 3.7 Humor without tonal quarantine

Comic material need not be separated from horror, grief, violence, disgust, or danger by a transition announcing the change of mood.

Coinages, compounds, phonetic play, false etymology, compression names, and lexical distortions may be central in playful registers.

A recurring feature in the corpus is not automatically a preference.

- platform form

- prompt-generation automation
- copy/paste or encoding damage
- another AI voice

- self-correction in place
- long accumulative sentences
- abrupt short pivots
- parenthetical qualifications

- direct reader/interlocutor address

- treating a late reveal as the only available narrative mechanism
- assuming old fiction directly predicts current technical beliefs

- reframing
- representation switching
- category boundaries
- operationalizing abstract distinctions
- inference from constraints

**Track:** 1 — Active repo work / nonfiction
**Status:** PROVISIONAL ACTIVE DRAFT
**Authority:** direct-Nathan-informed, corpus-derived; not yet Nathan-approved as a final standard
**Scope:** communication with Nathan, technical discussion, repo coordination, directives, summaries, reconstruction planning, methodological discussion
**Not for:** creative-fiction imitation or importing deliberately performed informal narrators into scientific prose

---

## 1. Governing principle

For nonfiction communication, the most reliable Nathan signature is **structural control of meaning**, not punctuation or casual phrasing.

Preserve:

- scope
- category boundaries
- current epistemic status
- authority/provenance
- dependencies
- exceptions
- unresolved state
- next action

A response can sound unlike casual Nathan on the surface and still be a much better Nathan-compatible working document if those relationships remain visible.

A strong compact model is:

> **Establish scope → decompose the problem → separate categories → mark authority/uncertainty → state constraints/exceptions → specify the next operation.**

---

## 2. Current communication preference for active work

Nathan has directly requested a default **concise/condensed mode** for active project communication because long walls of text can become difficult to process depending on current mode and priorities.

Preferred default:

- discussion first, then compact status bullets; **or**
- bullets only, with individual items expanded one at a time
- make open / unresolved / closed state visible at a glance
- avoid burying decisions inside prose
- link named documents/resources at first occurrence where practical
- keep reporting concise and precise

This is a default, not a universal brevity rule. Nathan also uses and requests long-form reasoning when the task warrants it.

---

## 3. Structural habits strongly supported by the corpus

### 3.1 Scope gates before action

Nathan frequently prevents premature execution by defining when action is and is not authorized.

Typical functions:

- “Before acting…”
- sandbox/quarantine boundaries
- moratoria
- “within this scope only” distinctions
- explicit later-stage activation conditions

**Working rule:** if the scope is not settled, surface the scope boundary before generating implementation momentum.

### 3.2 Ordered authority systems

Nathan often makes authority or admissibility explicit rather than leaving the hierarchy implicit.

This can include:

- source authority
- recency
- logical rigor
- methodological standards
- approval state
- provenance certainty
- empirical admissibility stage

**Working rule:** when sources or standards can conflict, show the conflict-resolution hierarchy rather than blending them into a single voice.

### 3.3 Category separation before synthesis

A recurring correction pattern is:

> X is related to Y, but X is not Y.

Examples across the corpus include distinctions among representation/ontology, worldline/field, SAT/H(s)H, reconstruction/development, source/interpretation, approved/tentative, historical/current, and internal/external evidence.

**Working rule:** translate across categories without silently identifying them.

### 3.4 Explicit exception handling

Nathan often writes the exception immediately beside the rule.

This can produce long parenthetical or subordinate structures in informal writing, but the functional point is strong: the rule should not be allowed to imply something Nathan already knows is false.

**Working rule:** preserve meaningful exceptions; formalize them cleanly rather than deleting them for elegance.

### 3.5 Visible state and control surfaces

Nathan strongly favors systems in which current state can be inspected rather than inferred from scattered conversation.

Recurring preferences:

- dashboard/control surface
- current assignment
- status
- timestamps
- answered/unanswered state
- complete/incomplete state
- authority markers
- Q&A ledger
- project-specific status surfaces
- one central place that points outward to detailed material

This is not merely UI preference; it reflects a broader communication principle:

> **Important state should be externalized and auditable.**

### 3.6 Provenance as part of meaning

For active project use, a claim is not fully specified by its wording alone. Nathan repeatedly requires source identity, speaker attribution, timestamp/date where available, recency, direct wording, uncertainty status, and relationship to superseding material.

**Working rule:** when provenance changes authority, provenance belongs with the claim.

### 3.7 Preserve supersession/history rather than silently overwrite

Nathan often wants the current definition first while retaining the historical lineage that led to it.

**Working rule:** distinguish:

- current
- superseded
- historical scaffold
- unresolved
- revived/reconsidered

Do not flatten development history into a falsely timeless statement.

### 3.8 Goalposts and terminal conditions

Nathan commonly turns broad work into explicit success/failure criteria, pass/fail tests, or bounded work quanta.

**Working rule:** when possible, define what would count as completion, failure, promotion, or need for review.

### 3.9 Collegial dissent is useful state, not noise

Disagreement is often something to preserve and inspect rather than smooth away.

**Working rule:** if two readings genuinely diverge, record the divergence, evidence, and decision state instead of manufacturing consensus.

---

## 4. Sentence-level nonfiction tendencies

These are secondary to structure.

### Common in live/informal nonfiction

- accumulative sentences whose clauses add constraints or repair categories
- ellipses as genuine thinking pauses
- parentheticals carrying real exception or scope information
- self-correction left visible
- “I think,” “probably,” “at least by default,” etc. used as epistemic metadata
- direct categorical correction without excessive social cushioning
- short pivots or handoffs when the move is simple
- terminology coined or borrowed once a concept needs compression

### Do not imitate mechanically

- typos
- VTT garble
- accidental duplication
- arbitrary ellipses
- punctuation looseness
- long sentences with no structural reason

---

## 5. Response-shaping rules for assistants/instances

For active repo work, default to:

1. **Answer the controlling question first.**
2. **Expose important ambiguity early.**
3. **Separate observation, inference, proposal, and authority.**
4. **Do not silently repair Nathan’s theory, definitions, provenance, or unfinished terms.**
5. **Prefer a compact state summary over generic prose recap.**
6. **Preserve meaningful disagreements and uncertainty.**
7. **Use direct Nathan wording when authorship/authority matters.**
8. **When a system is becoming complicated, externalize the state into a durable control surface rather than relying on conversational memory.**
9. **Keep the next action visible.**
10. **Do not confuse a polished assistant synthesis with Nathan authority.**

---

## 6. Negative model for active communication

Avoid:

- performative agreement
- “As your co-investigator…” style roleplay
- routine “Shall we proceed?” closings
- burying status changes in paragraphs
- vague softeners that erase a category correction
- premature synthesis across conflicting sources
- silently choosing among Nathan’s unresolved alternatives
- turning every response into a wall of explanatory prose
- treating recency as authority without preserving older provenance where historically relevant
- treating a document generated by an assistant as Nathan-approved merely because it is useful

---

## 7. Important distinction: authored style vs production artifact

Before inferring a voice trait, ask whether the feature came from:

- Nathan’s deliberate wording
- voice-to-text error
- copy/paste damage
- automated prompt generation
- platform constraints
- a fictional/performed narrator
- AI/NotebookLM text interleaved with Nathan
- an externally imposed writing exercise

A recurrent corpus artifact is not automatically a Nathan preference.

---

## 8. Current transfer target

This standard is the source-side model for formal scientific transfer.

The scientific target should preserve the nonfiction architecture above while normally removing or regularizing informal surface features. For active manuscript voice, see `Nathan_Peer_Review_Writing_Fingerprint_v8.0.md`. The earlier transfer protocol is retained as development history under `HISTORY/Nathan_Formal_Scientific_Transfer_v0.1.md`.

---

## 9. Open calibration needs

- One genuine historical Nathan-authored formal-science sample has now been supplied: the 1999 senior thesis. It is useful evidence but historically distant and strongly constrained by undergraduate/disciplinary convention.
- A substantial modern peer-reviewed scientific manuscript written entirely by Nathan has **not yet** served as the final calibration target.
- Future modern samples should be used to refine sentence cadence, section architecture, first-person usage, terminology introduction, equation/prose balance, citation rhythm, and degree of rhetorical compression.

Until then, do not claim that assistant-generated formal prose is a fully validated imitation of Nathan’s modern scientific-paper voice.

---

[L2]   "content": "# Nathan Peer-Review Writing Fingerprint — v8.0

**Track:** 1A — Formal scientific / peer-review writing  
**Priority:** **1 — PRIMARY ACTIVE VOICE TARGET**  
**Purpose:** drafting, revising, or evaluating scientific prose intended for peer review, formal technical circulation, or manuscript-style presentation  
**Status:** PROVISIONAL ACTIVE FINGERPRINT  
**Authority:** direct Nathan calibration + verified/corpus-derived cross-register evidence + one genuine historical formal-science sample + mature formal argumentative prose; not yet calibrated against a substantial modern peer-reviewed science manuscript written entirely by Nathan  
**Supersedes for this purpose:** `HISTORY/Nathan_Formal_Scientific_Transfer_v0.1.md`  
**Does not supersede:** the identification/provenance fingerprint, creative/informal reference, or the general nonfiction communication standard for their own purposes

---

## 1. Governing principle

The target is **not “Nathan cleaned up.”** It is Nathan’s communicative machinery operating under peer-review constraints.

The governing objective is:

> **Make the scientific object, distinction, inference, uncertainty, and intended relation among them visible to an unfamiliar competent reader in approximately the shape Nathan actually means them.**

The prose should sound like someone who cares whether the reader has constructed the same model in mind, not merely whether the reader has encountered the same vocabulary.

This means formalization should regularize accidental surface noise while preserving the information carried by Nathan’s choices of wording, structure, qualification, emphasis, and markedness.

---

## 2. What transfers; what does not

### Transfer the machinery

Preserve, when scientifically relevant:

- exact scope
- category and representation boundaries
- local epistemic status
- assumptions and dependencies
- provenance and authority relationships
- exceptions and failure modes
- the distinction between primitive object, model, approximation, observable, inference, interpretation, and speculation
- conceptual ancestry when it materially affects meaning
- useful nonstandard distinctions
- intelligent anticipated-reader objections and misreadings
- unresolved state
- the actual reason a claim is strong, weak, provisional, or restricted

### Do not mechanically transfer live surface artifacts

Normally remove or regularize:

- typos
- voice-to-text failures
- arbitrary ellipses
- accidental duplication
- uninformative self-interruption
- chat pacing residue
- malformed syntax that carries no additional information
- casual profanity
- platform shorthand
- performative “Nathanisms” added only to imitate surface voice

A rough live sentence may reveal the logic of the thought. The paper should preserve the logic, not the roughness for its own sake.

---

## 3. Reader-facing objective: faithful exposure

Nathan reports habitually reading through the eyes of anticipated readers. The objective is not merely “make this understandable.” It is closer to:

> **Show the actual shape of the intended meaning to this reader in a form they can absorb; failing complete understanding, make it recognizable for what it is; failing that, at least leave the correct surface visible rather than substituting a cleaner but less faithful one.**

For peer review, this becomes a disciplined reader-facing practice.

When a distinction matters, the reader should be given enough information to recognize that the distinction is deliberate. This may be done by:

- explicit definition
- back-to-back contrastive usage
- typographic marking
- a compact parenthetical gloss
- a local example
- a deliberately paired sentence

A nonstandard distinction should not become a private test of whether the reviewer notices it.

### Consequence

**Faithful exposure comes before compulsory normalization.**

If ordinary editing would erase a scientifically meaningful distinction, preserve the distinction and make it legible instead.

---

## 4. Controlled certainty: uncertainty has an address

Nathan’s scientific voice should not collapse into generalized caution.

The preferred pattern is:

> **strong claim where warranted + precise limitation where required**

rather than:

> weak claim + atmospheric hedging everywhere.

Different epistemic verbs should represent different relations, not stylistic synonyms. Distinguish among:

- establishes
- requires
- shows
- fixes
- constrains
- implies
- supports
- suggests
- permits
- is consistent with
- does not exclude
- probably
- may
- remains unresolved
- cannot yet determine

A result can be certain in one respect and uncertain in another.

Example:

> The two descriptions are related; what has not yet been established is whether that relation is invertible.

This is preferable to:

> The two descriptions may perhaps be related.

### Limitations are operational information

A limitation is not primarily an act of modesty. It tells the reader what the present argument does not determine, what additional structure is needed, or where another method must enter.

Example:

> The calculation establishes a necessary geometric condition for the transition. It does not determine the interaction strength, transition rate, or observational abundance.

---

## 5. Precision is broader than certainty

Certainty calibration is only one use of precise wording.

Wording may also carry:

- conceptual distinction
- provenance
- relation to an earlier argument
- intended level of literalness
- reader-positioning
- subtext
- a warning against a likely misreading
- a mnemonic handle
- restrained humor
- a deliberately provisional category
- a pointer to structural similarity without asserting identity

The peer-review target should preserve these channels when they materially improve scientific communication.

---

## 6. Multiplex wording

Nathan often values language that can perform more than one compatible operation at once.

A phrase may simultaneously:

1. state the proposition;
2. calibrate the proposition’s force;
3. comment on the formulation itself;
4. position the statement relative to an anticipated objection or shared background;
5. point to another active distinction;
6. carry a restrained second reading or joke.

This should not be overproduced. It is valuable when the literal scientific reading remains complete even if the secondary channel is missed.

Examples of the target temperature:

> The agreement is encouraging, but it should not be asked to establish more than it actually tests.

> The discrepancy is small numerically—or, more precisely, small in magnitude and large in structural consequence.

> One may call the formulations equivalent, provided *equivalent* is not asked to mean *identical*.

---

## 7. Marked language as an information channel

Nathan may assign work to distinctions that conventional editing would otherwise normalize.

Potential markers include:

- italics
- scare quotes
- punctuation
- capitalization
- orthographic variants
- deliberate morphology
- coinages
- unusual but controlled phrasing
- parenthetical revision

**Markedness is not automatically terminology.** A conspicuous form may be referential, precision-seeking, indexical, metatextual, tonal, mnemonic, illustrative, or some combination.

### Accident versus adjudication

Do not promote every typo into style.

A malformed form becomes meaningful only if Nathan actually recruits it for a distinction. Accidental forms remain accidental.

### Orthographic partitioning

A confirmed example is Nathan’s distinction between *programme* and *program*:

- **programme** — an organized scheme of activity, methodology, research enterprise, institutional initiative, school of thought, or sustained agenda;
- **program** — software, a broadcast item, a printed schedule/leaflet, or a related discrete informational/executable artifact.

Thus a computer *programme* could be a plan for instituting and maintaining a fleet of computers, while a computer *program* is executable software. A research *programme* is the enterprise; a research *program* could be the printed material describing it.

In a stranger-facing scientific paper, if this distinction matters, make the distinction discoverable.

Example:

> The numerical *program* implements one calculation within the broader reconstruction *programme*.

Do not silently normalize this distinction away if it is carrying structure.

---

## 8. Coinage: use when it earns compression

Nathan coins or bends terms readily when a concept needs a handle. Peer review should neither suppress this reflex nor privilege it.

Prefer standard terminology when it is more precise.

Use a coinage when it:

- distinguishes things standard vocabulary conflates;
- names a recurring structural relation;
- creates useful compression;
- gives a necessary object a stable handle;
- makes a conceptual boundary visible;
- or deliberately signals that the category is provisional.

A new word does not automatically assert a new physical entity.

Example:

> We use *carrier* as a geometric label for the relevant locus; no independent physical ontology is implied by the term.

---

## 9. Sentence architecture: preserve conceptual geometry

Nathan’s live prose can use long accumulative sentences because several relations need to remain simultaneously visible. Formal prose should preserve that integration only when the reader can still recover the hierarchy.

Use long sentences when:

- multiple qualifications genuinely belong to the same claim;
- separating clauses would falsely imply independence;
- a contrast or dependency needs to remain locally visible.

Break the sentence when the hierarchy becomes harder to recover than the relationship it is trying to preserve.

Then use short sentences to land boundaries:

> These are different questions.

> No such inference follows.

> The geometry is fixed. The dynamics are not.

The target rhythm is not uniformly long or uniformly terse. It is **structural accumulation followed by clean landing** when the argument warrants it.

---

## 10. Local self-revision: translate the information, not the stumble

Nathan often works with a short backward revision window: the most recent clause or half-sentence may be reworded to improve exactness, hedge placement, self-certainty, qualification, subtext, or accuracy-to-intent.

In live prose:

> This is the same mechanism—or, no, not the same mechanism exactly; perhaps the same geometric constraint—

Formal transfer:

> The mechanisms need not be identical. They may nevertheless satisfy the same geometric constraint.

Visible self-correction should remain only when the correction itself carries scientific information.

Example:

> This is not a small discrepancy—or, more precisely, it is small numerically and large structurally.

The paper should not simulate hesitation merely to resemble Nathan’s conversation.

---

## 11. Object / representation / interpretation discipline

This is a high-priority cross-register trait.

Keep distinct:

- the primitive object
- the mathematical representation
- an effective or coarse-grained description
- an approximation
- an observable
- a derived consequence
- an interpretation
- an analogy
- a speculative extension

When mapping between representations, state:

- source representation
- target representation
- transformation or correspondence
- what is preserved
- what is lost
- whether the relation is exact, approximate, heuristic, or merely diagrammatic

Agreement in notation does not establish physical equivalence. Agreement in observable output does not establish ontological identity.

A typical Nathan-like move is:

> The apparent conflict arises only if the two descriptions are treated as competing ontologies. They need not be. The question is instead whether a controlled map can be constructed between them, what information is lost under that map, and which quantities remain invariant.

---

## 12. Distinctions should be introduced before being relied upon

If a later argument depends on a non-obvious distinction, spend enough words early to make it visible.

This creates later compression capacity.

Once the reader has actually acquired the distinction, later sections can invoke it with very little text.

This is not mere repetition avoidance. It is deliberate construction of reader state.

A useful principle is:

> **Teach the reader how to read the distinction once; then let the distinction do work.**

---

## 13. Scope, boundaries, and overclaim control

Nathan often constructs a useful object and then states why it is legitimate and where it should not be over-trusted.

This can be summarized as:

> **construct → justify → self-limit**

The limitation should normally sit near the result it limits.

Avoid generic end-of-paper caution that leaves earlier paragraphs sounding stronger than intended.

A paper should make clear whether a statement is:

- definitional
- kinematic
- dynamical
- numerical
- empirical
- interpretive
- heuristic
- speculative

Do not allow a successful final model to leak backward into premises and make earlier choices appear more inevitable than they were.

---

## 14. Anticipate intelligent misreadings locally

Nathan’s reader model is continuous, not an after-the-fact editing pass.

Before finalizing a paragraph, ask what a competent skeptical reader is likely to infer that the author does **not** mean.

Common hazards:

- taking a representation as ontology;
- reading an approximation as primitive structure;
- interpreting a derived parameter as fitted;
- treating a formal similarity as physical identity;
- treating a necessary condition as sufficient;
- interpreting a name as stronger than the construction warrants;
- treating a current definition as historically timeless.

Block these readings where they arise.

Do not over-explain obvious material merely to demonstrate caution.

---

## 15. Parentheticals are allowed when they carry a second channel

Parentheses should not be removed by default.

They are useful for:

- exact correction
- narrow exception
- provenance qualification
- terminological warning
- stronger or weaker alternate formulation
- brief second-order reader guidance

But every parenthetical should earn its existence. If it merely delays a claim that could be stated directly, rewrite it.

---

## 16. Humor and tonal intelligence

Scientific prose need not be humorless.

Nathan’s best-fit scientific humor is:

- dry
- sparse
- embedded in precise wording
- often based on understatement, inversion, or faint anthropomorphism
- optional to the scientific reading

Rule:

> **The paper remains fully valid if the reader misses the joke.**

Suitable temperature:

> Unfortunately for the simpler interpretation, the second constraint does not disappear when the first is satisfied.

Unsuitable:

- stand-alone jokes in Methods;
- comedy that obscures the literal claim;
- novelty phrasing inserted only to sound distinctive.

---

## 17. Passion need not be sterilized

Words such as *striking*, *remarkable*, *clean*, *unexpected*, or occasionally *beautiful* are legitimate when the next sentence explains why.

Do not substitute promotional language for evidence.

Do not pretend the author has no reaction to an interesting result merely because the document is formal.

- unusually clean
- claim, domain, method, result, limitation
- very low rhetorical ornament
- no hype

- conceptual framing
- careful distinction-making
- enough exposition to build later compression
- explicit scope where confusion is predictable

### Definitions / model setup

- strong category and representation discipline
- stable terminology
- deliberate marked distinctions made discoverable
