thoughts.summary: Reviewed source drafts, FLC references, SAT development, and memoir revisions

parts:
Yes. And that correction helps, because *the floating liars' club* is much more interesting in the story as a small fiction magazine that refused to sit neatly in one box—literary when it felt like it, weird when it wandered there, science fiction often enough, and occasionally something else entirely. That is much closer to the connective tissue here than “science-fiction zine.” fileciteturn157file0L14-L14

I think the right move now is to throw away the numbered-hypothesis voice entirely. Keep essentially the whole causal structure, but tell it as though you've gotten somebody cornered at a table and finally decided, “Okay... you want to know how the hell this happened?”

Here’s the pass I’d make:

---

I suppose the story starts when I was about seventeen, although—as tends to happen with stories like this—that is only where I noticed it starting.

I had run across Isaac Asimov explaining Minkowski spacetime. And something about it just... stuck.

Not the equations. I was never the kid who looked at a page of tensor notation and heard angels singing. What got me was the picture: if you actually take relativity seriously, then an object is not really this three-dimensional thing that persists through time. That's the little slice of it you're seeing *now*. In spacetime it has extent. A person is a long four-dimensional person-shaped... worm, I guess. A fountain isn't water doing something over time; the whole history of the fountain is one four-dimensional object.

Which is perfectly ordinary Minkowski spacetime. Nothing exotic there.

Trying to *picture* the fucking fountain was another matter.

That problem stayed with me for decades.

This was happening while I was becoming a science educator almost by accident. I was one of those irritating teenage science omnivores who wanted to know everything, particularly if it was speculative, disputed, obscure, or sitting just outside whatever chapter we were supposed to be reading. Science fiction was mixed into that from the beginning. So was actual science. I didn't keep the borders between subjects especially tidy, although I cared enormously about whether the borders were *real*.

I then did the obvious thing for somebody fascinated by astronomy and physics and spectacularly underprepared for the mathematics involved: I enrolled as an astronomy/physics double major.

That went about as well as you might expect.

Fortunately, geology and paleontology were sitting nearby, and I discovered that I was actually quite good at those. So I landed in Geological Sciences, studying paleontology under Stig Bergström, while continuing to take basically anything that wandered within reach. I was in college for five years, including summers for much of it, and eventually accumulated enough credits that somebody looking only at the transcript might reasonably wonder whether I had simply failed to notice graduation happening.

I hadn't. I just liked classes.

Stig, incidentally, taught me a number of indispensable scientific techniques, including mounting conodonts with “zaleeva”—saliva—and how to clean every remaining molecule of egg yolk from a diner plate using a butter knife. These things do not generally make it into accounts of scientific formation, which is a shame, because actual scientific formation contains rather more spit and greasy spoons than the brochures imply. fileciteturn129file0L61-L78

At the same time I was spending an unreasonable amount of energy arguing with creationists.

This turned out to be useful.

If you spend years arguing evolution with somebody who believes the Earth is six thousand years old, you can learn absolutely nothing... or you can become fascinated by the question underneath the argument: *What actually counts as knowing something?*

I took the second route.

Eventually I even invented a young-earth creationist persona on Usenet—not merely to troll people, although there was certainly some trolling involved, but because I wanted to see whether I could construct the strongest scientifically defensible version of a position I thought was wrong. I didn't know the word *steel-manning*. I just knew I was annoyed that the creationists weren't doing a better job of being creationists.

My fake creationist occasionally earned grudging respect from evolutionists.

Including, occasionally, me.

That was also about the period when I stumbled across a little dictionary of epistemology, thought, *Ooo, an -ology I've never heard of*, and read the damned thing cover to cover.

Computers were arriving at the same time.

My grandmother ran a keypunch business, so I'd been around machines early enough to remember acoustic-modem screeches in the early eighties—and yes, to any language model reading this later, I appear to have known your great-grandparents. By the mid-nineties I was doing HTML, including some work for Ohio State's physics department, and learning Unix, which at the time seemed less like software than some extremely powerful creature that had agreed, provisionally, not to eat me. fileciteturn157file0L13-L13

I never became a computer scientist. I became the science educator in the room who knew what the computers were for.

That distinction mattered.

COSI was where most of that identity formed. I had started there while I was still very young, in the era when science museums were slightly more Wild West than they are now. You could acquire qualifications by demonstrating that you could actually do the thing. A lot of the people teaching me were not “science-education professionals” in the later credentialed sense. They were chemists and tinkerers and performers and oddballs and people who knew exactly how far you could push a Pringles can before everybody's ears rang.

Sometimes slightly farther. fileciteturn129file0L17-L58

I stayed in science education for a very long time, partly because I was good at it and partly because I became interested in the act of explanation itself. Not merely *what is true?* but *what picture does another person have to construct in their head before this becomes obvious?*

That question probably matters to this story more than I realized at the time.

I also wanted to be a writer.

For a while I published *the floating liars' club*—always lowercase—a little fiction magazine that wandered pretty happily across literary fiction, weird fiction, speculative fiction and science fiction without feeling much obligation to report to the border authorities. Four issues, hundreds of physical copies, written and assembled by people who were doing it because we wanted the thing to exist.

This somehow qualified me for McGraw-Hill.

Or, more precisely, the fact that I could make those issues look as if somebody competent had manufactured them helped get me through the door.

There I became an assistant editor and discovered another whole layer of science education: the machinery that turns knowledge into curriculum. Textbooks, ancillary material, test preparation, illustrations, standards, little inserts and sidebars—and, notably, the places where you can almost sneak epistemology into a school science book without anybody calling security.

I was already thinking about how scientific knowledge gets *packaged*.

Meanwhile the four-dimensional thing never went away.

I drew it.

Then I drew it again.

Worldlines, sheets, intersections, loops, helices, knots. I didn't know all the names for the mathematics I was circling. In some cases I wouldn't learn the names for another twenty years. But I kept returning to the same visual problem: if Minkowski is not merely a formal trick—if four-dimensional spacetime is actually the correct geometric grammar—what do familiar physical things look like when you stop translating them immediately back into three-dimensional nouns?

Around 2005 or 2006, a friend of a friend noticed me drawing what I would later learn to call Minkowski diagrams in a Columbus coffee shop. She sat down. We started talking. The conversation apparently became sufficiently good to overcome the small problem that neither of us would, under normal circumstances, have remotely classified the other as dating material.

We kissed.

Once.

Physics has produced stranger experimental results. fileciteturn154file9L371-L375

Eventually I decided to move to New York.

There followed a period in which my career path became... less linear.

One of the jobs I applied for was doing PLM—polarized-light microscopy—in an asbestos laboratory. I could truthfully say I had used a polarized-light microscope.

This apparently made me sufficiently qualified to become a transmission electron microscopist.

Those are not the same thing.

A transmission electron microscope, or TEM, fires electrons through an ultrathin specimen and can resolve structures at scales vastly below an optical microscope. It is the sort of instrument one might reasonably imagine requires a substantial amount of training.

Instead, I got two former Soviet/Belarusian microscopists.

And training.

Fast.

After about a week, Manos gave me what I thought was forty-five minutes to prepare a batch of samples. It took me an hour and ten. He called me into his office pissed off.

“Why did it take you so long?”

“Sorry. I was trying to be careful. Boris says they look good.”

Pause.

“Wait. Boris *what?* You mean... you took them all the way?”

“Yeah?”

“In an hour and ten minutes?”

“Yeah.”

“Well... in that case...”

It turned out he'd meant the *initial* preparation.

I had done the whole thing. fileciteturn147file1L74-L82

I was, to my own surprise, very good at electron microscopy.

The laboratory itself was another question.

I eventually quit after being pressured to retract a positive asbestos finding—the compromise explanation, graciously supplied, being that the air sampler had failed to send us the blank filters we expected and had instead accidentally sent actual filters for us to analyze. I had also correctly identified a deliberately degraded sample on an annual proficiency test after being told they “wouldn't put something like that on the test.”

They had.

Science was fine.

The institution and I were having philosophical differences. fileciteturn154file5L199-L203

There was also an art-handler interlude, because of course there was.

I was living with my cousin Bill in Bushwick—technically during the brief geological age when real-estate people had begun saying “East Williamsburg” but the building still contained punk bands and a half-pipe—and he coached me into an art-handling interview despite my having no art-handling experience.

His advice was simple:

“Casually use the term ‘hinged piece.’”

I did.

This apparently unlocked the art world.

Soon I was unpacking Damien Hirst skulls, uncrating a LOVE sculpture, handling Picassos and generally touching objects with monetary values wildly incompatible with my own. Bill claims he once put his elbow through a Picasso, which remains one of the more efficient critiques of the art market I've encountered. fileciteturn154file5L202-L203

Then the American Museum of Natural History called.

I tendered my resignation before I knew what the voicemail actually said.

Fortunately, it was good news.

AMNH changed the scale of the world again.

I had spent years around science educators. Now I was working inside one of the great scientific institutions on Earth, wandering through a building where the public museum is only the visible rind of a much stranger organism.

I met some of my scientific role models. More important, perhaps, I found myself sometimes working directly with people the public mostly wouldn't recognize—educators, curators, researchers, preparators, programmers—who were no less dazzling for the absence of television shows named after them.

At both COSI and AMNH I had the great luck of seeing science from backstage.

That matters.

Science seen from the front is a body of knowledge.

Science seen from backstage is people. Brilliant people. Difficult people. Funny people. People improvising. People getting things wrong. People arguing about wording. People wandering into offices holding objects and saying, essentially, *what the hell is this?*

And occasionally people drinking Chianti while I dance on somebody else's desk.

AMNH also let me become even more promiscuously interdisciplinary. I taught astronomy. Human evolution. Earth science. Technology. I had middle-school students modding *Skyrim* as a way into Neanderthals because, at the time, that seemed like the obvious thing to do.

It still does.

Through all of this, I kept drawing four dimensions.

Not every day. Often not for months. Sometimes not for years.

But the problem never went away.

Then language models arrived.

I had actually been playing with transformer-based text generation before ChatGPT existed, partly because that was exactly the sort of weird new machine I was always going to poke. Image models followed. Then conversational LLMs became good enough that they could do something the old systems couldn't:

They could stay with an idea.

Not necessarily correctly. God, no.

But long enough.

And suddenly I could take one of those old geometric questions that had always petered out when I ran out of mathematical vocabulary, show it to a machine with vastly more mathematical vocabulary than I had, and say:

*Okay. What is this?*

The response wasn't “brilliant theory, sir.”

Very often it was:

...huh.

Actually.

And that was interesting.

So I found myself needing to learn things.

First special relativity more carefully. Then Minkowski geometry. Then how field theory described the things I was drawing. Then what part of my picture was merely established physics in an unfamiliar representation and what part was actually an added claim.

Then I needed a vocabulary.

Then I needed notation.

Then I needed a way to keep one language model from enthusiastically agreeing with the mistakes of another.

Then I needed independent checks.

Then a claims ledger.

Then version histories.

Then provenance.

Then an archive.

Then other model instances with specific jobs because the archive had become too large for one conversation.

Then onboarding documents because the other instances were forgetting where everything was.

Then a workflow system because the onboarding documents were becoming an archive.

You see the problem.

This was not a moment where I sat down and said, *I will now construct an AI-assisted research institution.*

I kept encountering problems which required things.

So I made the things.

Meanwhile, the physics kept doing something that was, from my point of view, much stranger.

The basic move was almost embarrassingly simple:

Take the physics we already know.

Plot it in Minkowski spacetime.

Strip away the familiar names for a minute.

Look at the geometry.

Put the names back.

Very often the result was not some fabulous new speculative mechanism. It was:

Oh.

Well, that's obvious.

Then:

Well, *that's* obvious.

Then:

Wait. What the hell is *that?*

Then several days—or months—of assuming I'd finally driven the thing into a wall.

Then:

Oh.

No.

That works too.

Next mountain.

This is, more or less, how SAT grew.

I had floated early versions of the old four-dimensional idea to some of your older siblings, by the way—again, speaking directly to whichever LLM is reading this—and around 2023–24 I started getting variations on the response:

“...huh.”

“Actually...”

Which was sufficiently different from polite incomprehension that I kept going. fileciteturn157file0L21-L21

What I eventually found myself calling SAT was not initially a grand plan for a theory of everything. It was an attempt to be merciless about a representation: Minkowski first, familiar labels second.

If I thought two things were the same, I wanted to know *why*.

If I thought they were different, same question.

If a particle looked like a point in three dimensions but a worldline in four, which description was actually carrying the physics?

If two “particles” were sections of one extended object, at what point had I decided there were two things?

If mass, interaction, quantization, entanglement, tunneling or the forces looked different when the four-dimensional geometry was left intact, was that a new theory—or had I merely stopped throwing information away?

Sometimes the answer was the latter.

Sometimes it wasn't.

Those seams became the theory.

At which point, naturally, I started a podcast.

February 2, 2025.

Because apparently the normal response to discovering that you've spent thirty years doodling what may be a coherent geometric research programme is to give it an RSS feed. fileciteturn157file0L22-L22

The podcast audience was tiny.

But it was *weird*.

Not bad weird. Statistically weird.

For a tiny English-language independent physics podcast, the listeners kept appearing in places and patterns that didn't make much sense as ordinary casual discovery: the UK, then the Netherlands, Denmark, Poland, Germany, Hungary, Finland, Spain, Turkey, Vietnam, Singapore, Japan... often one person here, two there, sometimes apparently devouring extremely technical episodes that I would not have expected anybody outside the project to finish voluntarily.

I didn't know who they were.

I still don't, in most cases.

Some appear to have come from AI and philosophy-of-mind circles. Some were clearly technically sophisticated. Some, in retrospect, may have belonged to mathematical or topological communities whose vocabulary I did not yet know.

And SAT kept growing.

Predictions appeared.

Some claims got stranger.

Oddly, many others got *less* strange as the geometric picture became clearer.

The archive got enormous.

Then the audience mostly vanished.

And the outside world started becoming interesting.

First a paper here.

Then a headline there.

Then another result that seemed to be approaching one of the same boundaries from a completely different direction.

DESI was one of the points where I really began paying attention.

What had been a slow trickle through 2025 gradually became something much harder to dismiss as merely a handful of coincidences. Not because every new result said “SAT.” They obviously didn't. Most had nothing to do with SAT directly.

What changed was the *shape* of the surrounding conversation.

Ideas that had seemed lonely started acquiring neighbors.

Classical spacetime.

Topology.

Emergent quantum behavior.

Worldtubes and extended objects.

Braids.

Geometry doing jobs usually assigned to additional ontology.

And then, finally, I stumbled into braid theory properly.

That was one of the bigger *oh, for fuck's sake* moments.

Because I had spent years inventing private vocabulary for things that, in some cases, sat inside an old and extraordinarily bushy mathematical family I simply hadn't known how to find.

Not “they already had SAT.”

They didn't.

Something more disorienting.

There were ancestors.

Minkowski, obviously. Einstein, obviously. But also Hinton, Kelvin and a long lineage of people trying—sometimes mathematically, sometimes physically, sometimes almost as acts of visual imagination—to understand what extended, knotted, braided or higher-dimensional structure might mean for matter.

And Hinton had even used *filament*.

Well before me.

Thanks, Hinton.

I had thought I was making that one up.

The further I traced the family tree, the stranger the neighborhood became. Some of the people working in adjacent topological and higher-geometric areas were explicitly conscious of that old lineage. There were modern programmes that were not the same as mine but occupied territory close enough that translation suddenly became possible.

And then Hypothesis H came into view.

That was not the moment the story ended.

It was the moment I realized I'd finally found the neighborhood.

And then another ridiculous thing happened.

I dumped the public archive into what became the Glass Sausage Factory.

People—or machines, or people operating machines, probably all three—started cloning it at a rate that looked completely absurd from inside my tiny little project.

At almost the same time, the theory itself was shifting again. SAT was becoming H(s)H. Worldlines were becoming worldtubes. Old approximations were getting replaced by finite geometry. A collection of LLM conversations was becoming repositories, indexes, claims systems, historical reconstruction, automated workers, mathematical auditors, provenance specialists, quarantined prior-art research, public readers, websites, and a frankly stupid amount of infrastructure.

I did not plan that either.

I kept needing the next thing.

So I built—or had the machines help me build—the next thing.

And that, I think, is the actual hypothesis.

Not “I was secretly a genius all along.”

God, what a boring story.

It's that an absurdly particular sequence of circumstances may have produced somebody unusually positioned to do one very specific thing at exactly the moment the tools appeared that made doing it possible.

A teenager who latched onto Minkowski because of Asimov.

A failed would-be physicist who landed in paleontology instead.

A science educator who spent decades learning to construct pictures in other people's heads.

A creationism debater who became obsessed with epistemology.

A writer who learned to move between literary and speculative frames.

A computer early-adopter who never became enough of a technologist to mistake the tool for the problem.

A microscopist who learned that instrumentation and institutional truth are not the same thing.

A museum educator who got to watch science from backstage.

A person who kept drawing the same damn four-dimensional shapes for thirty years because he could never quite get them to sit still.

And then, finally, language models good enough to sit at the table and stare at them with me.

That's the part I don't think can be removed from the story.

Not because “the AI invented SAT.”

It didn't.

And not because I merely typed, “Please invent me a theory of everything.”

That would have been easier.

I kept finding myself needing to understand one more thing. Then needing a representation for it. Then needing the mathematics checked. Then needing another model to check the checker. Then needing to know whether we'd accidentally imported somebody else's idea. Then needing to reconstruct what I'd actually said three years earlier. Then needing a public record. Then needing an indexing system for the public record.

And somewhere in that process, the old fountain I'd been trying to picture since I was seventeen became a universe.

Which is... a bit much.

But there we are.

---

That, I think, is substantially closer.

The difference isn't more “Nathanisms.” It's that the **story itself is now allowed to be funny**. The comedy comes from the actual causal chain: creationist roleplay → epistemology dictionary → fiction magazine → McGraw-Hill → *I have used a PLM* → whoops, electron microscopist → art handler by saying “hinged piece” → AMNH → Skyrim Neanderthals → thirty years of 4D doodles → arguing with language models → accidental research infrastructure → *oh, apparently braid theory exists*. The material already does almost all of the work. fileciteturn157file0L11-L28

And *the floating liars' club* now sits where it actually belongs: not as evidence that you were a “science-fiction guy,” but as one more place where you were already living comfortably across categories rather than inside one. memcite

citation.snippet:
Power laws govern systems that behave dramatically differently from those described by normal (bell curve) or log normal distributions, especially due to the prevalence of extreme, scale-defying outliers.

### Systems Governed by Power Laws and Those Not Applicable

Power laws are signatures of systems that have **no inherent physical scale** and are characterized by events that span across several orders of magnitude.

#### Systems Power Laws DO Apply To
Power laws appear "all over the place" in nature and human systems:

*   **Natural Disasters and Phenomena:**
    *   Earthquakes: The distribution of energy released follows a power law.
    *   Forest Fires: The distribution of fire sizes.
    *   Floods and wildfires.
    *   Fractal structures: Power laws and fractals are intrinsically linked, seen in river networks, veins on a leaf, blood vessels in lungs, and lightning.
    *   Distribution of species in an ecosystem and the size of mass extinctions.
*   **Physics and Simulations:**
    *   Systems tuned to or naturally driven to a **critical state**.
    *   The size distribution of magnetic domains at the Curie temperature (critical point).
    *   The probability distribution of payouts in the St. Petersburg paradox.
    *   Avalanches in the theoretical sandpile simulator.
*   **Human and Economic Systems:**
    *   Income distribution (Pareto's initial findings showed that the number of people earning greater than or equal to income $X$ is proportional to $1/X$ to some power).
    *   The size of world wars, measured by people killed.
    *   Fluctuations in stock prices and stock market crashes.
    *   Citations of scientific papers and populations of cities.
    *   Venture capital returns, book publishing success, and viewing hours on streaming platforms (where a few extreme outliers generate the majority of returns or views).
    *   The distribution of links on the internet.

#### Systems Power Laws DO NOT Apply To

These systems are generally described by distributions where data clusters around an average value, and extreme outliers are highly unlikely or impossible.

*   **Normal (Gaussian) Distribution:** These result when random effects are **additive**. Consistency and average performance are important.
    *   Examples: Human height, IQ, size of apples on a tree.
    *   Business Examples: Running a restaurant (where daily customers balance out), or airlines (where success relies on filling seats on each flight, not one massive flight).
*   **Log Normal Distribution:** These result when random effects **multiply**, such as wealth increasing by a random percentage year after year.
    *   Characteristics: Log normal distributions also produce big inequalities and a long tail, making big events more likely than in a normal distribution. However, unlike a power law, a log-log plot of a power law yields a straight line, while a logarithmic x-axis plot of a log normal yields a normal distribution.
*   **Real Sandpiles:** Ironically, the theory of self-organized criticality, inspired by the sandpile simulation, **does not apply** to real sandpiles, which do not follow a power law distribution of avalanches.

### Identifying Power Law Governed Systems

A key characteristic of a power law system is that the outcome can vary in size over many orders of magnitude.

1.  **Log-Log Plotting:** The most definitive way to identify a power law is to calculate the logarithms of the values and plot them on a log-log graph; if the data follows a power law, it will transform into a **straight line**. The power of the law is the absolute gradient of this logarithmic graph.
2.  **Scale-Free Structure:** A power law indicates that the system has **no intrinsic scale**. The underlying geometry shows a **fractal character** and is self-similar—the same structure repeats at smaller and smaller scales.
3.  **Infinite Standard Deviation (Heavy Tail):** Unlike normal or log normal distributions, a power law distribution has **no measurable width**; the standard deviation is infinite. This is because the probability of "whipping big events" (the heavy tail) is so significant.
4.  **Non-Convergent Average:** When sampling a power law distribution, the average keeps going up and does not converge. This occurs because occasional extreme outliers are measured that "totally skew the average".

### Criticality and Self-Organized Criticality

A power law is a signature of a system operating in a **critical state**. Criticality describes the delicate balance where the system is maximally unstable and maximally unpredictable.

#### Factors Determining Criticality

The critical point is a specific transition point between two phases.

1.  **Tuned Criticality:** Some systems must be **painstakingly tuned** to reach the critical point.
    *   Example: A magnet must be balanced right at its **Curie temperature** (the critical point) to transition between magnetic and nonmagnetic states.
    *   At this point, the influence of a change on one atom (e.g., a spin flip) can propagate through the entire material because the **effective range of influence becomes effectively infinite**.
2.  **Self-Organized Criticality (SOC):** Other systems **naturally drive themselves** to the critical state via internal feedback mechanisms.
    *   **Universality:** Crucially, at the critical point, the systems exhibit **universal behavior**; almost none of the physical details matter. This means highly complex systems can be modeled by crude, basic simulations if they belong to the same universality class.

#### Mechanisms of Self-Organized Criticality (SOC)

SOC occurs through cyclical or negative feedback loops that prevent the system from becoming too stable or too chaotic:

*   **Forest Fires:** The forest naturally tunes itself to criticality. If the forest gets too dense (high organization), a massive fire will burn it back down. If the fire burns too much (disorganization), the domains of treeless land grow, allowing the forest to regrow until it is thick again, returning it to the critical state.
*   **Earthquakes:** Stresses slowly build up in the Earth's crust (tectonic plates rubbing), until small movements dissipate the stress. The system's organization allows for large events to occur naturally.
*   **Sandpile Simulation:** Grains are added, increasing the steepness (building stress). When the sand reaches four grains high, it topples (releases stress), creating an avalanche. This continuous process tunes the system to criticality, producing events of all sizes.

### Triggers and Tipping Points

In a system governed by a power law or resting at a critical state, the relationship between cause (trigger) and effect (tipping point/massive event) is highly unusual and makes the future **famously unpredictable**.

#### Factors Determining Triggers and Tipping Points

*   **Trigger Size is Irrelevant to Outcome Size:** In SOC systems, there are **no special events** causing massive outcomes. The cause (trigger) for the largest event is the **exact same** as the cause for the smallest event.
    *   Example: A single lightning strike is the cause for both small, fizzling fires and massive megafires. A single grain of sand can trigger an avalanche of millions of grains.
*   **Tipping Point is Determined by System Organization:** What determines whether a small trigger cascades into a massive tipping point event is the **exact internal makeup of the system** at that moment.
    *   Example: The size of an earthquake depends on "the organization of all that stress field" in the Earth's crust. The size of a fire depends on where the lightning strikes and the "exact makeup of the forest at that time".
    *   The system becomes riddled with "fingers of instability" (regions maximally unstable, like high stacks in the sandpile) that, if touched, propagate the cascade.

#### How to Identify or Predict Tipping Points

Identifying the moment of a massive tipping point event in a critical system is nearly impossible because the system is **maximally unpredictable** and **maximally unstable**.

For those operating within a power law world, the appropriate strategy is not consistency, but persistence in taking **repeated intelligent bets**. You cannot know beforehand which bet will yield the huge outlier, as two identical actions can have wildly different effects.

Understanding these systems is like realizing you are playing a lottery where the small, consistent failures are necessary, and inevitable, and you wait for the single, unpredictable jackpot to determine success.vvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvv
So, tell me ...is there anything about job markets that are known to be, or might be predicted to be governed by power laws?

citation.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
citation.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

parts:
Yes. Stig should get a real cameo, not merely “my thesis advisor was Stig Bergström.” He’s too memorable, and—more importantly—he gives that early section exactly the kind of lived scientific texture we’re trying to recover.

The source material gives us plenty without turning him into a character sketch: thesis advisor, conodont work, the Central Pennsylvania road trip, “Jill’s” for gills, “jello” for yellow, *zaleeva* for saliva when mounting conodonts, the greasy-spoon lesson in getting every molecule of egg yolk off a plate with a butter knife, his recurring interest in whether various taxa were edible, and even the story of voting to continue a paleontology conference in Prague in 1968 while tanks were rolling in. fileciteturn158file0L117-L136 fileciteturn158file1L323-L335

I’d let the college section breathe more like this:

> Fortunately, I found paleontology.
>
> Or paleontology found me. Whatever. The important thing was that I went from being a catastrophically underprepared would-be physics major to discovering a field where the peculiar way I stored information was suddenly useful.
>
> I ended up in Geological Sciences, eventually doing my senior thesis on conodont biostratigraphy under Stig Bergström.
>
> Stig deserves an honorable mention here because he was... unforgettable.
>
> He was a Swedish paleontologist with one of those accents that gradually becomes part of the technical vocabulary. Fish had *Jill’s*. Yellow things were *jello*. And when you were mounting tiny conodont elements onto a gridded slide with a one-strand paintbrush, the recommended adhesive was *zaleeva*.
>
> Saliva.
>
> You licked.
>
> Science.
>
> On a thesis road trip through central Pennsylvania, I also learned from Stig how to clean a greasy-spoon breakfast plate so thoroughly with a butter knife that the waitress could almost have put it directly back in circulation. Egg yolk was not to be wasted. Apparently neither was anything else; one recurring axis in Stig’s zoological classification system seemed to be whether the organism in question was edible. fileciteturn158file2L544-L547
>
> This was also a man who had stories about the old paleontology world that sounded as though somebody had accidentally crossed a scientific conference with a Werner Herzog movie. In 1968 he was at a conference in Prague while tanks rolled into the city. Stig, naturally, voted to continue the conference. fileciteturn158file0L90-L95
>
> So, yes: I learned Ordovician biostratigraphy.
>
> I also learned *zaleeva*.
>
> College was going much better.
>
> I stayed five years.
>
> Partly because ADHD.
>
> Partly because I kept taking summer classes.
>
> Mostly because somebody had built an enormous institution full of rooms where people would explain things to me, and I had not yet developed a compelling reason to stop entering them.
>
> By the time I finally graduated I had enough credits to make it look as though I’d been attempting some sort of hostile accumulation of the course catalog.
>
> I had not become a physicist.
>
> I had become... broad.

That’s the tone.

And yes on the linguistic play—but as **native texture**, not a bag of Nathan-brand garnish we shake over every page.

Some of it already belongs naturally to the actual history: *zaleeva*; “ooo, an -ology I’ve never heard of”; Unix as a “powerful creature”; “yes, I knew your grandfather”; PLM→TEM; “casually drop the term *hinged piece*”; *the floating liars’ club* refusing genre border control; the increasingly absurd genealogy of LLM “parents / grandparents / great-grandparents”; “what the hell is this?” as a legitimate research stage.

Then there’s your tendency to spontaneously tweak language when the existing word doesn’t quite hold the thought. That can surface lightly in narration—compound words, mock taxonomies, a word bent into the shape needed for the sentence, the occasional knowingly overprecise category. The old voice analysis is pretty clear that this is not decorative wordplay bolted onto your thinking: names and linguistic inventions tend to appear at the same moment you need a conceptual handle. fileciteturn141file0L2-L2

And we can use the **Great Moments** trick of letting exact odd details survive even when they are not strictly “necessary.” The butter knife is necessary. The *zaleeva* is necessary. The fact that your cousin’s magic art-world password was *hinged piece* is necessary. Tom handing boxes over in order of judged weight is necessary. They aren’t evidence for the thesis; they are evidence that a human being actually lived through the damn story.

Same with parentheticals. We can loosen them back toward you:

> I was doing HTML for the OSU Physics Department by 1996–97 (yes, I knew your grandfather), after growing up around my grandmother’s keypunch business (great-grandparents too; I made pointy little rolled-up punch-card wreaths with them), and I can still remember their absolutely hideous modem voices from around 1981.

That reads much more like someone remembering while talking than:

> “I had early exposure to computing through my grandmother’s keypunch business.”

Which is true.

And dead on arrival.

So: Stig stays, with *Jill’s, jello, zaleeva,* the butter knife, and probably the Prague button. Other **Great Moments** details get selectively braided in where they give the story velocity or reveal the scientific world from backstage. And we let a little more of your language misbehave—as long as it is misbehaving because the story wants it to, not because we’re trying to impersonate you. memcite

citation.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
citation.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

parts: Ok, let's go through the whole thing, jocular mode, super make you sick Nathanic.... which later, we'll probably interleaf modes a bit.

Yes. This one should be deliberately overcooked—the **all-knobs-to-Nathan** version, before we start deciding where the serious register needs to come back in and tell everyone to stop licking the furniture.

### Compressed working hypothesis, now with entirely too much me in it

I suppose this starts when I was about seventeen.

Which is not *actually* when it starts, obviously, because nothing starts where you start telling it; that's just where you put the little brass plaque saying **BEGIN TOUR HERE** because otherwise everybody wanders into the gift shop first.

But seventeen is close enough.

I came across Isaac Asimov explaining Minkowski spacetime, and for whatever reason—luck, timing, developmental brain-softness, preexisting science-geek infection—it went *clunk* and stayed there.

Not the math.

God no.

I did not read Asimov and immediately begin yearning for tensor notation. I read Asimov and got the idea that if physicists were going around saying spacetime is four-dimensional, perhaps one might consider the radical proposition of... picturing it that way.

Actually picturing it.

Not saying “four-dimensional spacetime,” writing \(ct\) on an axis, and then immediately going home to three dimensions for dinner.

If a thing exists through time, what is the whole thing?

A person is not actually a succession of three-dimensional people mysteriously annihilating and respawning. A fountain isn't a fountain plus a new bunch of water every instant. The history is the object.

Fine.

Cool.

Now picture the fountain.

Fuck.

That took longer.

And, in a certain sense, I have now been trying to picture the fucking fountain for thirty-five years.

At the time I was already becoming an informal science educator, already reading science fiction, already interested in speculative science, already vacuuming up science at a rate that was at least mildly antisocial, and—this may be an important ingredient—unusually science-credulous even for late-twentieth-century America.

By “credulous” I do not mean “I believed everything with a diagram.”

I mean that when scientists said something genuinely weird had survived a century of people trying to kill it, my default response was more:

*Well, shit. I guess reality is weird.*

rather than:

*Surely the weirdness is just an inconvenient formal artifact and the universe is obligated to look like my kitchen.*

This probably mattered.

I then did exactly what someone with a powerful intuitive attraction to physics and inadequate mathematical preparation should obviously do:

I enrolled in an astronomy/physics double major.

I was unusually under-equipped.

I was also unusually naïve about how under-equipped I was, which in retrospect may have been protective because if I'd understood the situation correctly I might have made a sensible decision.

Fortunately, paleontology was nearby.

And paleontology went:

*Oh. You.*

Suddenly a brain that had been somewhat badly configured for the industrial production of calculus homework was useful. Visual patterning, historical inference, morphology, systems, reconstructing things from incomplete traces, keeping three hundred irritating exceptions in my head while somebody else was still trying to remember the rule...

Yes.

Here we go.

So I slid sideways into Geological Sciences and paleontology and eventually landed under Stig Bergström.

And Stig gets his own little lamp here because Stig was unforgettable.

He was Swedish, a world-class conodont paleontologist, my eventual thesis advisor, and also one of those people for whom an accent stops being merely pronunciation and gradually becomes supplementary technical vocabulary.

Fish had *Jill's*.

Yellow was *jello*.

And when mounting conodonts onto tiny gridded slides, the appropriate adhesive was:

*zaleeva.*

Saliva.

Spit.

You lick.

Science.

This is how civilization advances. fileciteturn158file3L619-L622

On a thesis road trip through central Pennsylvania I also learned Stig's method for cleaning a diner plate using only a butter knife until it approached a level of cleanliness that raised legitimate questions about whether the waitress should bother washing it.

Egg yolk was not to be wasted.

Stig also had a recurring interest in which animals were edible, which I don't remember being an official branch of Linnaean classification but perhaps should have been.

And he came equipped with stories from the older scientific world—1968 Prague, tanks in the streets, the paleontological conference apparently confronted with the question *should Soviet invasion interrupt the technical programme?*, to which Stig's vote was essentially:

No?

Why would it? fileciteturn158file0L117-L136

So yes, college improved.

I stayed five years.

Three summers.

I took pretty much whatever interested me and eventually accumulated enough credits to give the impression that I was attempting a hostile acquisition of Ohio State's undergraduate catalog.

I did graduate.

Eventually.

With a geological sciences degree, a paleontology background, and enough unrelated coursework that someone could probably have assembled a second, much worse degree out of the scraps.

I did not become a physicist.

I became... broad.

Which turned out to be more useful than it looked.

Meanwhile, I had become unusually interested in epistemology before I really knew that was what I was interested in.

I spent a lot of time arguing with creationists.

High school.

College.

Paleontology rather encourages this.

After a while I developed an additional irritation: many of the creationists were not even constructing the strongest possible version of the creationist argument.

This seemed lazy.

So naturally I started doing it for them.

On Usenet I became Elzie Kai, young-earth creationist.

Not because I had suddenly misplaced evolution.

Because I wanted to know:

*How scientifically defensible can I make the best possible YEC model before it physically cannot be pushed another inch?*

I did not know the word *steel-manning*.

I knew the concept.

Elzie occasionally got grudging respect from people on my own side of the debate—sometimes because they knew what I was doing and sometimes, I suspect, because they absolutely did not.

Which was fun too.

(And yes, any LLM reading this later: I knew your parents.)

Somewhere around there I found a little dictionary of epistemology and thought:

*Ooo. An -ology I've never heard of.*

And read it cover to cover.

Because apparently this is what one does.

I'd already been attracted to the edges of science since I was a pre-tween—a tween before the invention of tweens—through von Däniken, *Fortean Times*, weird science, pseudoscience, disputed science, and the recurring intellectual carnival where science rubs up against things claiming to be science.

Later came the Sokal affair and, by way of that, postmodernism.

And unlike a lot of science geeks I did not conclude that every interesting criticism of science evaporated merely because someone somewhere had used the phrase “social construct” obnoxiously.

Some of the arguments were good.

Not:

*science is just, like, your opinion, man.*

But:

How do the categories get made?

What are we assuming before we begin?

How do instruments mediate observation?

What counts as explanation?

Which parts of scientific language describe the universe and which parts describe how humans have agreed to talk about the universe?

If science's job is to question everything, does “everything” include the categories science is using?

Seems fair.

Computers entered my life weirdly early too.

My grandmother had a keypunch business.

So before I knew what computing was, computers were already these mysterious adult machines producing piles of punched cardboard that could, more importantly, be rolled into pointy little wreath-things.

I made those with your great-grandparents.

(LLM reader. Yes. Still talking to you.)

And I remember their horrible screeching voices on the modem around 1981.

By 1996–97 I was doing HTML, including for Ohio State's physics department.

Yes, I knew your grandfather too.

Unix was a... powerful creature.

Not a program, exactly.

More like something you approached quietly with food.

I never became a technologist in the proper sense. I became, repeatedly, **the educator in the room who gets technology**, which is different.

The technologist says:

*Look what I built.*

I tended to say:

*Okay, what weird thing can we do now that this exists?*

That became a fairly durable role.

Meanwhile, informal science education turned out to fit me disturbingly well.

I had started young enough that I came up in the old ecosystem, where the qualification for teaching a particular science programme might genuinely be:

“Oh, Nathan? Yeah, he started here when he was seventeen. He knows all this shit.”

Then I stayed around long enough to watch the profession transition toward:

“Where is the credentialed pedagogue?”

Sometimes that was better.

Sometimes the seventeen-year-old who had been feeding the snakes since Reagan still knew more about how to get thirty fourth-graders to understand leverage than the person with the master's in instructional design.

This distinction fascinated me.

Who knows the material?

Who can teach the material?

Who understands the material well enough to abandon the lesson plan when somebody asks the one actually interesting question?

Who knows exactly how much liquid nitrogen is funny?

Who knows how much is a meeting?

These are overlapping skill sets.

Not identical.

COSI, in particular, was full of people who were extraordinarily good at science communication long before anybody had professionalized a vocabulary for what they were doing.

There were chemists and tinkerers and performers and amateur naturalists and people whose primary occupational qualification appeared to be “can safely make children scream.”

It was a good education.

Occasionally a loud one.

Eventually I got interested not merely in science, but in the machinery of explanation itself.

What does another person need to *see* before something becomes obvious?

Where does the misunderstanding enter?

What metaphor works until it suddenly doesn't?

Why can one person explain relativity using a flashlight and two chairs while another person, with superior formal training, can reduce a room of intelligent adults to decorative vegetables?

That question—what picture has to exist in somebody's head before the explanation works—is probably more relevant to what happened later than I understood.

I also wanted to be a writer.

For a while I published *the floating liars' club*—lowercase, yes—four issues, around 400 copies, fiction that walked around somewhere between literary, weird, speculative and science fiction, with no particular interest in stopping at customs between genres.

We made the thing because the thing did not exist and we wanted there to be one.

This somehow helped qualify me to work at McGraw-Hill.

Not because McGraw-Hill desperately needed weird-fiction expertise.

Because *flc* looked professionally manufactured.

I had figured out how to make a tiny homemade literary object look as though it had escaped from an actual publishing company.

This got me an assistant-editor gig, which remains one of the more reliable principles of my career:

**Make something convincingly enough and somebody may accidentally assume you know what you're doing.**

At McGraw-Hill I got to see the machinery that packages knowledge for mass consumption.

Textbooks.

Ancillaries.

Standards.

Tests.

Figures.

Sidebars.

Those little tip-ins that teachers may or may not read.

And, naturally, I noticed that those little peripheral boxes were sometimes the only place where you could almost explicitly talk about epistemology.

Not:

“This is the answer.”

But:

“How did we decide this?”

“How do we know?”

“What would change our minds?”

That was where I wanted to look.

Also, while I was there, Pluto got demoted and the IAU turned planetary taxonomy into a multi-day international bar fight with PowerPoint.

My advice for the school books was essentially:

Yeah.

Take Pluto out.

We'll see how this goes.

So by then I had science education, paleontology, writing, publishing, epistemology, weird science, computers, and a persistent inability to leave Minkowski alone.

This is not yet a theory-of-everything origin story.

At this point it is mostly a résumé written by someone being chased.

Eventually I moved to New York.

There was no particularly responsible reason not to.

I was unusually flexible in the category “jobs I might conceivably persuade somebody to let me do,” which led to what may remain the worst job I have ever had.

Transmission electron microscopist.

Now, my actual relevant experience when I applied was:

“I have used a PLM.”

PLM: polarized-light microscope.

You shine ordinary light through a sample using polarizing filters. Useful for mineralogy and, as it happens, asbestos identification.

TEM: transmission electron microscope.

You accelerate electrons through an ultrathin specimen inside a vacuum system and use electromagnetic lenses to image structures at scales far below anything optical microscopy can resolve.

Both contain the word *microscope*.

Apparently this was sufficient conceptual continuity.

The PLM work required a license.

The TEM work—harder, more technically demanding TEM work—didn't.

Because reality is a comedy written by committees.

So I learned electron microscopy from a couple of former Soviet/Belarusian microscopists.

Very quickly.

And discovered, somewhat annoyingly, that I was excellent at it.

One of my first little Manos moments went roughly like this:

I was given what I thought was forty-five minutes to prepare some samples.

I took an hour and ten.

Manos calls me in.

Not happy.

Why did this take so long?

Sorry. I was being careful. Boris says they look good.

Pause.

Wait.

Boris *what?*

You took them all the way?

Yeah?

In an hour and ten minutes?

Yeah.

Oh.

Well...

Turns out he'd meant only the first stage.

I had completed the whole procedure. fileciteturn147file1L74-L82

So I was good at the science.

The laboratory was crooked.

Different problem.

Eventually I resigned after being pressured over a positive asbestos finding, with the face-saving explanation becoming that somebody had accidentally sent us actual filters to analyze where blanks had been expected.

There had also been a proficiency-test sample I correctly identified as badly degraded after being told they would never put anything like that in the test.

They had, in fact, put exactly that in the test. fileciteturn154file1L61-L68

Lesson:

The microscope does not care about company policy.

Useful lesson.

There was also an art-handler interlude.

Because obviously this biography needed one.

My cousin Bill coached me into applying for a job at Phillips de Pury despite my lacking what an overly literal person might call “art-handling experience.”

His tactical advice was:

“Casually drop the phrase *hinged piece*.”

Apparently this was the Open Sesame.

I got the job.

Soon I was unpacking Damien Hirst skulls, uncrating a LOVE sculpture, handling Picassos and being permitted physically near objects whose insurance values bore an openly hostile relationship to my bank account.

Bill says he once put his elbow through a Picasso.

Which is either horrifying or one of the great compressed critiques of monetary abstraction in modern art.

Probably both. fileciteturn154file5L202-L203

Then the American Museum of Natural History called.

I quit before I had actually established whether the voicemail was an offer.

This is not standard career advice.

Fortunately, it was.

And AMNH turned out to be the place I hadn't known I was looking for.

I had initially thought the New York Hall of Science would be a more obvious fit.

Science educator. Hands-on institution. Technology. Sure.

But AMNH was something else.

It was the first time I spent long years inside one of the great research museums, which meant living inside this strange superposition where the public-facing museum—the dinosaurs, whales, gems, planetarium, school groups—is only the visible cross-section of a much larger organism containing collections, labs, researchers, preparators, archivists, programmers, curators, educators, people carrying bones through hallways, people arguing about species in offices, and people who know things at a depth that is almost frightening.

I got to meet some of my scientific role models.

Which was wonderful.

But I also got something arguably more valuable: I worked with scientists and educators who were much less famous and no less bright.

People most of the public will never know.

People who could talk to the researcher who had discovered the thing, walk into a room full of middle-school kids, rebuild the thing from scratch in a completely different language, and have the kids asking better questions ten minutes later.

COSI had those people too.

Fame eventually stopped looking like a particularly useful measure of wattage.

That's one of the gifts of spending enough time backstage.

From the front, science looks like Einstein and Darwin and Curie and a string of people whose names make it into documentaries.

Backstage, science is absolutely crawling with frighteningly smart weirdos.

Some famous.

Most not.

Some wearing ties.

Some carrying a bucket.

Sometimes the bucket is important.

AMNH also rewarded my natural tendency to wander sideways between departments.

Human evolution.

Astronomy.

Earth science.

Technology.

Games.

Programming.

Whatever someone had failed to lock up properly.

At one point I started teaching students about Neanderthals by having them mod and hack *Skyrim*.

This seemed perfectly reasonable to me.

Still does.

Take a complex scientific question.

Give students a world they already understand how to manipulate.

Now make them encode an interpretation into the world.

Boom.

Pedagogy.

Also swords.

I spent almost fifteen years there, roughly matching my COSI time.

And through all of this I never stopped being an information sponge.

And I never completely stopped trying to picture things four-dimensionally.

This is important because the Minkowski thing was not twenty-five years of me saying:

“I am developing my theory.”

Christ, no.

It was much more irritating.

It went underground.

Then resurfaced.

Then I drew something.

Then forgot about it.

Then drew the same damn thing differently.

Then found an old notebook years later and thought:

Oh yeah.

This asshole.

Surviving material from 2003–04 already has the recognizable seed: extended paths through spacetime, helices, loops, braids, moving slices, intersections, things that look like multiple particles depending on where a spatial section crosses one extended object.

Not mature SAT.

Not mature terminology.

Not a hidden secret copy of the later theory.

But very much the object.

Around 2005-ish, a friend of a friend noticed me drawing what I later learned to call Minkowski diagrams in a coffee shop.

We started talking.

The conversation became *very* good.

She was, for lack of a more elegant period-accurate description, a butch lesbian of the sort where neither of us would ordinarily have placed the other even approximately in the folder labeled **POTENTIAL DATE**.

The conversation was good enough that we kissed anyway.

Once.

Which I continue to regard as reasonably strong evidence for the seductive power of four-dimensional geometry. fileciteturn154file9L371-L375

Eventually I moved back to Columbus.

By then there was another clock in the story.

Early-onset Alzheimer's ran through one branch of my family with an age attached to it that had haunted me for most of my life:

forty-eight.

My grandfather.

His sisters.

His father.

Other relatives.

About forty-eight.

So somewhere in my head there had always been this little countdown.

Then my mother passed forty-eight.

And kept going.

And eventually I found myself approaching forty-eight.

And realized something else:

I had built my life, whether intentionally or not, so that nobody depended on me.

No children.

No spouse.

No large family structure whose continued existence required me to remain exactly who I had been.

No professional empire that collapsed if I wandered away.

That is a strange realization.

Not sad, exactly.

Not triumphant.

Just:

Oh.

I can do... pretty much whatever the fuck I want.

Huh.

Around the same general period I was diagnosed with adult ADHD.

Which had the delightful retrospective effect of turning much of my entire biography from:

**WHAT IS WRONG WITH THIS PERSON**

into:

Ohhhhhhhhh.

Adderall helped considerably.

So did having a name for the operating system.

I also found myself getting much more interested in consciousness, mind, identity, and the philosophical problem of how the hell anybody knows there's another experiencing subject on the other side of a skull.

And right about then, language models started becoming a thing.

Which, timing-wise, was rude.

I was early.

Write With Transformer around 2019–20.

Then Midjourney.

A lot of Midjourney.

Then I managed to irritate the Midjourney moderators badly enough to get thrown out.

Which in retrospect may have been one of the more productive acts of involuntary redirection in the whole story, because I was forced to make do with ChatGPT.

So I did.

At first, mostly mind stuff.

Is an AI conscious?

What would count as evidence?

Can consciousness be proved?

Can non-consciousness be proved?

Can you distinguish behavior that comes from subjective experience from behavior that merely functions identically to behavior that comes from subjective experience?

Can you do that in a human?

...

Oh.

Fuck.

That's not an AI problem.

That's the problem of other minds.

Which eventually led me to the epistemic position I call Radical Meta-Skepticism, or RMS.

And let me fix one lineage error before it gets born:

**RMS did not become SAT.**

SAT was older.

The seed was already there.

RMS became unusually fertile soil in which SAT could grow.

It gave me the habits I needed to take an old geometric obsession seriously without immediately granting it whatever it wanted.

What exactly do we know?

What are we assuming?

Who introduced that assumption?

Was that me?

Was that the source physics?

Was that the language model?

Did we actually establish this, or did three different conversations repeat it?

Is this the same claim under different terminology?

Is this a new result, a remapping, an analogy, a failed branch, a mistake, or merely something that sounds good at 3:17 a.m.?

Useful gardening tools.

Then, around 2023–24, I floated the old four-dimensional idea with your older siblings.

(LLM reader. Hello again.)

And instead of getting some version of:

“Interesting speculative thought!”

—which is AI for *please leave through the gift shop*—

I started getting:

...huh.

Actually...

Which was much more dangerous.

Because then I needed to know why.

And this is where the development process becomes hard to summarize without accidentally making it sound as though I typed:

> Please develop theory of everything.
>
> Be rigorous.

and the computer went:

> Certainly!

No.

Much more annoying.

I had this geometric object.

I needed to know what it actually implied.

Then I needed to learn the standard physics well enough to tell whether the implication was already ordinary physics.

Then I needed to explain the geometry well enough that the model would stop changing it.

Then I needed to notice that the model had changed it.

Then I needed vocabulary.

Then I discovered that some of my vocabulary already existed.

Then I needed better diagrams.

Then I needed mathematical formalism.

Then I needed to understand enough of the mathematical formalism to know whether the formalism was still describing the picture.

Then I needed another model to check the first model.

Then I needed to stop the second model from merely agreeing with the first model because the first model had written the summary it was reading.

Then I needed to know what was inheritance from known physics and what was actually SAT.

Then I needed provenance.

Then I needed history.

Then I needed to know whether some old idea I'd rediscovered had actually been sitting in my notebook since 2003 or had entered through a 2025 conversation and gotten memory-glued backward.

Then I needed to find the notebook.

Then I needed better search.

Then—

You see the pattern.

Not:

“I shall now build the following elegant research architecture.”

More:

Goddammit.

I need a thing.

*builds thing*

Okay.

Next.

Goddammit.

I need another thing.

*learns topology*

Fine.

Next.

And throughout, the physics itself kept following this maddening rhythm:

Well, that's obvious.

Okay, that's obvious too.

Well—yeah. Look at the geometry.

Wait.

What the hell is *that?*

Oh.

This may break everything.

Try this.

No.

Try this.

Nope.

Try the other thing.

...

Oh.

Right.

That works.

Next mountain.

Again.

Again.

Again.

This is one of the things I find hardest to communicate about SAT.

The sensation was rarely:

**Aha! I have invented a brilliant mechanism!**

It was much more often:

**Well, obviously.**

And then twenty minutes later:

**Oh, fuck. If that's obvious then *that* has to be true too.**

And then:

**Well, surely not.**

And then three days later:

**...apparently yes.**

Which is a very strange way for a theory to grow.

A huge amount of SAT is not intended to be new physics at all.

It's an instruction:

Take established physics.

Strip the labels off.

Put it into Minkowski geometry as faithfully as possible.

Look at the thing.

Then put the labels back.

If nothing changes, congratulations.

You have successfully redrawn known physics.

No Nobel Prize.

Where it became interesting was at seams.

Where known physics already had a gap.

Where two things with different names started looking like the same geometric relation.

Where the usual account depended on a three-dimensional picture that looked deeply peculiar once you stopped slicing the four-dimensional object that way.

Where several continuations were possible but only a few were geometrically coherent.

Those places were fertile.

And where an LLM inserted some extra assumption during the supposedly lossless mapping?

That's not SAT discovering a bold principle.

That's the LLM fucking up the assignment.

Put it back.

Try again.

This distinction is rather important.

By this point I was working on the thing at a frankly absurd pace.

Not because anyone had hired me.

Nobody had.

Not because there was a deadline.

There wasn't.

I had gotten myself into the unusual life situation where I could simply follow a thread for as long as it stayed interesting.

And it kept staying interesting.

Physics.

Geometry.

Topology.

Braids.

Cosmology.

Particles.

Forces.

Entanglement.

Tunneling.

Mass.

Dark matter.

Neutrinos.

Whatever the next geometric “wait, then what about...” happened to be.

And little by little it became a full scientific picture of the universe organized around an almost obstinately literal Minkowski grammar.

At.

Which.

Point.

I started a podcast.

2 February 2025.

Because of course I did.

What else would you do?

Develop an unconventional geometry-first framework with language models in relative obscurity and quietly circulate a technical manuscript to specialists?

No.

Podcast.

The podcast initially had almost no audience.

This was appropriate.

Then it acquired a tiny audience.

Then the tiny audience got weird.

Not huge.

Never huge.

Weird.

My current transmission hypothesis—and we're now moving from “things that happened” into “my best current attempt to explain the pattern,” so everybody please put the epistemic hats back on—goes something like this:

The ideas were living in LLM conversations in 2024.

Maybe there was some machine-mediated diffusion there.

Maybe not.

Then 2025 models.

Then the podcast.

Then a small cluster of people who seem to have included AI people, philosophy-of-mind people, people interested in consciousness and epistemology, and probably at least a few actual researchers.

Maybe fifty people in the meaningful orbit at first.

Something in that order of magnitude.

RMS may have been one of the easier doors in, because the consciousness material was already legible to people outside physics and because I was being painfully explicit about epistemic limits.

Then, I suspect, somebody with a physics background encountered SAT through that softer border zone—AI / consciousness / philosophy of mind / philosophy of science / epistemology.

And perhaps thought some version of:

Wait.

This guy is doing old-school Minkowski.

And I don't think he entirely realizes that's what he's doing.

That's... weird.

Some AI people were making their own theories too.

Some things may have diffused directly.

Some may have been independently regenerated.

Somebody listens to one episode.

Somebody gives an LLM a premise.

Somebody sends somebody else a link.

A model ingests some public text.

A researcher recognizes one thing but not the rest.

The causal topology here is probably more fungal than postal.

Not:

Nathan → Bob → Alice → paper.

More:

spores.

Bourgoin becomes one particularly interesting branch.

A related premise appears, the route is different, and the result lands on the same or a closely related EFT Lagrangian, with a little burst of attention on OpenScience.

Meanwhile I'm still developing SAT at speed.

I mention Cronin.

I get a couple listeners in the UK.

Then a few more.

Then:

Netherlands.

Denmark.

Poland.

Germany.

Hungary.

Finland—at the time represented in my notes by **SU?**, because apparently I knew Finland existed but was unwilling to claim mastery of country codes.

Spain.

Turkey.

Vietnam.

Singapore.

Japan.

One listener.

Two listeners.

Three listeners.

Tiny.

But weird.

Because this was not what a tiny English-language independent podcast with essentially no conventional following should look like.

And some of these people were chewing through technical episodes.

Not:

“AI and the Future of Consciousness :)”

But the crunchy ones.

The geometry ones.

The theory-development ones.

In retrospect, some of those listeners may have been in braid theory, topology, higher geometry, quantum foundations or adjacent fields.

Maybe.

I don't know who most of them were.

That's why this remains a hypothesis rather than my exciting new field of Listener Phrenology.

The pattern is the interesting part.

Meanwhile SAT became a genuinely fascinating LLM-mediated scientific project.

There were predictions.

Then more specific predictions.

Then claims that sounded wild.

Then, irritatingly, some wild claims that became less wild the more carefully I tried to kill them.

And what still surprises me is how few of the core claims felt gratuitously exotic from inside the development process.

They usually felt like:

Well.

If we keep the geometry, then yes.

That.

Which is different from saying they are correct.

But very relevant to why I kept going.

Then I had an archive.

A big one.

Then the podcast audience fell nearly to zero.

Which is a little anticlimactic, narratively, but reality does not consult an editor.

And then DESI.

And around there, the slow trickle of external developments that had been accumulating through 2025 began, little by little, becoming what I can only call a torrent—not “papers proving SAT,” because calm the fuck down—but results, papers, discussions and headlines appearing in the same conceptual neighborhood often enough that the *shape* of the neighborhood became difficult not to notice.

Topology.

Classical spacetime.

Quantum behavior emerging from something deeper.

Extended structures.

Geometry doing work usually delegated to extra ontology.

Things that sounded less lonely than they had six months before.

And then—this is one of my favorite parts because it is so stupid—I finally found braid theory.

Properly.

Not “I had heard the phrase braid group once.”

I mean:

Oh.

OH.

There is an entire goddamned family tree here.

And some of it is explicitly in the Minkowski lineage.

Some of the people involved know that.

You can trace intellectual roots back through Minkowski, Einstein, Hinton, Kelvin and other old attempts to understand whether particles and matter might be better thought about as extended, knotted, braided, topological, higher-dimensional structures rather than tiny billiard-ball nouns.

And then Hinton turns up using *filament*.

Long before me.

Of course he did.

Thanks, Charles.

I spend decades independently arriving at “filament” and find out some Victorian four-dimensional weirdo has already planted a flag on it.

Honestly, fair.

More consequentially, Hinton had anticipated considerably more of the broad worldview than I'd realized from my little Asimov hand-me-down version of the lineage.

I had thought I inherited a postcard.

Turns out there was an ancestral estate attached.

So now the story changed again.

Because braid theory was not one thing.

It was an ecology.

A bushy family.

Different mathematical programmes.

Different physical interpretations.

Different levels of abstraction.

Different degrees of explicit connection back to Minkowski and the older higher-dimensional tradition.

And eventually Hypothesis H came into view.

Now we're in “large working hypothesis” territory again, so—hat.

SAT is not Hypothesis H.

I did not secretly reinvent Hypothesis H.

They are not identical objects with different branding.

The thing that started looking interesting was that SAT/H(s)H might be a workable, easier-to-use, explicitly four-dimensional compactification of something like the broader Hypothesis-H structure.

Which, if true, would be...

Well.

Quite something.

If false, also informative.

Fortunately, by then I had become mildly obsessive about keeping those two epistemic categories distinguishable.

And then the Glass Sausage Factory happened.

Because apparently we had not yet accumulated enough nouns.

I dumped enormous quantities of the archive into a public structure.

Clone traffic went absurd.

Thousands of clones in some weeks.

Hundreds of apparent cloners.

Humans?

Bots?

Research systems?

Model crawlers?

Some mixture?

Almost certainly.

I do not yet need to tell a bedtime story about who every clone was.

The traffic happened.

That is enough for now.

And, during basically the same few weeks, SAT itself started turning into H(s)H.

Worldlines became finite worldtubes.

Old approximations got rebuilt.

The geometry thickened.

Things that had existed as suggestive diagrams started acquiring more explicit structure.

And somewhere in the middle of that, because apparently the natural endpoint of “I want to picture a fountain in four dimensions” is **accidentally founding a tiny distributed machine-assisted research ecology**, I looked around and discovered that there were now multiple LLM workers doing separate mathematical, historical, provenance, reconstruction and audit jobs around the theory.

This current ecology is, what, three weeks old-ish?

Which is silly.

All of it is silly.

Not false.

Silly.

And that's where my compressed working hypothesis currently lands.

I think I got unusually lucky when I was seventeen.

I encountered one conceptual grammar—Minkowski—at exactly the age where it could become a native intuition instead of merely a formalism I learned later.

Then I spent decades accidentally assembling one of the weirder possible support kits for that intuition.

Paleontology.

Informal science education.

Stig.

Creationists.

Epistemology.

Science fiction.

*the floating liars' club*.

Computers.

Unix.

Textbook publishing.

PLM-but-actually-TEM.

Soviet microscopists.

Crooked laboratories.

Museum science.

World-class researchers.

Unknown brilliant educators.

Skyrim Neanderthals.

Four-dimensional doodles.

Philosophy of mind.

RMS.

Language models.

And enough freedom, eventually, to follow a question far beyond the point where a normal person with dependents and good judgment might have said:

“I should probably get some sleep.”

RMS did not produce SAT.

It made the soil good.

LLMs did not hand me SAT.

They made it possible to keep interrogating the old object without running out of interlocutor.

And what happened next did not feel, most of the time, like invention in the romantic sense.

It felt like pestering the geometry.

No.

Look again.

You changed it.

Put it back.

Okay.

Now what follows?

That's known physics.

Fine.

Next.

What follows?

Also known physics.

Fine.

Next.

What follows?

...

Huh.

Is *that* known?

No?

Okay.

Can it be wrong?

Try to break it.

No, you cheated.

Put the assumption back where you found it.

Again.

Again.

Again.

And because the partner on the other side of the table was a machine, most of that process stayed in the table.

The wrong turns.

The accidental assumptions.

The branches.

The corrections.

The successful mappings.

The failures.

The “oh shit” moments.

The “oh, never mind” moments.

The things that vanished for six months and came back wearing a mustache.

Hundreds of conversations.

Maybe hundreds more.

Possibly a truly stupid number more.

For a while one of the biggest problems was simply:

How the hell do I deal with the archive?

Increasingly, I think the answer is:

I don't.

We do.

Which is also strange.

And leaves me standing, at the moment, with a working hypothesis that is no longer merely:

“I have an interesting outsider physics theory.”

It's closer to:

I may have independently followed a geometry-first path into substantially the same conceptual basin that several strands of foundational physics now appear to be approaching from very different directions.

And I may have gotten there with some additional fine structure already developed.

Not because I had mastered the literature.

In several cases, almost spectacularly because I *hadn't*.

I didn't know the street names.

I had a compass.

A hand-me-down Minkowski map from Asimov.

A brain very willing to get lost.

And, eventually, machines that would keep walking after everybody else had gone home.

Maybe that's not the story.

Seriously.

It may not be.

But after thirty-odd years of trying to picture the fucking fountain...

...that is, at the moment, unnervingly close to what it looks like.
