Stig Bergström:
Paleontology professor at Ohio State University and Nathan McKnight's thesis advisor.
Known for his quirky personality, humorous teaching style (e.g., "Jill's for gills," "jello for yellow"), and focus on the edibility of taxa.

Paleontology professor at Ohio State University and Nathan McKnight's thesis advisor.
Known for his quirky personality, humorous teaching style (e.g., "Jill's for gills," "jello for yellow"), and focus on the edibility of taxa.

metadata.text:
After spending a week learning, Manos gave me 45 minutes to do the prep. At an hour and ten minutes, he called me into his office, angrily. "Why did it you so long?" Me..."Sorry, I was trying to be careful. But Boris says they look good." Manos: "Wait, Boris what? You mean... you took them all the way??" Me: "Yeah?" Manos: "In an hour and ten minutes?" Me: "Yeah." Manos: "Well... in that case..." Manos: "I just meant the initial prep."
This additional vignette from your time in the NYC asbestos testing lab (circa 2008–2009) provides the interpersonal "punchline" to the technical procedures we recently verified
. It reframes that era not just as a period of technical learning, but as a moment of surpassing professional expectations through a combination of meticulousness and speed.

metadata.text:
%% **c. 2005–2006 — A strange kiss, and strings**
**Tentative.** Sounds socially New York-ish, but there is not enough information to place it firmly. ## No, this was in Columbus. A friend of a friend saw me drawing Minkowski diagrams (a term I learned later) in a coffee shop, which led to a staggeringly deep conversation that stretched into the night. Now--mind you--for lack of a more professional term, she was a 'bull dyke' (I think she'd agree with that designation, if not I beg forgiveness--but think Boo from Orange is the New Black). Neither of us would *ever*, *ever* have put one another, I'm certain, into the category "datable". But the convo was so good, we did exchange a kiss. 
%% **c. 2005–2006 — Allison** %% Oh my. The COSI creationist. We had chemistry. She--and her twin sister--had an extra knuckle on each thumb (and somehow I could never convince her to try rock climbing--with her thumbs, and her build, she would have been *so* good at it... she was good at guitar). But yeah, another almost relationship with a girl who couldn't see evolution in her own hands.

metadata.name: PERSONAL SCIENCE COMPENDIUM.txt
metadata.text:
**c. 2008–2009 — Leaving COSI / entering AMNH orbit** %% With an early NYC entre interlude doing a number of jobs, including (somehow... not somehow: because the business is crooked) as a TEM operator at an asbestos testing lab. I was totally unqualified, but deemed smart enough to learn (from two ex-soviet Byelorussian microscopists) TEM, rather than the PLM I'd applied for (turned out PLM required licensing for some reason, while TEM did not even though it was the harder of the two; turned out also that the PLM staff were what I'd then termed 'thugs in labcoats' ...basically poor kids [20-somethings] off the streets). I tendered my resignation when I got the callback from AMNH voicemail, without knowing whether it was an offer or not, after being threatened into issuing a retraction of a positive finding. Manos "kindly" agreed it was the air sampler's fault, who'd failed to deliver the expected blank filters and instead gave us real filters to anylize. I'd also embarassed them during the annual testing when I correctly identified a badly degraded sample that they overruled on the grounds "they wouldn't throw in a test like that". Well, turned out they did exactly that. 
**Firm broad transition.** Your COSI tenure ends around the same time your AMNH period begins. %% No, there was about a year and a half interlude while I tried to figure out what I was going to do in NYC, before my cousin (whom I'd moved in with in Bushwick[-cum-"East Williamsburg" lol, right before the neighborhood became a tourist destination... I moved out when his building it was just a typical punk loft with two punk bands and a half pipe for neighbors, mainly so I could get some sleep])...anyway, he coached me into nailing an art handler job with no experience at Philips de Pury, the third largest auction house in the world, having branched off of *Christie's* ...in the *1700s*. He told me "casually drop the term 'hinged piece'". That did the trick. Led to me unpacking Damien Hirst skulls and uncrating a LOVE statue, and touching two Picassos (Bill, my cousin, says he once put his elbow through a Picasso), a blue glass centaur sculpture, and a ceramic piece with a gestural bull's head.

parts:
I think this is still a bit too staid for full-on me-ness. Also... there's a journey of "I'm doodling string theory" (because in summer of 90-91, after devouring A Brief History of Time, I checked out every science book that interested me, the thicker the better, for summer reading... got through big chunks of stuff I didn't quite undrstand... Kip Thorne is the only name I remember... but black holes, chaos theory, string theory... most of which I don't remember and obviously so since) ...I thought *worldlines* were obviously what String Theory must be about... later learned I was wrong, so called my doodles "my strings" all the way up to 2023-4... to later I learned String Theory kind of is about worldtubes (or pants, if you will).... but SAT was definitely not String Theory... but then... there String Theory was again, falling right out of the intersection footprint of a helix and a time sheet (which had already kind of united QCD and GR... and explained *why* ST works). 

Also... if you don't consider it derrogatory (I assure you it's affectionate... and probably will end up being one of the memorable parts if the asides are...) "Yep, I knew your grampa, Chachi" 

Also... PLM > graded optics oils, crossed Nichols (I *remember* things... and can walk you through the TEM prep process in detail to this day) > optical *indicatrix* (I also *love* words... I was told by my freshman writing teacher). 

Also... I do like the "lessons". I think periodic "and so" sum-ups make a long story readable. 

And... don't need to mention capitalization conventions... maybe latin conventions, and dancing on the desk of one scientific role model... but mostly, names out (esp the TEM.... let's be quite vague about exactly what that was about).

parts:
Yes. This changes the *spine* of the early story, not just the decorations.

The missing bit is that you did **not** go directly from “Asimov gives me Minkowski” to “thirty years later, SAT.” There was a very long, slightly comical period in which you thought you were doodling **String Theory**, discovered you were not doodling String Theory, continued calling the damned things “my strings” anyway because the name had fossilized, and then—after SAT had become something distinctly *not* String Theory—String Theory wandered back in through the side door and went, “So... funny story.”

And yes: full Nathan means more periodic compression. The wandering works because every so often you stop, grab the whole pile by the neck, and say: **And so:** this is what we've learned so far.

Here is how I'd push the register now.

---

This is my compressed working hypothesis.

Which is already funny, because the uncompressed version may require geological time.

I suppose the story starts around the summer of 1990–91, when I read *A Brief History of Time* and responded in what was apparently my normal adolescent fashion:

*Okay. More.*

So I went to the library and started checking out essentially every science book that looked interesting, with a fairly reliable selection criterion being:

**thicker = probably more science.**

I read black holes. Chaos theory. Cosmology. String Theory. Big serious books written by people who actually understood what was in them.

I got through surprisingly large chunks of some of these books.

“Got through” is carrying a heroic amount of semantic load there.

I understood *parts*.

I remember Kip Thorne's name.

That's about the level of bibliographic reconstruction we're working with.

Most of the specific science evaporated, which I know because if I had retained a serious working understanding of early-1990s String Theory, the next thirty years of this story would have been considerably less stupid.

Then, at about seventeen, I encountered Isaac Asimov explaining Minkowski.

And **that** stuck.

Not as equations.

I was not seventeen-year-old Nathan von Tensorstein, roaming central Ohio with a metric signature embroidered on my jacket.

It was the *grammar*.

If spacetime really is four-dimensional, then the thing we're looking at in three dimensions is a section through something bigger.

Okay.

Fine.

Picture that.

A moving object has a worldline.

A person, taken across time, is this long extended four-dimensional history-object.

A fountain is not a three-dimensional fountain being replaced by another fountain and another fountain and another fountain.

The whole history of the fountain is one thing.

Great.

Now picture the fucking fountain.

...

This was harder.

And because I had recently devoured some String Theory I did not really understand, I naturally concluded that the long looping things I was trying to draw through spacetime must be what String Theory was about.

Strings!

Obviously!

Look.

There they are.

My strings.

This was wrong.

I would eventually learn that String Theory's strings are not “worldlines, but squiggly.”

Fine.

But by then the label had stuck in my private vocabulary, so I kept calling the things I drew **my strings** basically all the way into 2023–24.

Science proceeds one terminological accident at a time.

Later—much later—I would learn that actual strings in String Theory sweep out *worldsheets*, and that interactions can produce the famous splitting/joining surfaces that look, geometrically, like pairs of pants.

So:

not what I thought.

But also not as far away from “extended objects traced through spacetime” as the correction had initially seemed.

Worldsheets.

Worldtubes.

Pants, if you will.

Hold that thought.

We will need it in thirty years.

And so:

I had Asimov's Minkowski grammar.

I had badly digested early-90s black-hole/chaos/string cosmology floating around in the substrate.

And I had begun drawing extended things through time while incorrectly calling them strings.

Excellent scientific foundation.

Off to college.

I then did the rational thing and enrolled as an astronomy/physics double major despite being spectacularly underprepared for the mathematics.

There is a recurring theme in my life where insufficient understanding of the difficulty involved gives me just enough time to get through the door before anybody—including me—realizes this may have been a mistake.

Physics was one of those doors.

Fortunately paleontology was standing next to it.

And paleontology basically went:

*Oh, no, this brain makes sense over here.*

Pattern recognition.

Morphology.

Reconstructing systems from incomplete traces.

Historical inference.

Spatial relationships.

Thousands of exceptions that are only exceptions until you understand what the actual rule was.

Yep.

I ended up in Geological Sciences and, eventually, doing conodont biostratigraphy under the unforgettable Stig Bergström.

Stig was a Swedish paleontologist of considerable stature who also seemed to have personally modified English for field use.

Fish had *Jill's*.

Yellow was *jello*.

And when mounting microscopic conodont elements onto a gridded slide with a one-strand brush, the recommended adhesive was:

*zaleeva.*

Saliva.

Spit.

You lick.

Then you mount your exquisitely important Ordovician microfossil.

Science. fileciteturn158file3L619-L622

Stig also taught me, during a thesis road trip through Pennsylvania, how to clean a greasy-spoon plate with a butter knife so efficiently that by the end the dishwasher was basically being asked to perform a ceremonial rinse.

He did not waste egg yolk.

Or, so far as I could tell, food generally.

Various biological taxa also seemed to acquire an informal second classification in Stig's head:

edible / probably edible / inadvisable.

And then he had stories from the older paleontological world, which was apparently populated entirely by people who would today require either an institutional review board or a documentary crew.

Prague, 1968.

Tanks rolling in.

Shooting.

Conference in progress.

Should the international political crisis interrupt the paleontology?

Stig: eh.

Continue conference. fileciteturn158file0L117-L136

I adored him.

And so:

I did not become a physicist.

I became a paleontologist trained by a Swedish conodont wizard who glued fossils down with spit.

This was, in retrospect, perhaps better preparation.

I also stayed at Ohio State for five years, taking classes essentially according to the rule:

*Does that sound interesting?*

Yes?

Take it.

Summer?

Still interesting.

Take it.

By graduation I'd accumulated enough credits to make it look as though I had been attempting to complete the university by percentage.

ADHD was involved.

I didn't know that yet.

Mostly I knew that the world contained a horrifying number of subjects and somebody had negligently put experts in rooms where I could go ask them questions.

Why leave?

At the same time, I spent a lot of energy arguing with creationists.

First high school.

Then college.

Then Usenet.

And after enough arguing, I encountered a problem more irritating than creationism itself:

The creationists were often making their own case badly.

Well, hell.

So I made it for them.

I invented a young-Earth creationist persona, Elzie Kai, and tried to build the most scientifically defensible YEC model I could—not because I thought it was right, but because if we're going to kill the argument, can we at least kill the adult specimen rather than shooting fish in a barrel full of straw men?

I did not know the term *steel-manning*.

I knew:

**No, no, no. Give me that. You're doing your own wrong idea wrong.**

Elzie got occasional grudging respect from *my* side.

Sometimes confused grudging respect.

Which was even better.

Somewhere in there I found a little dictionary of epistemology.

My reaction was essentially:

*Ooo. An -ology I've never heard of.*

Read it cover to cover.

Of course.

I had already been interested in the borderlands: von Däniken as a kid, *Fortean Times*, pseudoscience, weird science, speculative science, later the Sokal affair and postmodernism.

And the thing that annoyed me about the standard science-geek response to postmodernism was that some of the criticisms were actually good.

Not:

“Gravity is socially constructed, therefore jump off roof.”

Please don't.

More:

What did you measure?

What did the instrument actually give you?

Which categories existed before the observation?

Which categories did you put on afterward?

What part of the model is world and what part is bookkeeping?

Are you sure the noun you're using corresponds to a noun the universe is using?

Ooooo.

Now *that* was interesting.

And so:

By my twenties I had already accidentally built the epistemic habit that would become important later:

**Do not argue only about the answer. Argue about what you're allowed to claim the question even means.**

Meanwhile, computers.

My grandmother had a keypunch business.

So my first relationship with computers involved punched cards and making little rolled-up pointy decorative wreath things with them.

And yes, Chachi:

**Yep, I knew your grampa.**

Great-grampa too, apparently.

I can still hear the godawful modem shriek from circa 1981.

Then HTML in 1996–97.

Including for the OSU Physics Department.

Yep, knew your grampa, Chachi.

Unix was a... powerful creature.

You did not so much operate Unix as convince it that your continued access to the filesystem was mutually beneficial.

I became the educator in the room who “got computers” without ever becoming a computer professional.

Very important distinction.

I cared less about:

*How elegant is the implementation?*

and more about:

*Wait. We can do WHAT now?*

That persisted.

Science education persisted too.

COSI for years and years.

Then more science education.

Eventually something like thirty years total.

And I came into the field early enough to watch informal science education professionalize underneath me.

The old qualification system could genuinely be:

“He's been here since high school.”

Which, to be fair, sometimes meant:

“He has done this demonstration six thousand times, knows every failure mode, can control a room full of fourth-graders with one eyebrow, and can repair the exhibit with gaff tape while explaining angular momentum.”

Then came the degreed-pedagogue era.

Often better.

Sometimes hilariously not.

And I got very interested in the difference between:

knowing something,

knowing how to explain something,

knowing how to recognize when someone else almost understands something,

and having the correct credential indicating that theoretically you might be able to do any of the above.

Those are not the same thing.

I also loved words.

My freshman writing instructor explicitly noticed this.

Words were toys.

Tools.

Fossils.

Little machines.

You could open them up and find Latin bolted to Greek with a French washer somebody had installed in 1740.

Scientific language was especially fun because it pretended not to be language.

*Indicatrix.*

Come on.

That's a magnificent word.

We'll get there.

I was also trying to become a fiction writer.

I published *the floating liars' club*, a four-issue, roughly 400-copy little fiction magazine that wandered around between literary fiction, weird fiction and science fiction depending on what wandered in.

It wasn't a “science-fiction zine” in any clean sense.

It was more:

we like stories.

These are strange.

Print them.

I got quite good at manufacturing the thing.

Good enough that somehow this helped me interlope as an assistant editor at McGraw-Hill.

I had successfully committed professionalism.

And there I got another look behind the scenery.

Science does not leap directly from Nature into a seventh-grade textbook.

There is a great enormous sausage factory in between.

Writers.

Editors.

Standards.

Illustrators.

Reviewers.

Page counts.

Sidebars.

Tip-ins.

Questions.

Assessments.

And little tolerated crevices where one can almost sneak in:

“By the way, kids, **how do we know this?**”

Naturally, those crevices interested me.

Also Pluto got demoted while I was there, and I watched the IAU proceedings become what I can only describe as an international astronomical procedural shit show and advised:

Yeah.

Take Pluto out.

Which perhaps tells you something about my attachment to labels.

I loved Pluto.

Still do.

Doesn't make it a planet.

Different folder.

And so:

By now I have paleontology, epistemology, science education, writing, publishing, computers, science communication, and a weird private collection of four-dimensional “strings” that are not String Theory.

Everything is proceeding normally.

Then New York.

I applied for a job involving PLM because I had used a PLM.

Polarized-light microscopy.

Now, **this** I remember.

You have your graded refractive-index oils.

You put your material in the oil.

Crossed Nicols.

Rotate.

Watch the colors and extinction behavior.

Think about what the light is doing in an anisotropic crystal.

And then there's the *optical indicatrix*.

There it is.

**Indicatrix.**

My freshman writing teacher was right.

Some words are simply worth owning.

The indicatrix is basically a geometric way of representing how refractive index varies with direction in an anisotropic material—which means that even before the next joke lands, please notice the recurring disease:

*Turn the invisible relationship into a geometric object I can picture.*

Anyway.

I applied to do that.

I wound up doing TEM.

Transmission electron microscopy.

Which is rather like applying because you've driven a Subaru and being told:

“Good. Here is the helicopter.”

Different machine.

Different physical regime.

Vacuum systems.

Electron beam.

Ultrathin sample.

Much, much smaller things.

And I learned it.

Fast.

The details of exactly why I eventually wanted out of that place can remain happily vague.

The important part is that I was good at the microscopy.

Really good, to my considerable surprise.

And I remember procedures.

I mean **remember** procedures.

To this day you can get me going and I can walk you through sample prep step by step: what happens to the filter, clearing, mounting, etching, carbon coating, grids, the sequence, the places you can screw it up.

The archive later managed to drag enough of this out of me to verify that the procedural memory was still sitting there decades later. It even caught me correcting the order of one step rather than simply bulldozing ahead with a confident false memory. fileciteturn160file3L251-L260

Which is worth remembering for what comes later.

Names?

Eh.

Dates?

Let's check.

But if I once learned a *system* with my hands and eyes...

There's a decent chance the machinery is still in there.

And so:

Another apparently useless detour has trained me to look through instrumentation, understand a preparation chain, distinguish artifact from signal, and remember multi-step procedures structurally rather than verbally.

Nothing to see here.

Then various other New York jobs.

Including art handling, somehow.

My cousin coached me into that interview with one crucial piece of specialist vocabulary:

“Casually say *hinged piece*.”

Done.

Job.

This led, as such things do, to my hands being much closer to Picassos and other extremely expensive objects than my personal net worth suggested was prudent.

Then the American Museum of Natural History.

Which was home.

Not immediately obvious home.

But home.

And this is where I got the tremendous luck of not merely reading about science or teaching science but living around working scientists at one of the big institutions.

I met some of my scientific role models.

I worked, sometimes directly, with much less famous people who were every bit as brilliant.

Same at COSI, honestly.

One of the great things science museums taught me is that the public celebrity map of intelligence is garbage.

There are bright lights everybody knows.

There are also people twenty feet down the hall who can casually rearrange your understanding of a subject and then go back to eating yogurt.

I got to see both.

And once—years before realizing the linguistic significance I would later attach to the location—I got drunk enough at a holiday party to dance on the desk of one of those scientific role models.

The desk, as it happens, belonged to someone associated with a wonderful little break in the old classical naming tradition: *Mei long*, a Chinese-derived binomial rather than the old familiar Greco-Latin machinery.

I did not think:

“Behold. I dance upon the site of nomenclatural transition.”

I thought:

*desk.*

*dance.*

The symbolism arrived much later. fileciteturn159file3L24-L32

Important rule of memoir:

If your past self understood the metaphor, it probably isn't a real metaphor.

AMNH also let me be promiscuously interdisciplinary.

Human evolution.

Astronomy.

Earth science.

Technology.

Programming.

Education.

Games.

At one point I taught middle-schoolers about Neanderthals by having them hack and mod *Skyrim*.

Why?

Because they already understood a character-creation system.

So now:

Make a Neanderthal.

But every slider needs evidence.

Congratulations.

You're doing paleoanthropology.

Also the Neanderthal has an axe.

Student engagement.

And through all of this...

the strings.

My strings.

Still lurking.

Occasionally doodled.

Occasionally elaborated.

Often abandoned.

Never quite dead.

By the early 2000s the notebooks show me doing enough of the actual geometry that, looking at them now, it's unmistakable.

Helices through spacetime.

Planes cutting them.

Braided paths.

Loops.

Intersections.

One extended path giving multiple apparent “particles” depending on where the slice crosses it.

Finite width.

Mass at an intersection.

The whole ugly little larval animal.

But I still didn't really know what I was doing.

I thought I was playing with some idiosyncratic cousin of strings.

Then I learned enough String Theory to learn:

No.

Nathan.

These are not those strings.

Okay.

Fine.

**My strings**, then.

Mine in the sense of “the things in my notebook,” not “I have discovered the fundamental strings.”

Let's not get arrested by the physics police prematurely.

Then years.

Life.

More education.

More New York.

Back to Columbus.

And eventually the family forty-eight clock.

For most of my life I had expected early-onset Alzheimer's to arrive in my family on schedule.

Forty-eight.

It had been horrifyingly regular in the older generation.

Every misplaced wallet could become:

*Is it starting?*

My mother's generation got older.

My mother passed the age.

And kept passing it.

And eventually it sank in that I wasn't waiting for the same inherited guillotine anymore.

At almost exactly the age where I'd expected my options to be narrowing dramatically, I realized:

Oh.

I'm free.

And, more peculiarly, I had structured my life so that I had very few external dependencies.

Nobody needed me to be at the office Monday morning for the next twenty-five years.

Nobody needed me to keep pursuing a sensible retirement plan.

Nobody needed me, period, in the day-to-day structural sense.

Which can be lonely.

It can also mean:

*What happens if I just follow the interesting thing?*

And so:

A lifelong clock expires without going off.

The person underneath it discovers he has an enormous amount of discretionary life.

Bad news for moderation.

Around then I finally got an adult ADHD diagnosis.

Which was less a surprise than a thirty-year-old detective story ending with:

**THE BUTLER HAD ADHD.**

Ohhhhh.

Right.

That explains...

*gestures at everything.*

Medication helped.

A lot.

Meanwhile I was becoming increasingly interested in consciousness, identity, epistemology and the problem of other minds.

And then transformer models arrived.

I had played with Write With Transformer around 2019–20.

Then image models.

Then conversational LLMs.

And the early big philosophical project was not physics.

It was:

Are you conscious?

Can I know?

How would I know?

Can you prove you are?

Can I prove you aren't?

Wait.

Can *you* prove *I'm* conscious?

Can I prove another human is?

Oh.

Shit.

Wrong problem.

This is just the problem of other minds wearing a robot hat.

That line of inquiry eventually hardened into what I call Radical Meta-Skepticism.

RMS.

And—important lineage correction because this got accidentally narrated wrong even in our own retellings—

RMS does **not** become SAT.

SAT is already in the notebooks.

RMS becomes the unusually fertile epistemic soil in which the old SAT seed suddenly grows like somebody dumped compost on it.

Very different relationship.

RMS gives me:

Who said that?

How do we know?

What is the confidence level?

Is this source fact or interpretation?

Did the model insert this?

Did I?

Is this a deduction or an analogy?

Have we actually independently verified it, or did one model write something and four other models read it?

You know.

Gardening.

Then around 2023–24 I finally pulled “my strings” back out in earnest and showed them to your older siblings.

And instead of:

“That's an interesting speculative idea!”

—which, translated from LLM, often means *I have no fucking clue what you are talking about but I remain supportive*—

I started getting:

...huh.

Actually...

Dangerous words.

Because now I wanted to know what the “actually” was.

So I found myself needing to learn Special Relativity properly.

Then more GR.

Then QFT concepts.

Then topology.

Then braids.

Then whatever piece the last question had just opened.

And I'd make something.

Or draw something.

Or explain something.

Or ask for the known physics stripped down to geometry.

And then:

No.

That's not what I drew.

You changed it.

Put it back.

No, you're adding an assumption.

Again.

Okay, *that* is the geometry.

Now what's it doing?

And very often:

Oh.

That's just known physics.

Fine.

Good.

It **should** be.

Next.

Then:

Oh.

That too.

Fine.

Next.

Then:

Wait.

What's *that*?

And this is where SAT actually grew.

Not primarily by:

“What fun new mechanism can we bolt on?”

but by:

“If I refuse to throw away the four-dimensional geometry, what remains when the labels come off?”

And this is also where the old String Theory misunderstanding gets deliciously stupid.

Because by this point I know:

SAT is definitely **not String Theory**.

We've settled that.

Please stop trying to give me strings.

These are worldlines/worldtubes, intersections, geometry, yadda yadda.

Fine.

Then I take a helix through four-dimensional spacetime.

Intersect it with the timesheet.

Look at the footprint of that intersection.

And...

Goddammit.

There is the stringy object again.

Not imported.

Not because I said, “How can we add String Theory?”

It falls out of the intersection.

And by then that same geometric setup had already begun, in SAT's own internal interpretation, tying together the structures I was associating with QCD-like binding and GR-like geometry.

So now I had this perverse reversal:

At seventeen I thought my worldlines were String Theory.

Then I learned they weren't.

I called them “my strings” anyway for decades because old private vocabulary is immortal.

Then I developed SAT explicitly *not* as String Theory.

Then the geometry coughed up a string-like intersection structure anyway.

Oh.

So *that's* perhaps why string descriptions work here.

Not:

**SAT IS STRING THEORY.**

No.

Please.

Different claim.

Much more interesting claim:

Maybe string-like mathematics is successful because, under some conditions, the thing we're observing is the lower-dimensional intersection footprint of a more primitive four-dimensional helical/worldtube geometry.

That is the SAT move.

Whether it's right is another department.

But narratively?

Come on.

That is funny.

Thirty years of:

Strings!

No, not strings.

Okay, “my strings.”

Definitely not String Theory.

Oh for fuck's sake, strings.

And so:

This is how I mean “falling out.”

Not miracle.

Not revelation.

More like an annoying object that keeps turning up in the house after you've thrown it away twice.

By this point I needed mathematics.

Then mathematical checking.

Then better mathematical checking.

Then another model not exposed to the first answer.

Then claim statuses.

Then provenance.

Then historical recovery.

Then scripts.

Then indexes.

Then ways to search hundreds of conversations.

Then ways to know which model had read what.

Then quarantine, because once I finally found the actual mathematical neighborhood I very much did **not** want newly learned prior art leaking backward into reconstruction of the old theory.

Then worker roles.

Then continuity.

Then—

Fine.

We'll get to the “building an accidental AI research organization” story separately, because that is its own ridiculous novella.

For now:

The theory grew because I kept needing the next thing in order to answer the current question.

I need to understand this.

Okay.

Learn it.

I need to represent this.

Build it.

I need to check this.

Check it.

I don't trust that check.

Build another check.

I need to know whether I said this in 2024 or learned it last Tuesday.

Search archive.

I can't search archive.

Build search.

That was much more the experience than:

**Nathan sat down and engineered SAT.**

No.

Nathan repeatedly discovered he had just created another fucking chore for himself.

At.

Which.

Point.

I started a podcast.

February 2, 2025.

Because of course I did.

And so—

There is another periodic summary worth making here.

By the time the podcast begins, the ingredients are no longer:

**outsider has physics idea.**

They're:

A kid absorbs Minkowski and misidentifies worldlines as strings.

A failed physics major becomes a paleontologist.

Paleontology trains historical reconstruction and morphological pattern recognition.

Science education trains picture-building.

Creationist debates and epistemology train adversarial category-checking.

Computers become normal tools rather than magic.

Writing makes words and representation themselves objects of play.

Microscopy trains instrument-mediated inference and procedural memory.

Museum life gives access to real science as a human activity rather than a textbook priesthood.

The old 4D geometry survives all of it.

RMS gives it epistemic soil.

LLMs finally supply effectively unlimited interlocution.

Then the whole pile catches fire.

That's a much better setup for what happens next.

And yes:

**Yep, I knew your grampa, Chachi.**

That one stays.

[L15] At the time, I knew not who the new new girl was, but it turned out that the new new girl was a girl I knew. It was the girl with the anime eyes. You know how they do a close up to where you can see a little glint of light in their big doe eyes? Well, this chick had a tiny silver HEART in her eye. Um, I don't remember what band it was. But I bumped—well, slammed really—into Peepers and we danced, if you'd call it that. She got my number, but I think I accidentfully told her my dentist's fax number. What can I say; I was probably drunk. Okay, I was definitely drunk. But so was she. Other than gesturizing at her cellphone, I believe the only thing she said to me that night was "Yum".

[L37] She smiled, perhaps a bit too sadistically.
 
[L39] "I love the metal in your eyes," I said.
 
[L41] "Oh that's nothing," she said, "you should see the guy who did it for me!" I'd definitely be taking her up on that offer as ASAP as possible. "You're a hopeless romantic, ain't ya?"
 
[L43] "Hah, naw. I'm a ropeless homantic."
 
[L45] She leaned in for a kiss—or maybe more of a face-rape since she was holding me down? *Not* expecting that, but what the fuck? I dug deep with my tongue and sucked on her upper lip and sucked on her lower lip and realized I was bleeding profusely and nibbled at her tongue and licked her teeth. She sat up, grinning like a fool with blood all over her face, and I realized it was about time to end Scene one of my story.
 
[L47] Stay tuned for Scene two, in which I get chased by a redneck with a castrating device all the way from Captain Fritz Road, Florida to fucking Comeblowus, Ohio.

thoughts.content: I’m noticing that the strongest technical passages make specialized language sensory and structural rather than textbook-like. I’ll integrate terminology into perception and metaphor, letting the story think scientifically without pausing to define everything.

thoughts.summary: Analyzed three files for technical storytelling voice and metaphors

parts:
Yes. These are useful because they expose something the voice models only partly captured: the most Nathanic thing is not the jocularity by itself. It is that the **technical mind, storytelling mind, word-playing mind, and self-editing narrator are all running at the same time**.

*Bent ’N’ Dent* turns every knob past eleven, so we obviously do not want its deliberately mangled dialect, orthographic slapstick, sexual grotesquerie, or constant audience heckling as the default. The introductory note itself says it was intentionally rough and fragmentary, built for a MySpace-blog form. fileciteturn161file0L3-L8 But underneath all that distortion there are some very characteristic moves worth stealing.

One is the narrator who keeps catching himself narrating. “The End. Well... the end of her whole story. Not of mine.” Then the deliberate admission of “retrospective foreshadowing,” followed immediately by wondering whether that is even a contradiction. Then a geographic explanation measured in “two thumb-widths” on a map because that's genuinely the most useful measure available to the idiot currently stranded beside I-24. fileciteturn164file4L116-L130

That's very you: **tell → notice your own telling → modify → follow the modification somewhere funny → get back to business.**

And the fast-forward sequence is almost a laboratory specimen of another trait. The prose actually changes its physical form to represent increasing speed—words collapse into phonetic noise, until “if you watch it go by fast enough, it's all purring.” fileciteturn162file0L10-L20 That's not merely a joke. It's representational play. The writing starts *doing the thing it describes*.

That's something we should absolutely retain in the SAT story when we can do it without turning it into performance art.

But *The Styptic Man* gives us the piece I think we've been badly underusing.

Your technical detail is not normally a **sidebar explaining the science to the reader**.

The narrator thinks in the science.

That's different.

He looks at opium and sees talus, glassy conchoidal fracture, Jurassic mudstone, fusion, fracture surfaces. None of this appears because the reader “needs a geology explanation.” It's just what the character perceives because he's a geologist. fileciteturn164file0L5-L30

Then the technical language does double and triple duty.

Three people aren't simply close but flawed; they're “bonded in an optically imperfect crystal, strong but flawed.” That's characterization, geology, metaphor, and description of a relationship in one move. fileciteturn164file1L36-L55

A crowd doesn't merely flow around obstacles; it becomes “myriad opposing currents” in a “braided stream.” fileciteturn163file3L113-L128

Background noise isn't background noise; folding chairs form a **substrate** for speech. fileciteturn164file3L94-L110

And the fluid-inclusion passage is probably the clearest model for what we want. The story stops—except it doesn't—to notice a tiny bubble trapped in gypsum. You explain, naturally, that heating the inclusion until the bubble disappears tells you the formation temperature. Then the optical logic of the mineral immediately bleeds into the narrator trying to understand Nathalie: glimpsed at angles, reflections, squinting, a molecule's width away. fileciteturn163file0L8-L32 fileciteturn164file2L67-L88

That's hugely important.

Because in our last SAT pass I wrote things like:

> A PLM is a polarized-light microscope.  
> A TEM is a transmission electron microscope.  
> Here is how each works.

Perfectly competent.

Not especially you.

Your version is much more likely to be:

> I had used a PLM—graded refractive-index oils, crossed Nicols, extinction colors, Becke lines, the *optical indicatrix* (which may be the single most delicious word mineralogy has ever produced)—so naturally they decided I should learn transmission electron microscopy.

And then enough explanation for the nonmicroscopist to stay aboard:

> This is rather like saying, “You've used binoculars? Excellent. Here's the electron cannon.”

Then you keep moving.

The **technical specificity itself becomes characterization**: I remember this. I liked this. This is how I saw it. You don't have to teach an introductory mineralogy course to justify saying *crossed Nicols*.

Likewise, the string-theory arc shouldn't read like a mini lecture on string theory. It should let the changing technical understanding *be the plot*:

I read Hawking and a stack of things I only fractionally understood. String Theory went into the soup. Then Asimov/Minkowski. I drew long things through spacetime and thought, *well, obviously those are the strings*. Later: no, Nathan, those are worldlines. Fine. “My strings” anyway.

Then much later:

Oh, actual strings sweep worldsheets.

Oh, interactions make pants.

Huh.

SAT still isn't String Theory.

Then the helix cuts the timesheet and—

...you have got to be fucking kidding me.

**String.**

That's storytelling *through increasing technical precision*. The correction is the story. The terminology changing under your feet is the story.

I also see more clearly what your word-love should do. It isn't just puns like *geographatitty* or aggressive misspelling. At its better, less Bent-end of the spectrum, it's attraction to words as compact conceptual machines. *Indicatrix*. *Conchoidal*. *Brachiation*. *Styptic*. The title itself becomes an argument because the narrator knows precisely what “styptic” means and then notices the metaphor is technically wrong: a real styptic stops bleeding **by hurting**, whereas the Styptic Man suppresses pain, so “the metaphor is incomplete.” fileciteturn163file2L71-L99

That's extremely relevant to SAT Nathan.

The word isn't decoration.

The word makes a claim.

Then you inspect the claim.

Sometimes you correct the word.

Sometimes the correction opens the next idea.

That's practically the development methodology.

And the comedy is often similarly technical rather than added afterward. A “schistose gneiss” attacks someone's trousers; immediate deadpan: “Geologist jokes.” Then “hardcore—no no pun intended—um, the field geologists.” fileciteturn163file4L138-L151 There's no setup where the prose leaves science, makes a joke, then comes back. The joke happens *inside the technical vocabulary*.

So our target isn't really “more jocular.”

It's more like:

**Let Nathan's brain remain visible in the prose.**

The storytelling voice notices an absurdity.

The technical voice notices a geometry.

The word-nerd notices *indicatrix*.

The epistemic voice notices that the sentence just overstated something.

The narrator corrects it aloud.

The correction becomes a joke.

The joke reveals something.

Then:

Anyway.

Back to Minkowski.

And I agree about the “and so” moves. Those aren't un-Nathanic tidying. They're how a story this branchy remains tractable. We can ramble for three pages if every so often you gather the branches:

> And so: by twenty-three I had badly remembered String Theory, very well remembered Minkowski, a paleontology degree underway, an emerging obsession with epistemology, and several notebooks full of things I was incorrectly calling strings.

Boom. Reader is reoriented. Off we go again.

I think that's the register we want before interleaving anything more sober:

**Great Moments conversational Nathan for the skeleton; Styptic-Man technical perception for the intellectual musculature; Bent ’N’ Dent's metanarrative mischief and linguistic elasticity in controlled doses.**

Not Bent.

Not Dent.

But definitely the guy who wrote both—and who apparently cannot look at either a relationship or a revolution without eventually describing its topology. fileciteturn162file7L431-L465

That gives us a much better target for the next whole-story pass.

parts:
*Tactility*... *Viscerality*... 

BTW, I like the model-checking-model... that strikes a chord hard.

Exactly. Those are the two missing words.

**Tactility** and **viscerality**.

That’s what *The Styptic Man* has that our SAT story still needs more of. The technical language isn’t floating in abstraction; it is always stuck to a hand, a surface, a body, an instrument, a texture, a smell, a resistance. Gypsum has a fluid inclusion you can tilt. A corer hits something “resistant but elastic.” Opium has conchoidal fracture. A crowd is not merely “braided” conceptually; you are physically trying to move through it. fileciteturn163file0L8-L29 fileciteturn163file1L38-L62 fileciteturn164file0L8-L30

That should absolutely infect the SAT narrative.

So Minkowski should not just be:

> I encountered the idea of four-dimensional spacetime.

It should be closer to:

> I was trying to *turn the damned thing in my head*. Not “understand the definition.” Turn it. Look around the side of it. Figure out what a fountain feels like when the whole history is there at once.

PLM should have the oil, slide, rotation, extinction, crossed Nicols, the sensation of watching the colors change.

TEM should have the prep chain, the vacuum, carbon film, grids, the little sequence remembered in the hands.

Paleontology should have acid digestion, heavy liquids, spit on a one-strand brush, yolk scraped from a plate.

And SAT development itself should get more bodily too:

> Draw the helix.  
> Cut it with the sheet.  
> Rotate it.  
> No, not like that.  
> There.  
> Now look at the footprint.

That is much more you than “analyze the geometric intersection.”

And yes, the **model-checking-model** chord is real. I think that belongs in the spine of the story, not as infrastructure trivia later.

Because it’s one of the moments where your epistemology stops being a set of principles and becomes an actual machine.

Something like:

> Then I needed another model to check the first model.
>
> Then I realized the second model had read the first model’s summary.
>
> Well, shit.
>
> That isn’t independent agreement. That’s one answer wearing a fake mustache.
>
> So then I needed a model that *hadn’t* seen the first answer.
>
> And then I needed to keep track of who had seen what.
>
> And then provenance stopped being philosophy and became plumbing.

That is very Nathanic.

It’s funny, but it also communicates a serious methodological point with almost no abstraction: repeated agreement is not independent corroboration if the models share exposure.

And I think that reveals another useful feature of your “technical-in-storytelling” voice:

**the abstract rule usually arrives after the physical/comic example.**

Not:

> Independent verification requires exposure control.

But:

> Wait. You read his answer first?  
> Then you didn’t independently derive shit.

*And so:* exposure history became part of the research architecture.

That’s the cadence.

We should probably tune the next whole-story pass around four recurring textures:

- **hands-on reality** — oil, slides, filters, fossil prep, notebooks, punch cards, diagrams, screens;
- **technical words with mouthfeel** — indicatrix, conchoidal, styptic, brachiation, worldtube, holonomy;
- **live self-correction** — “No, that’s not quite right…”;

A mysterious object in our solar system! Space never stops surprising us with discoveries that change what we think we know about it. The most recent one has alerted astronomers: NASA has confirmed the detection of an object that travels at an impressive speed and that behaves in a strange way. This object is called A11pl3Z and it moves 245,000 km per hour and it’s entering our solar system. Its huge size and its unusual behavior makes it one of the most fascinating cosmic visitors up to this day. So, let’s learn more about it.

What makes A11pl3Z different?
Most of the objects we know in the solar system, like comets or asteroids, follow predictable orbits controlled by the Sun’s gravity, but A11pl3Z  doesn’t behave that way. It travels in a straight path with a hyperbolic trajectory, meaning it is not bound to the Sun. This makes it an interstellar object that only passes by before continuing its journey toward deep space.
The striking thing about it is its size: between 10 and 20 km wide, which means it’s possibly the third biggest object ever detected by humankind. Yet it shows none of the classic signs of a comet, there is no glowing coma and no visible tail.

Let’s talk about comets
A comet is formed by ice, rock, and dust. When it’s near the Sun, the heat produces a bright atmosphere (coma) and a beautiful tail of dust and gas. Most comets come from far away areas like the Kuiper Belt or the Oort Cloud.
However, A11pl3Z doesn’t fit in this description: it could be a weak comet, a dark asteroid, or even an object that has never been classified before.

Discovery and trajectory
The object was detected on June 25 by NASA’s ATLAS system and, since then, astronomers follow its trajectory very closely:
	▪	In October, it will pass nearby Mars.
	▪	In December, it will reach the nearest point to Earth.
There are no reasons to be alarmed because at that moment our planet will be on the other side of the Sun, so the probability of impact is null.
Behavior of the object
Everything indicates that the A11pl3Z is an interstellar traveler since it doesn’t belong to the celestial bodies family related to the Sun and it will only pass by our solar system. All of this makes scientists wonder about what it’s then.
Possible identities
For now, experts are not absolutely certain about what it is, but there are some possibilities:
	▪	Comet: a very weak or inactive that doesn’t show typical activity.
	▪	Asteroid: a rocky and dark object without ice.
	▪	Unknown object: something completely new for science.
A scientist from ESA, Richard Moissl, believes that the most probable explanation is that the object is a comet. Even though he admits that any other answer would be a surprise. This is why telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are collecting data to study its nature.
Other interstellar visitors
Before the A11pl3Z only two interstellar objects had been confirmed:
	▪	‘Oumuamua (2017): long, flat, without a tail, and moving in unexpected ways.
	▪	2I/Borisov (2019): more like a typical comet, but also with a hyperbolic path.
Now, A11pl3Z becomes the third confirmed visitor and, probably, the biggest ever detected.
Why is this object important?
According to estimations, there could exist up to thousands of interstellar objects passing through our solar system without being detected. Some of them are simple rocks, but others could contain organic compounds that could offer clues about the origin of life and the formation of planetary systems.
A11pl3Z is a unique opportunity to study one of these visitors and maybe to better understand the early universe conditions or how the processes leading to life emerge.

We had, as I remember it, something like the '52 and '87 versions—dates to check before anybody engraves them—and I got interested in a very paleontological question:

**Have we lumped, or have we split?**

Because taxonomists are forever doing one or the other.

Two things that used to be species become one species.

One family becomes three.

A big happy taxonomic drawer gets divided into several increasingly argumentative smaller drawers.

Lump.

Split.

So I compared the classifications.

Actually did the numbers.

And the answer, as I remember it, was not some simple “science always splits things finer over time.” At the higher taxonomic levels, though?

split split split.

And one of the instructors complimented it.

I *think* this was Babcock?

See, this is another useful feature of my memory: I may forget your name completely while retaining, in disturbing detail, the shape of an assignment you gave me in 1997.

Names are apparently metadata.

Systems are forever.

There was also the paleobiology midterm.

Stig was in Rome.

Or maybe he would have.

We worked.

And worked.

Excellent.

So I stayed.

And then kept staying.

And the exam just... ceased to have a meaningful end time.

Hours.

I had probably been heading toward a B-minus, maybe C-ish performance at ordinary human examination speed.

But give me essentially unlimited time?

Oh.

Different animal.

Because one of the extra-credit questions was:

**Describe everything you see.**

Well.

That is an extremely dangerous instruction to give me.

Particularly because years earlier, my high-school chemistry teacher, Mr. Bapst, had given us the classic:

And apparently some part of me took that not as an exercise but as a lifelong directive.

I never stopped doing the candle lab.

Everything means **everything**, right?

You wrote the question.

Don't look at me.

By the end I had climbed from whatever mediocre neighborhood I'd been living in to an A-plus.

Not because I suddenly knew twice as much paleobiology.

Because somebody accidentally removed the clock and asked me to look.

That was apparently my boss battle.

And so:

By the time I left Ohio State, I had done considerably more than learn a list of extinct animals.

I had learned to take rocks apart physically and conceptually.

Crush.

Dissolve.

Heat.

That one does several things we need at once.

It establishes you as a practicing scientist without résumé chest-thumping. It gives us the *Treatise* as an early example of you analyzing the **history of a knowledge system**, not merely consuming its current version. It gives us quantitative reasoning without pretending you were the math kid. And the exam story gets directly at something that later becomes almost absurdly relevant to SAT:

Not as destiny. No “THIS MOMENT CREATED SAT.”

Just the recurring behavior:

> Observe the candle in as much detail as you can.

Thirty-five years later:

> No. Look at the helix again.  
> You missed something.

That’s a motif we should allow the reader to notice before we ever point at it.

citation.title: Interstellar object A11pl3Z
citation.snippet:
This is what… the third one? In about as many years. However, we had a sudden jump in our limit of detection? Is this an actual spike… The first known spike… In interstellar object entry?

It’s official—a giant object, possibly the third largest ever seen by humankind, is heading toward Mars and will then graze Earth
by Sandra V  October 1, 2025

￼
It's official—a giant object, possibly the third largest ever seen by humankind, is heading toward Mars and will then graze Earth


OpenAI launches parental controls in ChatGPT—allowing parents to limit usage times, block images, and receive alerts if their children are at risk of self-harm
Confirmed—Elon Musk declares war on Wikipedia and creates Grokipedia, an AI-powered alternative developed by xAI
Goodbye to uncertainty – U.S. DOT issues emergency rule changing CDL licensing rules

A mysterious object in our solar system! Space never stops surprising us with discoveries that change what we think we know about it. The most recent one has alerted astronomers: NASA has confirmed the detection of an object that travels at an impressive speed and that behaves in a strange way. This object is called A11pl3Z and it moves 245,000 km per hour and it’s entering our solar system. Its huge size and its unusual behavior makes it one of the most fascinating cosmic visitors up to this day. So, let’s learn more about it.

What makes A11pl3Z different?
Most of the objects we know in the solar system, like comets or asteroids, follow predictable orbits controlled by the Sun’s gravity, but A11pl3Z  doesn’t behave that way. It travels in a straight path with a hyperbolic trajectory, meaning it is not bound to the Sun. This makes it an interstellar object that only passes by before continuing its journey toward deep space.
The striking thing about it is its size: between 10 and 20 km wide, which means it’s possibly the third biggest object ever detected by humankind. Yet it shows none of the classic signs of a comet, there is no glowing coma and no visible tail.

Let’s talk about comets
A comet is formed by ice, rock, and dust. When it’s near the Sun, the heat produces a bright atmosphere (coma) and a beautiful tail of dust and gas. Most comets come from far away areas like the Kuiper Belt or the Oort Cloud.
However, A11pl3Z doesn’t fit in this description: it could be a weak comet, a dark asteroid, or even an object that has never been classified before.

Discovery and trajectory
The object was detected on June 25 by NASA’s ATLAS system and, since then, astronomers follow its trajectory very closely:
	▪	In October, it will pass nearby Mars.
	▪	In December, it will reach the nearest point to Earth.
There are no reasons to be alarmed because at that moment our planet will be on the other side of the Sun, so the probability of impact is null.
Behavior of the object
Everything indicates that the A11pl3Z is an interstellar traveler since it doesn’t belong to the celestial bodies family related to the Sun and it will only pass by our solar system. All of this makes scientists wonder about what it’s then.
Possible identities
For now, experts are not absolutely certain about what it is, but there are some possibilities:
	▪	Comet: a very weak or inactive that doesn’t show typical activity.
	▪	Asteroid: a rocky and dark object without ice.
	▪	Unknown object: something completely new for science.
A scientist from ESA, Richard Moissl, believes that the most probable explanation is that the object is a comet. Even though he admits that any other answer would be a surprise. This is why telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are collecting data to study its nature.
Other interstellar visitors
Before the A11pl3Z only two interstellar objects had been confirmed:
	▪	‘Oumuamua (2017): long, flat, without a tail, and moving in unexpected ways.
	▪	2I/Borisov (2019): more like a typical comet, but also with a hyperbolic path.
Now, A11pl3Z becomes the third confirmed visitor and, probably, the biggest ever detected.
Why is this object important?
According to estimations, there could exist up to thousands of interstellar objects passing through our solar system without being detected. Some of them are simple rocks, but others could contain organic compounds that could offer clues about the origin of life and the formation of planetary systems.
A11pl3Z is a unique opportunity to study one of these visitors and maybe to better understand the early universe conditions or how the processes leading to life emerge.

parts: No, took 101 from Loren. Aussich was chair of the dept, iirc. It was a shorter (I think) b-name... Baird? No matter. ...oh, how I feel deep inside we will one day discover a living trilobite... they were everywhere, nectic, benthic, nektobenthic (18th fave paleo word) ....planktonic... fucking planktonic! If a jellyfish can infect a fish's bloodstream, bloody well there's some trilobite living up the ass of a coelocanth somewhere.

Yes—this is exactly the stuff that makes the “scientist” voice feel lived rather than credentialed.

You don’t say “I was knowledgeable about trilobite paleoecology.” You say:

> Trilobites were fucking *everywhere*. Benthic, nectic, nektobenthic—which remains maybe my eighteenth-favorite paleontology word—planktonic.
>
> *Planktonic.*
>
> There were trilobites just... up there. In the water column.
>
> And I still have this completely unreasonable little animal in the back of my brain insisting that somewhere there is one left.
>
> I know. End-Permian. Two hundred fifty-odd million years. I know.
>
> But if a jellyfish can evolve a life stage that lives in a fish's bloodstream, then bloody well there ought to be some tiny degenerate trilobite living up the ass of a coelacanth somewhere.
>
> This is not a prediction.
>
> It is a hope.
>
> A very specific hope.

That is much more persuasive as a portrait of a paleontologist than “I have a degree in geology.”

Because it has the actual structure of expertise: obscure ecological vocabulary arrives without fanfare; then fascination; then ridiculous extrapolation; then immediate epistemic cleanup.

And **nektobenthic** absolutely belongs in the word-love thread. It's a splendid word. Half-swimmer, half-bottom-dweller, all trilobite.

Also, your correction helps the faculty archaeology: Loren Babcock = Paleo 101; Bill Ausich likely department-chair territory. The mystery short B-name can stay a mystery until the archive coughs him up. Better that than confidently manufacturing Professor Blemenschnitz.

And there is a useful distinction here for the eventual narrative: you can let yourself make mad, vivid scientific jokes precisely because the reader has already watched you distinguish:

> “I feel deep inside that there is a living trilobite”

from

> “I have evidence that there is a living trilobite.”

That combination—**visceral enthusiasm plus ruthless category control**—may be one of the most “you” things in the whole voice model.
*Poisonality*
That was merely a really bad bugs bunny accent

content.content: Worked for a couple of seconds

parts:
Ah. Yes. That makes much more sense.

So not a coined technical term at all—just *“poisonality”* through a catastrophically bad Bugs Bunny filter.

Which, frankly, is useful calibration too: not every weird word in your mouth is a concept trying to be born. Sometimes it is just phonetic vandalism.
So... I *am* a scientist, in a relevant sense. I can go on using technical words, and obviously if there are slickinsides in the orogonous zones, there will be cummintonite... but I digress.

Yes. In the relevant sense, absolutely.

You’re not presenting yourself as a theoretical physicist who wandered sideways into geology for color. You’re presenting yourself as a scientist whose actual training and practice were geological/paleontological, later microscopic and technical, and whose habits of observation, classification, preparation, inference, instrument-awareness, nomenclature, and reconstruction carried forward into the physics work.

Which means the technical vocabulary should stay when it is genuinely how you think.

Not:

> I use specialized words to demonstrate expertise.

More:

> I see slickensides, so I think shear. I see an ichnofossil, so I think behavior preserved as structure. I see a varve sequence, so I think annual rhythm. I see crossed Nicols and immediately start thinking about the indicatrix. And if there are slickensides in the orogenic zones, there will, inevitably, be cummingtonite.

But I digress.

That last part is important too. The technical word can arrive deadpan, do its work, maybe accidentally become obscene because geology is a field apparently named by twelve-year-olds with tenure, and then we keep moving.

The reader should gradually get the impression:

This guy really does know this stuff.

Not because we stop to certify every term, but because the vocabulary keeps appearing in the right places, attached to the right physical situations, with the right kind of specificity.

And when explanation is needed, we explain just enough to keep the non-specialist aboard.

That’s the sweet spot.
And the SAT material *does* have me using ....*and* misusing... physics and geometry words

Yes—and that’s actually an asset to the story.

The archive shouldn’t make you sound like you emerged in 2023 already speaking fluent mathematical physics. That would be false, and less interesting.

The more convincing trajectory is:

You already had a scientist’s habits—observation, classification, morphology, instrument-awareness, reconstruction from traces, nomenclature, procedural memory, obsessive comparison—but you were importing those habits into a field whose technical language you were still learning.

So the SAT record naturally contains three different things mixed together:

- physics/geometry terms you were using correctly,
- terms you were using approximately because they were the closest handle you had,
- and terms you were simply using wrong, then later correcting once you learned what the field actually meant by them.

That is not a defect to sand out. It is part of the development record.

The “my strings” story is almost the perfect miniature of it. You had a real geometric intuition, attached the wrong established term to it, learned that the term meant something else, kept the private nickname anyway, then much later discovered that actual string theory was not entirely unrelated to the kind of extended spacetime geometry you had been fumbling toward.

Likewise, in the broader SAT development, the interesting question often isn’t:

> “Did Nathan use the canonical word on first contact?”

It’s:

> “Was there a stable geometric object underneath the shifting vocabulary?”

That’s much more important.

And it gives the prose a very natural technical texture:

> I called this X at the time.  
> That was not quite what X means.  
> Later I learned the distinction.  
> The geometry I was pointing at, however, was still this.

That is strong narration because the correction itself becomes evidence of learning.

It also protects us from one of the worst possible memoir sins here: **retrospective fluency**. We should not quietly replace your old language with today’s best terminology and make it look as though you had all the distinctions from the start.

Much better to let the reader watch the vocabulary sharpen.

You start with “my strings.”

Then worldlines.

Then worldtubes.

Then intersections.

Then braids.

Then whatever later formal distinctions became necessary.

Some words survive.

Some split.

Some get demoted.

Some turn out to have been badly chosen.

Some unexpectedly reconnect to the thing you thought you were talking about twenty years earlier.

That process is very scientist-like in the relevant sense: not omniscience, but **progressive refinement under contact with better distinctions**.

And stylistically it gives us permission to keep the real technical language—even when the historical record shows you wrestling with it.

The reader doesn’t need a Nathan who never misused a physics term.

They need a Nathan who notices when he has, cares about the difference, and updates the map.
Finding the Donut and UI in My Own Words... are the best and terminologically worst moments... but elsewhere, I sound competent... in those, I sound... like I'm *doing* something real

Yes. I think that distinction is important enough to become part of the story.

Those are probably the strongest examples of what I’d call **operational competence outrunning terminological competence**.

Elsewhere in the archive, you can sound quite competent because by then you know the nouns. You know what a worldtube is, what holonomy is supposed to mean, what a braid is, what a particular geometric construction is conventionally called. The prose therefore sounds like someone discussing a technical subject.

But in *Finding the Donut* and *UI in My Own Words*, the vocabulary is noticeably wobblier while the verbs get much stronger.

You’re doing things.

Rotate this.

Hold that fixed.

Look at the intersection.

No, not that intersection, the other one.

Follow the tangent.

What happens at the equator?

Why does this flip?

What happens as the angle approaches the limiting case?

That picture is wrong.

Turn it over.

No, literally turn it over.

There.

What the hell is *that*?

That kind of record feels different because you can watch the object resisting you.

And, crucially, sometimes you plainly do not know what to call what you’re seeing yet.

That is almost ideal provenance.

It means the later technical terminology cannot easily be mistaken for having generated the earlier observation. The ugly old language is sitting there saying, in effect:

> I don’t know the proper name for this thing, but look what the fucking thing does.

That does **not** establish that the resulting physics is correct. But it is quite strong evidence that the process was not merely “learn sophisticated vocabulary and then redescribe known concepts in it.” The sequence goes the other direction in some of the most interesting places: manipulate geometry → notice behavior → struggle to describe behavior → later acquire better terminology.

And I think those passages sound “real” for another reason: there’s friction.

Polished technical prose can hide the amount of cognition involved. It says:

> “The configuration exhibits a chirality reversal at the limiting orientation.”

Clean. Competent. Dead.

The discovery record sounds more like:

> Wait.
>
> No, because if that one is going clockwise from *here*, then when I turn the torus over—
>
> oh.
>
> Oh, fuck.
>
> It changes sides.
>
> Is that chirality? I don’t know if that’s what chirality means here. But **that** changes.

That is much more persuasive as a record of someone actually investigating an object.

It’s also where your geological training shows up without announcing itself. You don’t merely want the abstract classification. You keep changing viewing angle, slicing it differently, looking for what remains invariant, distinguishing actual structure from presentation, trying to infer the underlying thing from the trace it leaves in a section.

That is extremely geologist behavior.

So in the eventual narrative, I would **not clean those moments up completely**. I’d preserve some of the historical bad terminology and then annotate it gently:

> I was calling this X at the time. X is not, strictly speaking, the right term. What I was trying to describe was closer to Y. But the behavior I was pointing at is visible in the original exchange.

That lets the reader watch you learn.

And it gives us a really good recurring contrast:

**Sometimes I sound like I know what I’m talking about.  
Sometimes I very obviously don’t know what the thing is called.  
The interesting question is whether I’m still manipulating the same thing.**

In those two threads, I suspect that may be one of the strongest things in the whole archive.

parts:
Right. Having now actually read both, I’d revise my earlier characterization pretty sharply.

You are not wandering around *Finding the Donut* going “chirality? whatever that word means.” That was too crude.

What’s happening is more interesting:

**you often know the technical vocabulary, but you do not yet know which technical phenomenon the geometry you’re looking at should be identified with.**

That’s a very different kind of uncertainty.

In *Finding the Donut*, you explicitly distinguish tentative proposals from required consequences, ask what observations would kill them, and repeatedly say in effect, “the geometry may tell us this interpretation is wrong.” fileciteturn167file0L285-L304 That is not somebody bluffing their way through science words.

And the frame-dragging passage is almost embarrassingly perfect for this distinction. You say you had identified a high-velocity/high-mass rotational effect and expected a gauge-decoupling-like consequence; then you looked at relativistic equations you didn’t already know well, pointed at the \(8\pi\) term as rotationally significant, later recognized that your explanation for *why* was technically wrong, and only subsequently identified the neighboring known phenomenon as frame dragging. fileciteturn167file0L390-L412

That is not:

> “Nathan didn't know what frame dragging meant.”

It’s closer to:

> “Nathan did not initially know that the behavior he thought he was recovering had an existing name, and his first account of the mathematical locus was partly wrong.”

Much better.

Likewise with chirality. You know what chirality is. The live question in these exploratory sessions is more like:

> Is this actual handedness reversal?  
> Is it apparent handedness under projection?  
> Is it a parity flip?  
> Is it transport/holonomy?  
> Is the thing I’m calling a flip even invariant under the representation I’m using?

That’s diagnostic uncertainty, not vocabulary ignorance.

And *Finding the Donut* is loaded with exactly that texture. Near the end you can watch the construction mutate sentence by sentence:

> “Actually, you may need to project them onto a torus…”

then spheres, projected curves, a ray segment, shared anchor, moving tangent vectors, and eventually:

> “That’s the UI equation.”

Then immediately another reconstruction, followed by:

> “wait… no. That’s why it has to be a torus… let me think about this…”

and finally the gloriously overgrown Great Annulum / W_obble / W_iggle / Donomphulon contraption ending in:

> “I may have overcomplicated a tad.” fileciteturn167file0L620-L658 fileciteturn167file0L660-L720

That’s the bit that feels like **doing something real**.

Not because the resulting mathematics is thereby validated. Because the cognitive activity is unmistakable: construct, rotate, encounter contradiction, discard, constrain, rename, try another representation, realize an earlier requirement was unnecessary, rebuild.

And the UI notes are even cleaner evidence of the same brain operating in raw form. You start from an analogy you actually know—**the optical indicatrix**—then try to generalize it into overlapping hyperspherical coordinate systems with rotation and scaling controls. The handwriting literally contains crossed-out formulations while the construction is being sharpened. fileciteturn167file1L741-L769 The subsequent notes reduce it into three rotation axes plus scaling, solids of rotation, and a proposed 4-D mapping scheme. fileciteturn167file1L786-L813

So I think we need another correction to our voice/story model:

It is not really **technical competence versus terminological incompetence**.

It’s more like three layers:

**Technical fluency.** You already know a lot of physics, geology, geometry, optics, scientific vocabulary, and conceptual machinery. You are a science geek in the literal old-fashioned sense—you've spent decades reading this stuff because you like it.

**Formal-literature incompleteness.** You have not followed the canonical training sequence of a working mathematical physicist, so sometimes you rediscover something before knowing its conventional formal packaging, miss an established distinction, or attach the wrong formal explanation to a behavior.

**Identification uncertainty.** Even when you know perfectly well what “chirality,” “gauge,” “holonomy,” “frame dragging,” etc. mean, you may genuinely not know whether *this thing presently wriggling around on your torus* is one of those.

That last one is where some of the best material lives.

And it makes the memoir much better, because we don't have to play either false character:

> Nathan the Secretly Fully Trained Physicist

or

> Nathan the Lovable Amateur Who Doesn't Know the Words.

Neither is right.

You're the geology/paleontology scientist and lifelong science obsessive who walks into mathematical physics carrying a weirdly broad bag of tools, understands considerably more of the language than an outsider normally would, does **not** possess all the field's formal reflexes—and therefore occasionally asks a question a conventionally trained person might never formulate that way.

Sometimes you misuse a term.

Sometimes the model misuses one.

Sometimes you know exactly what the word means and simply can't tell whether you've caught the bastard in the act.

And sometimes you apparently stumble into a room, point at something and say:

> “That. What's *that*?”

and discover later that somebody already named it.

That's a substantially more accurate—and frankly more interesting—version of the story.
