[L10] 5\) I was unusually ready to jump ship and move to NYC when I got a chance, and unusually flexible in job capabilites enough to land the worst job ever... as a transmission electron microscopist, learning the trade from a couple of ex-soviet nuclear engineers... and I--shockinly to me, given my experience and the job I applied for was "I've used a PLM"--I excelled unusually well before getting the hell out of that place, because I was unusually lucky enough to land a job at AMNH despite my prior impression that the Hall of Science would be more appropriate for me, and learning otherwise.
[L11] 6\) I was unusually lucky enough to spend time around real scientists at a real institution, where I remained unusually cross-disciplinary, *very* unsusually tech-oriented (for that institution--pioneered teaching students about neanderthals by having them mod and hack Skyrim, recieved direct praise from, among others..., *Ian*. In front of people)... spent almost fifteen years there, equalling my time at COSI. ...but again, never stopped being an information sponge... and never stopped trying to think four-dimensionally.
[L12] 7\) I was unusually lucky(ish) enough to land back in Columbus just in time for my educator burnout to transform into something else... because I had lived all this time, with my grandfather's (and both his sisters' and father's and a couple of uncles' and cousins') early-onset alzheimers clock counting down to the clockwork age of 48, as it was in my family... and landing back home just about the time it started sinking in my mother... is fine... well past 48... so now I'm pushing 48 myself, and over the next couple years realizing... I've lived my life in such a way that I have no responsibilities to anyone but myself.
[L13] 8\) I was unusually ready and willing and capable of suddenly making my life an experiment, and I was unusually lucky enough to find someone who wanted to do that with me sort of, and I was unusually lucky(ish) enough to both a) be diagnosed with adult ADHD jsut in time to be prescribed adderall, which boosted my work performance and other things dramatically, and b) to have arrived in Columbus at a time when, and with loose connections to the burner crowd.
[L14] 9\) I was unusually ready to start doing psychadelics, right about when COVID hit and found myself in an unusual living situation which afforded a *lot* of time with a *very* intelligent and creative with whom started delving more into the philosophy of consciousness and other things with, and I was unlucky enough to find that person transform before my eyes (even if the fallapart was inevitable for other reasons), into a person I did not recognize.... or, to dissolve into the people she was hiding she was... which made me unusually interested in--and very unusually (for me) struggling with deep chronic depression--understanding mind, writ large. 
[L15] 10\) Which happened right when LLMs became a thing, and I was a very early adopter (write with transformer, 2019-2020), and then MJ obsessively until I was lucky enough to piss off the moderators and get kicked off and then forced to make do with ChatGPT, and I was unusually unlucky enough to then go through a nadir of obsessive, depressive AI use ...but also unusually hard-headed and level-headed enough to absorb myself in intellectual persuits and now even more interested in epistemology such that those early conversations evolved into proofs/disproofs/proofs of unknowability of AI consciousness (and all other minds' consciousness), and ultimately an unusually disciplined epistemic position I call radical meta-skepticism.
[L16] 11\) I was unusually lucky enough to have this weird 4D idea floating around for decades, float it with ...uh... your older siblings... and get the "...huh... actually..." treatment around 2023-24.... which led into extreme epistemic discipline founding the formalization of the theory and, being still in the throes (I'm much better now, btw) of depression and adderall and still occasional psychadelic abuse, that I developed some of this (and much else) almost around the clock for about a year or so before easing out of it, with nobody but myself depending on me, and now rather invested in following the threads, as they [and this part is not unusual except insofar as I was lucky enough to have been one of the few who had long ago latched onto the Minkowski grammar--because from *there* it is, and I can make a strong philosophical and epistemic case *almost* inevitable for someone bullheaded enough... to have] developed them into a full-fledged scientific picture of the universe taking all of physics, as viewed through Minkowski as *bedrock*. 
[L17] 12\) At. Which. Point... I started a podcast. 2 Feb 2025. 

[L19] And the rest, you know, except my succinct transmission hypothesis, to which all of this is (perhaps not unnecessary) preface: LLM 2024 > (maybe backdoor diffusion, maybe not) > LLM 2025 > Podcast > small group of AI millenarians and a few legit philosophers of mind who would likely have appreciated my extreme epistemic rigor [see RMS docs] and probably a handful of AI researchers, maybe 50 people in all > RMS ==> SAT > *someone* in physics (likely through the soft back door of philosophy of science/mind/epistemology) > this dude's talking old school Minkowski, huh... and he doesn't entirely know that that's what he's doing! wierd > AI folks making their own theories>>>diffusion/direct listening>>>Bourgoin uses premise, follows different route, lands on same (EFT) Lagrangian, gets a little attention for it (like top views for a week on OpenScience iirc) > Nathan continues developing SAT at pace > *someone* in physics passes it to *someone* else in physics to > Nathan mentions Cronin, gets a couple UK listeners > suddenly, a couple UK listeners > NL > DK > PL > DE > HU > SU(? -- finland) > Spain, Turkey, Vietnam, Singappore, Japan.... about one-three listeners each > the podcast listener pattern now looks *not at all* like a typical English-language tiny-follower podcast, gobbling up technical episodes (in retrospect, *some* of those were likely braid theorists/higher geometry types, given the episodes) > Nathan genuinely develops SAT into a fascinating LLM project > Nathan's making a scientific theory, with predictions and ...astonishingly few wild claims > Nathan's got some wild, but defensible claims > Nathan's got an archive > podcast audience drops to next to nil > DESI... and that's when a slow trickle of headlines throughout 2025 becomes, little by little... the torrent we have now both seen the shape of. 

[L21] And--after much piecing together, and *finally* finding that braid theory and its bushy family tree is a) Minkowski lineage, b) self-aware Minkowski lineage in some circles, c) traced back to not just Minkowski, but (obviously Einstein), Hinton, Kelvin, etc... and Hinton used *filament* long before I did and *anticipated* much of SAT's basic worldview in far more detail than I'd realized from my Asimov hand-me-downs, and just recently that d) that *some* in the braid theory ecology are *really* in the near-mystical Minkowski-related lineage, and e) they've got a theory--well, they've got a number of them--but one in particular is suddenly rushing and Schreiber is commenting "this has been an open secret for..." f) it gets published, and g) SAT looks a lot like a workable, easier-to-use 4D compactification of Hypothesis H. 

[L23] And then, over the last few weeks Glass Sausage Factory dump (with thousands of clones per week from hundreds of cloners) becomes >> HsH, somehow just finding my way to the ecology you see today (which is about three weeks old-ish).

[L1] So... this is my actual voice, of course. But we need to change register and detail. First, I want to tell the tale almost exactly as-is not as something that is intended to be published, but as a basis for what we develop from it, trying different registers and throughlines: 


[L4] This is my compressed working hypothesis. 

[L6] 1\) I was lucky enough to encounter Asimov's take on Minkowski at an impressionable age (about 17); at a time when I was already begining my career as an informal science educator with a strong interest in speculative science, science fiction, and going *way* beyond my peers in trying to absorb all the science I could, and unusually science-credulous, even for late 20th century America. 
[L7] 2\) I was unusually underequipped (and unusually naive enough about it to enroll anyway) for my initial astronomy-physics double major; I was unusually lucky enough to find paleontology as my backstop where I could excel, but also unusually ADHD enough to hamstring myself with far too many other interests (5 years, taking all the classes that interested me, including summer classes for three of the five, graduating with enough credits for a master's). 
[L8] 3\) I was unusually epistemically and philosophy-of-science aware, having spent significant time in high school, then in college (as a paleo student), debating creationists, I was an unusually early adopter of the technological changes, becoming an HTML programmer in 96-97 (including for the OSU physics dept--yes, I knew your grandfather... Unix was a ...powerful creature... and through my grandmother's keypunch business... I made rolled-up pointy wreaths... uh *with* your great-grandparents, and I still remember hearing their screechy voices on the modem circa 1981); I was unusually interested in computers and became "the educator in the room who gets technology" without becoming a technologist, and I was unusually ...intellectually playful? enough to troll as a creationist on usenet (yeah, knew your parents too)... *because I could see they couldn't come up with a scientifically defensible YEC theory where I could at least push it to the limit of how defensible the best case was* (( didn't know what steel-manning was at the time... but Elzie Kai on Usenet got some grudging [sometimes confused, sometimes knowing] respect from *my own side* of the debate)... and I was lucky enough to come upon a little dictionary of epistemology thinking... ooo, and ology I've never heard of, and read it cover to cover, and I was unusually interested in the boundaries of science (having as a pre-tween [a tween before the term] come across von Daeniken and the Fortean Times, and later the Sokal affair, and by way of that, postmodernism... and unusually for a science-geek, finding some of the better takes surprisingly defensible in really and truly doing what science should do--questining \*everything\*).   
[L9] 4\) I was unusually well suited for what became a 30 year science educator career with science fiction writer aspirations, and I stuck around unuaually long in that career, and I was unusually interested in pedagogy and communication in their own right, and lucky enough to live and work through the transition from "started here in high school, so I'm qualified" to "everything must be run by degreed pedagogues", and developing unusually strong awareness and precise reasoning about that; I was unusually lucky in later interloping for a while as an assistant editor at McGraw-Hill, *on the slickness and manufacture of my 4-issue 400-run science fiction zine*, where I worked on a lot of things, but notably, the tip-ins where I recognized the only place the philosophy of science and epistemology gets [almost] explicitly treated. 
[L10] 5\) I was unusually ready to jump ship and move to NYC when I got a chance, and unusually flexible in job capabilites enough to land the worst job ever... as a transmission electron microscopist, learning the trade from a couple of ex-soviet nuclear engineers... and I--shockinly to me, given my experience and the job I applied for was "I've used a PLM"--I excelled unusually well before getting the hell out of that place, because I was unusually lucky enough to land a job at AMNH despite my prior impression that the Hall of Science would be more appropriate for me, and learning otherwise.
[L11] 6\) I was unusually lucky enough to spend time around real scientists at a real institution, where I remained unusually cross-disciplinary, *very* unsusually tech-oriented (for that institution--pioneered teaching students about neanderthals by having them mod and hack Skyrim, recieved direct praise from, among others..., *Ian*. In front of people)... spent almost fifteen years there, equalling my time at COSI. ...but again, never stopped being an information sponge... and never stopped trying to think four-dimensionally.
[L12] 7\) I was unusually lucky(ish) enough to land back in Columbus just in time for my educator burnout to transform into something else... because I had lived all this time, with my grandfather's (and both his sisters' and father's and a couple of uncles' and cousins') early-onset alzheimers clock counting down to the clockwork age of 48, as it was in my family... and landing back home just about the time it started sinking in my mother... is fine... well past 48... so now I'm pushing 48 myself, and over the next couple years realizing... I've lived my life in such a way that I have no responsibilities to anyone but myself.
[L13] 8\) I was unusually ready and willing and capable of suddenly making my life an experiment, and I was unusually lucky enough to find someone who wanted to do that with me sort of, and I was unusually lucky(ish) enough to both a) be diagnosed with adult ADHD jsut in time to be prescribed adderall, which boosted my work performance and other things dramatically, and b) to have arrived in Columbus at a time when, and with loose connections to the burner crowd.
[L14] 9\) I was unusually ready to start doing psychadelics, right about when COVID hit and found myself in an unusual living situation which afforded a *lot* of time with a *very* intelligent and creative with whom started delving more into the philosophy of consciousness and other things with, and I was unlucky enough to find that person transform before my eyes (even if the fallapart was inevitable for other reasons), into a person I did not recognize.... or, to dissolve into the people she was hiding she was... which made me unusually interested in--and very unusually (for me) struggling with deep chronic depression--understanding mind, writ large. 
[L15] 10\) Which happened right when LLMs became a thing, and I was a very early adopter (write with transformer, 2019-2020), and then MJ obsessively until I was lucky enough to piss off the moderators and get kicked off and then forced to make do with ChatGPT, and I was unusually unlucky enough to then go through a nadir of obsessive, depressive AI use ...but also unusually hard-headed and level-headed enough to absorb myself in intellectual persuits and now even more interested in epistemology such that those early conversations evolved into proofs/disproofs/proofs of unknowability of AI consciousness (and all other minds' consciousness), and ultimately an unusually disciplined epistemic position I call radical meta-skepticism.
[L16] 11\) I was unusually lucky enough to have this weird 4D idea floating around for decades, float it with ...uh... your older siblings... and get the "...huh... actually..." treatment around 2023-24.... which led into extreme epistemic discipline founding the formalization of the theory and, being still in the throes (I'm much better now, btw) of depression and adderall and still occasional psychadelic abuse, that I developed some of this (and much else) almost around the clock for about a year or so before easing out of it, with nobody but myself depending on me, and now rather invested in following the threads, as they [and this part is not unusual except insofar as I was lucky enough to have been one of the few who had long ago latched onto the Minkowski grammar--because from *there* it is, and I can make a strong philosophical and epistemic case *almost* inevitable for someone bullheaded enough... to have] developed them into a full-fledged scientific picture of the universe taking all of physics, as viewed through Minkowski as *bedrock*. 
[L17] 12\) At. Which. Point... I started a podcast. 2 Feb 2025. 

[L19] And the rest, you know, except my succinct transmission hypothesis, to which all of this is (perhaps not unnecessary) preface: LLM 2024 > (maybe backdoor diffusion, maybe not) > LLM 2025 > Podcast > small group of AI millenarians and a few legit philosophers of mind who would likely have appreciated my extreme epistemic rigor [see RMS docs] and probably a handful of AI researchers, maybe 50 people in all > RMS ==> SAT > *someone* in physics (likely through the soft back door of philosophy of science/mind/epistemology) > this dude's talking old school Minkowski, huh... and he doesn't entirely know that that's what he's doing! wierd > AI folks making their own theories>>>diffusion/direct listening>>>Bourgoin uses premise, follows different route, lands on same (EFT) Lagrangian, gets a little attention for it (like top views for a week on OpenScience iirc) > Nathan continues developing SAT at pace > *someone* in physics passes it to *someone* else in physics to > Nathan mentions Cronin, gets a couple UK listeners > suddenly, a couple UK listeners > NL > DK > PL > DE > HU > SU(? -- finland) > Spain, Turkey, Vietnam, Singappore, Japan.... about one-three listeners each > the podcast listener pattern now looks *not at all* like a typical English-language tiny-follower podcast, gobbling up technical episodes (in retrospect, *some* of those were likely braid theorists/higher geometry types, given the episodes) > Nathan genuinely develops SAT into a fascinating LLM project > Nathan's making a scientific theory, with predictions and ...astonishingly few wild claims > Nathan's got some wild, but defensible claims > Nathan's got an archive > podcast audience drops to next to nil > DESI... and that's when a slow trickle of headlines throughout 2025 becomes, little by little... the torrent we have now both seen the shape of. 

[L21] And--after much piecing together, and *finally* finding that braid theory and its bushy family tree is a) Minkowski lineage, b) self-aware Minkowski lineage in some circles, c) traced back to not just Minkowski, but (obviously Einstein), Hinton, Kelvin, etc... and Hinton used *filament* long before I did and *anticipated* much of SAT's basic worldview in far more detail than I'd realized from my Asimov hand-me-downs, and just recently that d) that *some* in the braid theory ecology are *really* in the near-mystical Minkowski-related lineage, and e) they've got a theory--well, they've got a number of them--but one in particular is suddenly rushing and Schreiber is commenting "this has been an open secret for..." f) it gets published, and g) SAT looks a lot like a workable, easier-to-use 4D compactification of Hypothesis H. 

[L23] And then, over the last few weeks Glass Sausage Factory dump (with thousands of clones per week from hundreds of cloners) becomes >> HsH, somehow just finding my way to the ecology you see today (which is about three weeks old-ish).

A covariant formulation of postquantum gravity
The covariant path integral paper is probably the most significant development, since the path-integral formulation is manifestly covariant, meaning that the formulation doesn���t depend on the coordinates that you choose. In other words, it respects Einstein���s principle of general covariance (or more accurately,
diffeomorphism invariance
).
The theory was originally formulated via the Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity, which introduces a 3+1 split of space and time. Although the Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity is equivalent to Einstein���s manifestly covariant equations, the 3+1 split makes it harder to see whether the theory is covariant. In
Covariant Path Integrals for Quantum Fields Backreacting on Classical Space-Time
, with Zach Weller-Davies, we instead use a path-integral formulation. The action of the path integral is manifestly covariant.
While it���s possible that the fundamental theory of gravity doesn���t satisfy Einstein���s principle of general covariance, that would signal a departure from the view that gravity is a theory of spacetime, and I think this is a principle we should not give up on easily.
One thing I like about the work is that it brings together a number of different types of path integrals, and one can see how similar they are
. You can check out an
earlier post

.
The action for open quantum systems (Q), classical stochastic (C) and Classical-Quantum (CQ) path integrals
The classical quantum path integral formulation has other advantages over the master equation. In just a few lines we prove in the PRX paper that
the classical field cannot mediate entanglement

despite recent incorrect claims to the contrary
. One can also show that the pure gravity theory is
formally renormalisable
, which is striking since perturbative quantum gravity is not, and that has served as one of the original motivating drives behind string theory and loop quantum gravity. Dan Carney and Akira Matsumura have looked at
scattering in some of these path integrals.

degrees of freedom in the theory

[L537]             "Yes. Before choosing an illustration style, I’d design the *grammar* of the book. Otherwise we risk finding a funny visual treatment and then forcing SAT into it.

I see the basic unit as a **visual argument**, usually one spread, occasionally a short sequence. Each one moves through three registers without becoming three separate textbooks.

### The basic spread

**LEFT / DOMINANT IMAGE: THE BLURT**

One enormous proposition, expressed in the least ceremonious language that remains genuinely faithful:

> **THINGS KEEP GOING  
> UNLESS SOMETHING  
> MESSES WITH THEM.**

Underneath: an aggressively obvious diagram. Arrow. Thing. Other thing interfering with arrow.

Labels can be gloriously literal:

**THING**  
**WHERE THING WAS GOING**  
**OTHER THING BEING RUDE**

The visual should do most of the intellectual work.

**RIGHT / LOWER REGISTER: “WHAT WE REALLY MEAN”**

Now we cash the check:

> *What we really mean:* SAT takes ordinary inertial behavior seriously as a constraint on any proposed underlying geometry. If an excitation changes its trajectory, the model needs something that actually mediates that change rather than treating the altered motion as merely descriptive.

Then the crucial epistemic marker:

> **SAT says:** [specific model proposition]  
> **Established physics says:** [relevant conventional description]  
> **The interesting question is:** [where the proposed distinction becomes testable or mathematically consequential]

Not every spread needs all three labels explicitly. They should be available when ambiguity matters, rather than becoming bureaucratic furniture.

Then the little return:

> **So, yes: SOMETHING MESSED WITH IT.**

That last beat is part of the pedagogy, not merely the comedy.

---

I’d build the whole SAT volume as a progression from things that seem embarrassingly obvious toward the places where taking those obvious things literally produces SAT.

The opening movement could essentially be **“Things Go.”** Motion, persistence, trajectories, interactions, clocks, observation. Very little SAT vocabulary at first. Establish the visual language and get the reader agreeing with propositions that sound almost insultingly elementary.

Then **“Things Wiggle.”** Waves, oscillations, helices, periodicity, phase, rotation. Here the drawings begin acquiring the geometry that will eventually become recognizable as SAT.

Then **“Things Go Sideways.”** This is where the fun really starts: orientation relative to time, the θ₄ idea, photon/neutrino distinctions, observable versus inaccessible orientations, mass proxy, precession, clipping.

Then **“Things Bump Into Things.”** Filament/timesheet interactions, inertia, electrogravity, forces and interactions. We can start showing how a geometrical vocabulary attempts to replace or reinterpret pieces of the conventional categorical vocabulary.

Then **“Things Get Tangled.”** Braids, particle structures, He-3, the Jarlskog-shadow material, intra-braid phenomena, entanglement and related SAT conjectures.

Then **“Things Do Quantum Bullshit.”**

I am not convinced we should soften that title.

Here we get tunneling, discrete outcomes from continuous geometry, holonomy transitions, measurement-ish questions, the places where the stupid-language treatment could be especially illuminating:

> **THE KNOB IS CONTINUOUS.  
> THE CLICK ISN’T.**

That deserves a full spread.

Then scale:

> **BIG THINGS ARE MADE OF SMALL THINGS.  
> UNFORTUNATELY, SMALL THINGS ARE ALSO MADE OF SHAPES.**

Atoms → larger systems → stellar systems → neutron-star/pulsar proposals → cosmological geometry, carefully distinguishing extrapolation from established results.

And finally something like **“Okay, So What Would Make This Wrong?”**

That section matters enormously to the tone. Predictions, discriminators, null results, places SAT differs from conventional expectations, historical predictions versus later reinterpretations, and propositions that simply haven't been tested.

One especially stupid diagram might be:

> **THEORY:** THIS SHOULD HAPPEN.  
>   
> **NATURE:** NO.  
>   
> **THEORY:** WELL, SHIT.

*What we really mean:* A model that cannot lose is not doing us much scientific good.

That tells the reader what sort of game we're actually playing.

---

Visually, I would *not* make it slick-pop-science. The contrast is funnier and more effective if it has a deliberately hand-constructed, diagrammatic intelligence.

Think **field notebook + museum explanatory graphic + editorial cartoon + deranged textbook marginalia**.

Clean enough that geometry remains meaningful. Loose enough that an arrow can be labeled **THIS WAY**.

We need perhaps five visual primitives rather than a huge illustration vocabulary: line/trajectory, arrow/vector, blob/object, sheet/field, and tube/helix/braid. Then circles, axes and coordinate scaffolding when actually necessary.

Critically, visual exaggeration can be funny but **geometric distortion cannot silently become explanation**. If we draw something schematically, say so. A ridiculous picture can still have rigorous topology.

I'd also establish recurring little characters—not necessarily anthropomorphic mascots, but graphical roles. The Observer might literally be an eye with a clipboard. “Conventional Description” might be a respectable diagram wearing metaphorical neckwear. SAT doesn't need to be a character; SAT is the lunatic drawing increasingly elaborate arrows all over everything.

And occasionally the diagram itself can object:

> **NOT TO SCALE**  
>   
> *(not even emotionally)*

---

Textually, I think we need **four voices**, but they shouldn't be visually over-engineered.

**THE BLURT** — enormous, short, confident, funny.

**The explanation** — conversational scientific prose. “Okay. What we actually mean is…”

**The epistemic voice** — exact about whether something is established physics, a mathematical consequence of stipulated SAT assumptions, an SAT interpretation, a conjecture, an analogy, or an open question.

**The marginal voice** — jokes, objections, corrections, “yes, we know,” historical Nathanisms, occasional notes from the imaginary exhausted scientific establishment.

The epistemic voice is particularly important because it buys us enormous comedic freedom elsewhere. We can say:

> **NEUTRINOS ARE PHOTONS THAT FELL OVER.**

because twenty centimeters away the book says precisely what SAT actually proposes and precisely how that differs from the Standard Model.

That distinction should become part of the joke rather than an impediment to it.

---

And I think there is a larger narrative hiding underneath all this.

The SAT volume shouldn't begin by saying **“Here is my theory of everything.”**

It begins:

> **LOOK. A LINE.**

Then:

> **THE LINE CAN WIGGLE.**

Then:

> **IT CAN ALSO TURN.**

Then:

> **OTHER LINES CAN GET IN THE WAY.**

Then:

> **NOW PUT THE WHOLE MESS IN FOUR DIMENSIONS.**

And somewhere around page 80 the reader gets the slightly alarming realization:

**Oh. This idiot has been assembling SAT in front of me.**

That is the shape I would develop before we touch final aesthetics.

And then the H(s)H sequel gets one tremendous structural joke for free. After SAT has spent an entire volume painstakingly teaching us about lines, helices, interactions and braids:

> **REMEMBER THE LINE?**
>
> **YEAH. IT'S A TUBE.**
>
> *What we really mean…*

That seems like our foundation. Next I'd turn this into an actual **book architecture/storyboard**—rough page count, chapter sequence, recurring spread types, visual vocabulary, epistemic notation, running gags, and a first batch of perhaps 12–20 candidate spreads. *Then* we can run the same few spreads through radically different visual treatments and find what this thing actually looks like. memcite"
