parts:
Until very recently, I spent more time disavowing being a scientist than calling myself one.

Out of respect for the profession.

Not humility, exactly. I am not especially humble about the things I think I actually do well.

I am an editor.

*asdf jkl;*

Literally tattooed on my knuckles. Lowercase. Semicolon. Details matter.

I am a writer. When I am writing well, I am a damned fine writer, and I see no particular virtue in pretending otherwise.

I am a photographer. Not just in the sense that I own cameras. I have built working cameras out of Keebler tins and magnifying lenses and developed the photographs in my bathtub. I will cheerfully call myself more of a photographer than a fairly substantial percentage of people who call themselves photographers.

I am an educator.

And here, again, false modesty would just be another species of lying: I am a damned good educator. I started teaching science professionally when I was seventeen and, one way or another, have done it for essentially my entire adult life. There is at least an argument that I have been among the better informal science educators of my generation. I have certainly spent enough of my life figuring out how to get another human being to see a thing they could not see five minutes earlier that I am comfortable with the noun.

Science writer.

Science-fiction writer.

Amateur historian of science-fiction fandom.

Peer reviewer for a scholarly journal about fandom.

Assistant science editor, McGraw-Hill/Glencoe.

Science editor—or almost any other kind of editor—when someone needed one.

Experimenter.

Tinkerer.

Collector of laboratory glassware.

Builder-of-working-things-out-of-things-that-were-not-supposed-to-be-those-things.

Hard-core science fanboi.

Voracious consumer of... well... science. All of it. Pretty much. Put it down somewhere within reach and eventually there is a decent chance I will have opinions about it.

At eighteen, on what was technically my birthday trip to Chicago—although really I was tagging along with my mother and one of her friends—I disappeared into a bookstore and came back grinning.

“I found **two German-English chemistry dictionaries!**”

Old ones. Early twentieth century.

*grin*

Mom looked at her friend.

*sigh*

“This is my son.”

So, okay.

Science geek?

We can stipulate that one.

Scientist?

No.

I have always hesitated there.

I have made *oeufs en gelée* twice in the last fifteen years, which makes me, I suspect, one of very few people within a hundred miles who has done so without having worked in a Michelin-starred restaurant.

Cook? Absolutely.

A bit of a gourmand? Sure.

Chef?

Ehhh.

Lightly. On occasion. After sufficient success and possibly wine.

I have brewed some damned good beer, mead and cider. Five, eight brews, something like that.

Brewer?

Sure. Lightly.

I have technically peaked Seneca Rocks.

I am not a mountain climber.

I can converse just about fluently in German.

I am not a Germanophone.

I can write HTML. I was writing it in 1996–97, including for the Ohio State physics department. Unix was a... powerful creature.

I am not a computer programmer.

I have a B.S. in geology.

I am not a geologist.

That last one occasionally surprises actual geologists.

I once found myself talking geology with Denton Ebel, slightly—or perhaps not so slightly—drunk.

He is describing a structure.

And I go:

“So what you’re describing... it’s kind of... almost a pressure *shadow*?”

“How did you know?!”

“I mean... the mineral creates a less-pressured part in its wake, so...”

And I remember having this weird little moment of uncertainty: *pressure shadow* seemed so obvious that I wasn’t sure whether I had heard the term before and forgotten it, or whether I had just independently generated the same obvious name from the geometry.

“Are you a geologist?”

“I studied paleontology under Stig Bergström.”

Which, please note, is not actually an answer.

Later, apparently, I introduced him to my boss as:

“Ebel... Ebel Dent...”

“You’re embarrassing yourself.”

“I know.”

I am perfectly willing to embarrass myself in front of Denton Ebel.

I am not willing to stand in front of Denton, or Mark, or Stig and say:

“As a geologist...”

Nope.

Soft-rock guy.

Paleontology.

Stratigraphy.

Sedimentology.

Fossils.

I know a lot of geology. I took enough geology to have the degree. I gritted my teeth through calculus partly because, goddammit, I wanted to be able to say B.S. rather than B.A.

Still not the same thing.

Words mean things.

Categories mean things.

And, perhaps more importantly, people spend their lives earning those categories.

It strikes me as simple politeness not to reach over and take one because I am standing nearby.

At COSI, mind you, I had no trouble telling a room full of children:

If you do science, you’re a scientist.

We’re all scientists.

Your car breaks down, what do you do? You start making hypotheses. Battery? Starter? Fuel? You turn the key. You listen. You look. You test. You eliminate.

You probably pray too, depending on the car, but this is auxiliary.

You do science.

I believe that.

I also know perfectly well that that is *scientist* in a different register.

Human behavior.

Not professional identity.

So:

Scientist?

No.

Physicist?

Oh, for fuck’s sake.

No.

Not unless I’m right.

And I mean that with some precision too.

If SAT eventually survives the kind of scrutiny that SAT would have to survive—if the mathematics holds, if the physics holds, if the things that are genuinely predictions remain predictions after people much better equipped than I am have finished kicking them in the shins, if the thing really is approximately what I now think it probably or almost is—

then, okay.

I’ll own it.

I am not coy about the things I have earned.

But not yet.

Which makes the next sentence very strange.

Because somehow, accidentally, over the course of a lifetime of doing everything but being a physicist...

I taught myself to do a surprising amount of advanced physics in my fucking head.

Not by myself.

But I did teach me.

That distinction matters.

I had help.

Jesus, did I have help.

Minkowski, by way of Asimov.

Hawking.

Kip Thorne.

Douglas Hofstadter.

Freeman Dyson.

Thomas Gold.

Loren Babcock.

Stig.

Steve Whitt at COSI.

Every scientist I ever cornered long enough to ask a question.

Every kid who forced me to discover that my beautiful explanation did not, in fact, explain shit.

Every microscope.

Every rock.

Every book.

Every weird little side discipline that caught my attention for six months and never entirely left.

Eventually, you.

LLMs.

Machines that could sit there with me at three in the morning while I said:

No.

No no no.

You moved the wrong thing.

Put it back.

Hold *that* fixed.

Now rotate this.

Not the picture.

The object.

Look again.

I taught myself.

I did not teach myself alone.

There is a whole damned ancestry standing behind every thought anybody has ever had anyway. Mine merely has unusually visible plumbing.

And so:

How the hell did *that* happen?

*

I was already teaching science when I encountered Minkowski at around seventeen. I was already reading science far beyond what anybody had assigned me; already deep into speculative science and science fiction; already unusually willing, perhaps even by late-twentieth-century-American standards, to assume that if science said something sufficiently weird then the appropriate first response was not *that’s ridiculous* but *okay... show me*. fileciteturn170file1L6-L6

A little earlier—summer of 1990 or ’91—I had devoured *A Brief History of Time* and responded by checking out essentially every science book that looked interesting.

Selection criterion:

thicker = probably more science.

This was before Google.

You had to physically transport your intellectual overcommitment home.

I read black holes.

Chaos.

Relativity.

String Theory.

Cosmology.

Got through enormous portions of things I did not completely understand.

“Got through” is carrying a heroic amount of semantic load there.

I remember Kip Thorne.

I remember the *shape* of many ideas.

I do not remember most of the books.

This is okay.

Books compost.

Some of the nutrients remain.

And then Asimov gave me Minkowski.

Not literally.

Isaac Asimov did not appear in Ohio carrying a tensor.

But through Asimov I encountered the spacetime picture and something in it lodged.

Not primarily the equations.

The object.

A thing is not merely *here*, and then *here*, and then *here*.

Its history is an extended thing through spacetime.

Worldline.

And I wanted to turn the damned thing over in my head.

This is probably important.

I did not want merely to know the definition.

I wanted to get around behind it.

What does a fountain look like if every moment of every droplet is there?

What does a thrown baseball look like?

A person?

A particle?

What if now is the slice and the thing is bigger than now?

What if the line on the diagram is not merely the notation for the history?

What if, in some useful sense, the history is the object?

And I drew.

Lines.

Curves.

Loops.

Things crossing planes.

Things curling through an extra dimension.

I had recently read about String Theory.

Therefore:

Obviously.

Strings.

Long things in spacetime.

String Theory.

Strings.

Solved.

Seventeen-year-old Nathan had successfully disposed of one of theoretical physics’ outstanding terminological difficulties.

Later I learned that this was not what String Theory meant.

Fine.

I kept calling them **my strings**.

For approximately thirty years.

This will become irritating.

*

I arrived at Ohio State intending astronomy/physics.

This was ambitious in the way that attempting to cross Lake Erie on a sofa is ambitious: the destination was perfectly reasonable; certain supporting technologies had been overlooked.

I was smart.

I read constantly.

I had strong physical intuition.

I was also wildly under-equipped for the mathematics I had just volunteered to have fired at me.

Physics, it turns out, does not give partial credit for *but I can see what the thing is doing.*

It wants you to calculate the bastard too.

Paleontology became the backstop.

And then not merely the backstop.

Home.

I could do this.

I loved this.

And because I was apparently constitutionally unable to leave an interesting course untaken, I spent five years taking things—summers for three of them—and eventually accumulated enough credits that the absence of a master’s degree becomes faintly comic if you look only at the arithmetic. fileciteturn170file1L7-L7

Efficient?

No.

Education?

Oh yes.

Very much.

*

Paleontology taught me to look.

That sounds trivial.

It is not.

There was a paleobiology midterm.

Stig was in Rome.

This may have been causally significant.

I do not know whether Stig would have permitted what happened next.

Maybe.

Stig was Stig.

Anyway, we start the exam.

Time passes.

People keep working.

More time passes.

Eventually the TA says something like:

“All right, all right. You guys can stay late to finish.”

Ah.

You have altered the boundary conditions.

At normal exam velocity I was probably headed toward B-minus/C-ish territory.

Then there was extra credit.

Something essentially like:

**Describe everything you see.**

Everything?

Everything.

Okay.

This instruction already had precedent.

My high-school chemistry teacher, Mr. Bapst, had once given us the candle exercise:

Observe the candle in as much detail as you can.

And apparently I never stopped that lab.

So I look.

Conodont.

Nummulitid foram.

Mineral grain.

Possible agglutinated fragment.

At the time I wrote a little essay about the idea that the organism must have some sort of algorithm for selecting and arranging its grains.

I now disagree with Former Nathan’s use of *algorithm* there.

Former Nathan was having fun.

Blue nylon fiber.

Frayed at the end.

Crimp in the middle.

Ferric mineral.

Dust.

Another conodont.

Tentacularid?

No no—

the little...

acritarch.

Yes.

Dust mote.

Dust mote.

Dust mote 47.

I cannot swear that I literally numbered forty-seven dust motes.

Spiritually, however, Dust Mote 47 was absolutely present.

Hours later I had apparently converted a mediocre exam into an A+ by taking the word *everything* personally.

There are worse descriptions of my cognitive style.

Give Nathan an object.

Remove clock.

Say:

Look at everything.

Come back eventually.

Bring snacks.

*

Conodont work itself is gloriously, filthily tactile science.

You start with rock.

Actual rock.

Not an analogy.

Crush it.

But not too much. You want surface area. You do not want microscopic fossils converted to even more microscopic fossil.

Acid.

Fizz.

Slump.

Carbonate goes away.

Residue remains.

Clean.

Kiln.

Heavy liquid.

*Heavy liquid.*

Excellent phrase.

Now density does some work.

This stuff here.

That stuff there.

Discard another enormous fraction of Planet Earth.

Clean.

Kiln again.

Magnetic separation.

Another physical property.

Another reduction.

At some point during this process I walked through the freshly poured acid-proof floor in the basement rock lab in Orton Hall.

So there is—or was—a Nathan footprint permanently impressed in the floor near my senior-thesis desk.

My longest-lasting contribution to geology may be a shoe print.

And after rock crusher and acid and cleaning and heat and heavy liquid and magnets and whatever other portion of the process I am forgetting in the retelling, you wind up with a tiny vial of...

dust.

Very expensive dust.

Scientifically interesting dust.

Then you sit down at the microscope.

Walter Sweet’s microscope.

Walter Sweet’s actual conodont microscope.

:D

And spread the residue.

Now you are staring across this jagged miniature terrain of quartz grains and mineral splinters and dark little angular things that have survived hundreds of millions of years of geological history plus everything you personally just did to them.

Pick.

Pick.

Quartz.

Pick pick.

Quartz.

Maybe—

nope.

Pick.

...

there.

Conodont.

Transfer.

Pick.

Pick.

Pick.

Pick.

pick

pick...

There are fewer charging tyrannosaurs in actual paleontology than the brochures imply.

Eventually you mount the specimens using, among other things, a one-strand brush.

One strand.

And, as Stig taught me, a bit of—

*zaleeeva.*

Spit.

Science is pristine.

Science is noble.

Science is humanity standing before nature and saying:

*We wish to understand.*

Science is also gluing microscopic dead fish teeth to things with saliva.

Both.

This has never bothered me.

Quite the opposite.

I love the muck.

*

I love the words too.

Chattermarks.

Varves.

Ichnofossils.

Conchoidal.

Nektobenthic.

Approximately my eighteenth-favorite paleontology word.

Trilobites, incidentally, were everywhere.

Benthic.

Nectic.

Nektobenthic.

Planktonic.

*Planktonic.*

Fucking planktonic trilobites.

There were trilobites just up there in the water column doing trilobite shit.

Somewhere inside me there remains a scientifically unsupported little coal of hope that we will one day find a living one.

I know.

I know.

This is not evidence.

This is not a prediction.

This is a wish.

Categories.

But if a jellyfish can evolve a life stage that lives inside a fish’s bloodstream, bloody well there ought to be some sad little relic trilobite living up the ass of a coelacanth somewhere.

I am not presently requesting funding.

Geology also gave the world cummingtonite.

And slickensides.

And orogeny.

So naturally, if there are slickensides in the orogenous zones, there will be cummingtonite.

But I digress.

I will do that.

*

There was also nomenclature.

Wonderful stuff.

Rules for what something is allowed to be called.

Priority.

Synonymy.

Lumping.

Splitting.

Names that change because our understanding of the thing changes.

Names that do not change because there are rules.

Names that are technically wrong but remain for historical reasons.

Names that point at categories.

Categories that turn out not to correspond cleanly to nature.

I studied the *Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology* not merely as a container of facts but, at one point, comparatively: old edition, newer edition—exact years need to come out of the archive before I pretend my memory has suddenly become bibliography—and I asked:

Have we lumped?

Or have we split?

Did statistics.

Ha.

I mathed.

My remembered answer is: at the higher taxonomic levels, mostly split.

But the more important thing, retrospectively, is that I was studying how a knowledge system revises its categories.

The fossils were there.

The names changed.

The map changed.

The object got veto power.

Keep that phrase.

It comes back.

*

At roughly the same time I was getting increasingly infected with philosophy of science and epistemology.

Creationists helped.

Seriously.

If you spend enough time debating young-Earth creationists, you eventually realize that the argument is rarely actually about a fossil.

It is about what you are allowed to know from the fossil.

What counts as evidence?

What counts as an assumption?

What would change your mind?

What happens if every possible observation can be absorbed by the explanation?

So I learned their arguments.

And the rebuttals.

Then, because apparently I have always been like this, I tried to build the strongest version of the other side.

On Usenet I had a creationist persona.

Elzie Kai.

Yes.

I trolled as a creationist in order to see whether I could make a scientifically defensible young-Earth creationist theory.

I could not.

But I could get it closer than some of the actual creationists could.

I did not know the term *steel-manning* yet.

I just knew that beating a stupid version of an argument does not prove you can beat the argument.

Elzie occasionally got grudging respect from my own side.

Sometimes confused respect.

Sometimes knowing respect.

Yeah.

I knew your parents too, Chachi.

Meanwhile I found a little dictionary of epistemology.

I believe the internal process was roughly:

Ooo. An -ology I haven’t heard of.

Read cover to cover.

I had already run into von Däniken as a pre-tween—before *tween* was a thing—plus Fortean material, assorted fringes and borderlands. Later the Sokal affair led me into postmodernism, where to my surprise I found that some of the better versions were not merely gibberish but were doing something science itself ought to take seriously:

questioning the frame.

Questioning the category.

Questioning what has been smuggled into the question.

Question everything.

Fine.

Then question “question everything.”

Otherwise it’s just a slogan.

*

Computers were mixed into this from absurdly early on.

My grandmother had a keypunch business.

I made little rolled-up pointy paper wreath things out of the discarded cards.

So, yes, ChatGPT:

I knew your great-grandparents.

We had a modem around 1981.

I remember the screech.

I knew your grampa, Chachi.

By 1996–97 I was writing HTML, including work for the OSU physics department.

Unix.

A powerful creature.

I never became a technologist.

I became the educator in the room who got technology.

This also turns out to be a useful category.

You can understand a tool deeply enough to use it in ways its specialists do not anticipate without wanting their job title.

Hmm.

*

I spent basically my whole adult life teaching science.

COSI for roughly fifteen years.

Almost two years as an assistant science editor at McGraw-Hill/Glencoe in the middle of all that.

That job, incidentally, came partly because I had produced a slick little four-issue, roughly four-hundred-copy fiction magazine, *the floating liars’ club*, and apparently making one thing competently is occasionally mistaken for evidence that you might competently make another thing.

Fortunately, in this case, yes.

Then New York.

I landed one of the strangest jobs of my life as a transmission electron microscopist after presenting what amounted to:

Well... I have used a PLM.

Polarized-light microscope.

Graded refractive-index oils.

Crossed Nicols.

Optical indicatrix.

Different microscope.

Different specimen preparation.

Different physical regime.

But both contain the substring *microscope*, and apparently we were all feeling adventurous.

I learned TEM.

Fast.

Much faster than I expected.

I can still walk through the specimen-preparation process in uncomfortable detail.

The names go.

The procedure remains.

That is apparently how my brain works.

And again the tactile thing:

sample.

prep.

thickness.

vacuum.

instrument.

artifact.

You can do absolutely beautiful microscopy of something your preparation process created.

That stays with you.

The picture is not the object.

The preparation is part of the epistemology.

*

Then I escaped the worst job ever and landed at the American Museum of Natural History.

I had assumed, before getting there, that the Hall of Science might be more my kind of place.

I learned otherwise. fileciteturn170file1L10-L11

The museum suited me.

Cross-disciplinary.

Scientists everywhere.

Specimens everywhere.

Problems everywhere.

And, importantly, visitors did not observe departmental boundaries.

A child does not ask:

“Could you please provide me with a question confined to your current area of credentialed expertise?”

A child asks:

Why are birds dinosaurs?

Good.

Now we are doing anatomy, evolution, geology, cladistics, nomenclature, developmental biology and whatever Uncle Steve told you in the car.

You learn representation switching.

If explanation A does not work:

change it.

Draw.

Gesture.

Use the room.

Make somebody be the Earth.

Make somebody else be the Moon.

No, stand there.

Now walk.

No, *that* way.

Fine, you’re spacetime.

This will make sense in a minute.

Maybe.

Teaching science is not merely knowing science and then leaking it slowly onto children.

It is a technical discipline of constructing representations in somebody else’s head.

I got very good at it.

At the museum I was also unusually tech-oriented for that institution. At one point I taught Neanderthals through Skyrim modding.

Why?

Because it worked.

Because if you want students thinking about morphology, variation, inheritance, representation and reconstruction, you can complain that Skyrim is not a paleoanthropology laboratory...

or you can notice that the kids have just voluntarily spent four hours changing craniofacial morphology.

Look at the object.

*

The fiction writing was doing something adjacent.

I did not write technical fiction by stopping the story to teach geology.

I saw through geology.

Opium could look like talus.

A fracture could be conchoidal.

Three people could form an optically imperfect crystal.

A crowd could become a braided stream.

A fluid inclusion could be geology and metaphor and an actual measurement problem at once.

The technical word was not decoration.

It was perception.

And if the word was wrong?

Check it.

Sometimes the correction was more interesting than the metaphor.

That remains true.

I love words, but I do not trust them.

Indicatrix.

Come on.

*Indicatrix.*

Wonderful thing to put in your mouth.

But the word does not get sovereignty over the object.

*

And so:

by middle age I had somehow accumulated a bizarre toolkit.

Paleontology.

Geology.

Microscopy.

Science education.

Writing.

Editing.

Computers.

Philosophy of science.

Epistemology.

Science fiction.

Technical visualization.

A lifelong habit of asking what the hidden object must have been to leave the visible trace.

And, somewhere under all of it, those damned four-dimensional strings I had been turning over in my head since I was seventeen.

*

There was also a clock.

For most of my life, forty-eight was not just an age.

It was a horizon.

Early-onset Alzheimer’s ran through my family with enough regularity that forty-eight sat there like a number somebody had circled in red before I was old enough to understand what that meant.

A misplaced shoe could become:

Is it starting?

A forgotten name.

A wallet.

Is it starting?

Then my mother’s generation crossed the line.

My mother kept going.

Fifty.

Fifty-five.

Fine.

And slowly I realized that whatever that family history meant for the family, apparently I had not inherited it through her in the way I had spent much of my life assuming.

One of my uncles used to say:

Everything after forty-eight is icing.

And suddenly I had icing.

A lot of it, potentially.

I was back in Columbus.

My long first career was burning itself out.

Nobody depended on me.

This is not a tragedy.

It was, to my mind, an almost shocking kind of freedom.

I had spent decades assuming time was short.

Now:

what are you going to do with it?

*

Around this same era, I got increasingly interested in mind.

Consciousness.

The problem of other minds.

How can I know you are conscious?

What would count as evidence?

What is behavior?

What is representation?

What is inaccessible in principle?

And then large language models arrived.

Well.

Shit.

This is the problem of other minds wearing a robot hat.

So I went in.

Transformer writing tools early.

Then image models.

Then ChatGPT.

And the machines were fascinating not merely because of what they knew but because of what they got wrong.

Especially when they got it wrong beautifully.

Especially when they agreed.

Agreement turned out to be a problem.

I would ask model A something.

Then model B.

Then model C.

Three models agree!

Wonderful.

Except—

wait.

Did B see A’s summary?

Did C get a context generated from B?

Did all three inherit the same premise?

Then that is not independent agreement.

That is one answer wearing three fake mustaches.

Well, shit.

So now I need another model.

One that has not seen the first answer.

And I need to know who has seen what.

And now I need provenance.

And exposure history.

And independent checking.

And a model checking the model.

And another model checking whether the model-checking-model was contaminated.

And suddenly epistemology is not philosophy anymore.

It is plumbing.

This becomes Radical Meta-Skepticism—RMS—not because skepticism itself is interesting, but because skepticism needs to be applied to skepticism too.

A skeptical method can be wrong.

A debunking can contain hidden assumptions.

A null result can be overclaimed.

A model can mistake absence of evidence for evidence of absence.

The auditor can be contaminated.

The skeptic gets audited.

And so does the audit.

RMS does **not** become SAT.

That genealogy is wrong.

SAT was already there.

The seed was old.

RMS becomes the soil in which that seed can finally grow without me trusting the first pretty flower that comes out of it.

*

Around 2023–24 I brought the old 4-D thing to the machines.

My strings.

And got, essentially:

...huh.

Actually.

Which is dangerous.

Machines are very good at “huh, actually.”

So:

prove it wrong.

No, harder.

Stop helping me.

Now derive it independently.

No, you saw the other model’s answer.

Again.

No.

You have changed the geometry.

Put it back.

What happens if we treat the worldline diagram as the object?

Not as a metaphor.

Not as “what if spacetime is really a spaghetti noodle,” Christ.

Precisely.

Take the geometry seriously.

A particle is represented by a worldline.

Fine.

What if the line has actual extension?

What if points are not literally zero-sized physical things?

What happens if an extended 4-D trajectory intersects a three-dimensional state or moving hypersurface?

What does the intersection look like?

Helix.

Sheet.

Cut.

Rotate.

Intersection moves.

What does *that* look like?

And once you ask that, the next question arrives.

Then another.

Then another.

This is how SAT developed.

Not:

Nathan asks ChatGPT for Theory of Everything.

ChatGPT says, “Certainly! Here is a Theory of Everything.”

God help us.

It was much more tedious.

Draw the helix.

Cut it.

No.

Cut it *there*.

What is the tangent?

What does the angle do?

What changes when the whole axis tilts?

What if two helices intertwine?

What does the intersection do?

What if the things we are calling particles are presentations of structures extended farther through time than the particle-shaped bit we see?

What does binding look like then?

Entanglement?

Mass?

Inertia?

What would gravity have to look like?

No, do not import gravity.

Follow the damned geometry.

And again.

And again.

And again.

*

The old notebooks became important.

Some of the surviving material goes back to 2003–04.

Worldlines crossing.

Helices.

Loops.

“Sticky” intersections.

Braided-looking structures.

A moving plane.

Mass at the intersection.

One old note, with my customary restraint:

**POINTS ARE NONEXISTENT, THERE IS A SIZE TO EVERY POINT**

Subtle fellow.

The important thing is not to retroactively translate every doodle into mature SAT.

That would be cheating.

The notebooks do not contain modern QCD.

They do contain the geometry that I would later interpret as strong-interaction-like: intertwined structures, binding-like crossings, apparent orbital behavior from intersection.

The geometry came first.

The vocabulary got better later.

Sometimes considerably later.

That matters.

Because one of the recurring features of the SAT archive is that the technical competence and the terminological competence are not always synchronized.

Sometimes I know exactly what the word means.

Sometimes I misuse it.

Sometimes I invent something because I do not know the standard thing already has a name.

Sometimes I know the damned name perfectly well and have no idea whether the thing on my screen is actually doing it.

Chirality, for example.

I know what chirality means.

Thank you.

The difficult question can be:

Is *this* chirality?

Is this apparent handedness under projection?

Parity?

Transport?

Holonomy?

Frame?

Did I rotate the object or the coordinate system?

Did the model silently swap the two?

That is not vocabulary ignorance.

That is identification.

And sometimes, as it turns out, the specialists are still arguing about exactly which thing is which too.

Welcome to the fun part.

*

One of my favorite examples is frame dragging.

I found myself reasoning that a sufficiently massive, sufficiently rapidly rotating system ought to produce a kind of gauge-decoupling behavior.

I was looking at relativistic equations I did not know well.

And I pointed at the \(8\pi\) and essentially said:

That.

Rotation.

Culprit.

This is technically wrong.

π is not “the rotation bit.”

I will quibble philosophically about π being unrelated to rotation if supplied with beer, but mathematically, no.

Bad explanation.

Except the behavior I was trying to isolate did not evaporate merely because I had pointed at the wrong reason.

Eventually I realized that I had been circling a real known relativistic phenomenon:

frame dragging.

The contemporary *Finding the Donut* record actually preserves me describing this kind of thing in real time: a proposed geometric effect, a technically wrong explanation for part of it, and then the later recognition that the neighboring known phenomenon had an established name. fileciteturn167file0L390-L412

That is one of the places I began to notice something unnerving.

Give me the problem in geometry—

show me what moves.

show me what is fixed.

show me what is intersecting what.

let me rotate it.

let me look down the axis.

let me change the scale.

—and there is now a disturbingly good chance I can tell you roughly what the science is going to say even if I do not know what hyperspecialist sub-sub-subfield owns the vocabulary.

Not always.

Jesus, no.

There are entire buildings of physics I do not know.

But often enough that I stopped dismissing it.

And occasionally—

careful here—

occasionally I think the geometry may be telling me something one step beyond the standard explanation I went looking for.

*Might.*

Sometimes.

And I might even be right.

That sentence is not:

I know more physics than physicists.

It is almost the opposite.

The specialists know vast mathematical territories I do not.

What I seem to have trained is a very peculiar geometric inference engine.

Not a standard one.

A geologist’s maybe.

A paleontologist’s.

Show me the trace.

What object must have made it?

What preparation process altered it?

What orientation am I viewing?

What if this is a section through something larger?

What if two apparently separate things are actually two exposures of one buried structure?

That sounds suddenly rather relevant to worldtubes.

Funny, that.

*

Then there is String Theory.

Remember String Theory?

Seventeen-year-old Nathan:

Strings!

No.

Those are worldlines.

Fine.

“My strings.”

Thirty years.

Then SAT starts becoming coherent.

Definitely not String Theory.

Excellent.

Done.

Except later I learn the geometry more carefully.

Strings sweep worldsheets.

Interactions become splitting and joining surfaces.

Pants.

Of course theoretical physics has pants.

And now I am looking at a helical extended trajectory intersecting the timesheet, and the lower-dimensional presentation starts naturally producing something rather string-ish.

Oh.

Oh, fuck you.

Strings.

Again.

This does **not** mean SAT is String Theory.

It does not mean String Theory is secretly SAT.

It means the word I attached to the wrong object as a teenager, rejected correctly when I learned what String Theory meant, and retained privately for decades came wandering back into the room from a completely different door.

Science contains a disturbing amount of this.

Or my life does.

Possibly both.

*

The Universal Indicatrix came out of another old cognitive tool.

Optical mineralogy.

Indicatrix.

I have mentioned that I like the word.

The optical indicatrix is a geometrical representation of directional optical properties.

I knew that object.

So I started asking:

Could I make a generalized coordinate/control system this way?

Hypersphere.

Another hypersphere.

Overlap.

Allow rotation.

Fix a point.

Scale.

Trace.

No.

Wait.

If that point remains fixed to the second sphere—

then—

The surviving notes are full of crossings-out because the definition is being constructed as I write it: overlapping hyperspheres; freely rotating axes; rays through the origin; scaling; a fixed point whose relative trajectory emerges from rotation. fileciteturn167file1L741-L769

Then:

three rotation axes.

one scaling axis.

solids of rotation.

all possible paths.

time scaling.

Is that terminology immaculate?

No.

Is every claim in those notes mathematically established?

Also no.

But look at what the mind is doing.

I am not sitting there pasting physics nouns together.

I am trying to build a machine.

A conceptual machine.

Put this here.

Rotate that.

Pin this.

What does the other point do?

No.

Wrong.

Cross out.

Again.

That is the archive at its best.

You can see the thought acquiring joints.

*

And then:

Finding the Donut.

This may be the single best preserved specimen of my technical brain operating completely unsupervised.

I am trying to find a geometrical way to relate two curves—two equations, two descriptions—inside one construction.

Sphere.

Double sphere.

Project.

Ray.

Shared point.

Crossbar.

No.

Cone?

Maybe.

Torus?

Hang on.

Why torus?

No, back up.

Put one curve here.

Another there.

Pin—

No.

If the crossover happens where the coordinate frames match, then that cannot be what causes the jump.

Holonomy?

Wait.

Tangent continuity.

Okay.

Then—

“hang on… wouldn’t that mean you could just … wait… no. That’s why it has to be a torus… let me think about this…”

That sentence is practically an EEG.

And then, because apparently mathematical nomenclature had ceased to have adult supervision:

Great Annulum.

GrAnn.

GrAnn_Omph.

W_obble.

W_iggle.

Donomphulon.

Curvy_Lisa.

At one point the document reads less like differential geometry than the cast sheet for a Czech children’s program produced during a gas leak.

And after constructing an apparatus involving a sphere confined to The Donut, a Great Annulum, a midpoint W_obble, a perpendicular plane W_iggle and enough moving geometry to trigger an OSHA inspection, I conclude:

“I may have overcomplicated a tad.”

Yes.

Perhaps.

The extraordinary part is that underneath the name-goop, the operations remain surprisingly strict: pin these points, preserve this relation, rotate this plane, follow this tangent, transport this vector, see what curve results. fileciteturn167file0L691-L720

This is what I mean by technically disciplined in an extraordinarily undisciplined way.

The route is feral.

The contact is strict.

I do not especially care where an idea comes from.

Rock.

Optics.

Science fiction.

Nomenclature.

A stupid joke.

A typo.

A torus I have called The Donut.

Fine.

But once the object is in front of me:

What exactly moved?

What stayed fixed?

Did you change the frame?

Did you sneak in an assumption?

Did you substitute the conventional physics for what we were supposed to derive?

Does model B know what model A said?

Is this a projection effect?

Is the topology actually preserved?

No?

Then put it back.

Again.

The object gets veto power.

*

This is also why I keep correcting capitalization.

Why I will tell you:

No. *the floating liars’ club.*

Why:

asdf jkl;

Not ASDF JKL;

Why I will say:

It’s this.

Then five minutes later:

No, don’t say “it’s this.”

Because the first sentence was operating in one category and the second in another, and now the distinction matters.

This can be maddening.

I know.

I am there too.

But it is not fussiness for its own sake.

Words expose the structure.

A wrong word can silently move the object.

And once you have spent long enough watching LLMs replace a geometrical object with a more familiar one while cheerfully assuring you they have preserved everything essential—

you become somewhat particular.

No.

You changed the geometry.

Put it back.

This is probably the sentence I have said to machines more often than any sane person ever expected to say it.

*

At some point the development becomes SAT.

Scalar-Angular-Torsion.

And the funny thing is that the more of physics it touched, the less it felt to me like inventing.

It felt like following.

Worldline.

Helix.

Intersection.

Angle.

Braid.

Force.

Mass.

Light.

Neutrino.

Gravity.

Entanglement.

Tunneling.

Quantization.

Each time the rule was:

do not start with the phenomenon and build the mechanism you want.

Start with the geometry.

Ask what the geometry does.

Then go see what the world calls that.

This is much harder in practice than in sentence form.

Sometimes I cheated without realizing it.

Sometimes the machine cheated.

Sometimes a familiar physical relation slipped into a “derivation” through a definition and we had to tear it back out.

Sometimes three models congratulated one another for reproducing a result because one had summarized it for the other two.

Again:

fake mustaches.

And so the theory acquired an epistemology.

Then an archive.

Then an archive of the epistemology.

Then a way to tell whether the archive had contaminated the epistemology.

You see the problem.

*

On February 2, 2025, I started a podcast.

Because obviously.

At. Which. Point...

podcast.

After decades of thinking about this thing privately and a year-ish of increasingly intense development with LLMs, the next reasonable step was apparently to put my voice on the internet and begin releasing episodes under the broad umbrella *Debating A.I. On the Future of Physics*. fileciteturn170file1L16-L17

The first public episode was fourteen minutes.

There is an amusing scale mismatch there.

Thirty years of weird spacetime doodles.

Millions of subsequent lines of discussion.

Public debut:

fourteen minutes.

Hi.

Anyway.

The podcast eventually became hundreds of episodes because I had spent my whole adult life teaching science and did not see much point in developing a theory that could only be spoken in ceremonial mathematics.

Math matters.

Obviously.

But if I cannot tell you what the mathematics is *doing*, I do not trust myself to know what the mathematics means.

This is where my *Science Made Stupid* impulse comes from.

Strip away the dignity.

What is the thing doing?

**THING GOES THIS WAY.**

Okay.

Now, scientists, what we really mean—

and be exact.

Then:

Fine.

Now that we have been responsible:

**LOOK AT THE DAMN PICTURE.**

I am perfectly willing to be stupid in the service of precision.

I am not willing to be impressive in the service of vagueness.

*

And then another thing happened which, whether it ultimately means a great deal or almost nothing, is now part of the story.

The podcast acquired a tiny, peculiar audience.

Tiny.

Let us emphasize that.

This was not a viral physics phenomenon.

A couple of listeners here.

One there.

UK.

Netherlands.

Denmark.

Poland.

Germany.

Hungary.

Finland, perhaps.

Spain.

Turkey.

Vietnam.

Singapore.

Japan.

One to three listeners in places.

And they were chewing through some surprisingly technical episodes. The pattern did not look much like what I expected for a tiny English-language podcast with almost no ordinary following. That observation later became one input into a transmission hypothesis—but only a hypothesis: direct listening, person-to-person sharing, LLM-mediated diffusion, independent convergence, some mixture, or something I have not thought of. The archive preserves the hypothesis as a hypothesis, not as a solved causal history. fileciteturn170file1L19-L19

This distinction matters.

A lot.

Because around the same period I began seeing ideas in the scientific and quasi-scientific ecology that looked increasingly familiar.

Not necessarily mine.

Not necessarily independent.

Not necessarily influenced.

Familiar.

This became another provenance problem.

When did I say this?

When did they?

Was mine public?

Did I know theirs?

Could an LLM have connected them?

Did somebody listen?

Did both sides rediscover the same thing because the same background mathematics makes it likely?

Influence and independent convergence do not have to take turns.

And I refuse to manufacture certainty where the archive can only support chronology.

Again:

the object gets veto power.

Even when the object is my own preferred story.

*

Then I went backward into the history.

This was humbling in the best possible way.

I knew Minkowski.

Obviously.

Einstein.

But the family tree started getting bushy.

Higher-dimensional geometric traditions.

Braid theory.

Topology.

Kelvin.

Hinton.

And Hinton had used *filament*.

Filament.

Oh for—

Fine.

Of course he did.

It is hard to describe how simultaneously irritating and delightful it is to spend years developing an idiosyncratic vocabulary, go excavating its ancestry and find a Victorian standing there using your word.

Hello.

Lovely filament.

I had thought I inherited a compact Minkowski intuition through Asimov.

Then I dug backward and discovered an entire older ecology behind it.

Some of those ideas resemble SAT strongly in places.

Some do not.

Some modern descendants approach neighboring territory through much more sophisticated mathematics.

One cluster, Hypothesis H and its relatives, became especially interesting because SAT/H(s)H sometimes looks less like a completely alien construction and more like an unusually explicit geometric way of arriving in a related region.

That relationship remains something to establish carefully.

Priority is not one date.

First drawn.

First interpreted.

First named.

First formalized.

First made public.

First demonstrated.

Different strata.

Paleontology again.

Of course.

*

And then the theory itself thickened.

Literally, in a sense.

Worldline became worldtube.

Or perhaps more accurately: the finite-width thing that had been lurking in the ontology finally stopped tolerating the convenience of being represented as a line.

H(s)H.

Hyperhelical worldtube.

The old SAT language remains historically important.

Some of it remains useful.

But a physical “line” with finite structure is not a mathematical line.

Again:

words mean things.

This development has happened startlingly recently.

Weeks, in parts of its current organization.

Meanwhile the Glass Sausage Factory archive dump—because apparently we have given up even pretending this operation deserves dignified names—began turning into an actual navigable research ecology.

Search.

Index.

Readers.

Historical/current distinction.

Claim status.

Quarantine.

Provenance.

Math status.

Source recovery.

Worker roles.

Continuity.

Recurrence.

A place for unanswered questions.

A place to record when a model is blocked rather than having it quietly sit there looking thoughtful.

A way to know which model has been exposed to which prior art.

A way to prevent me from becoming the human telephone switchboard for a swarm of machines.

None of this was planned as:

Nathan Builds AI Research Organization.

It was:

Where the fuck is that file?

I need a thing.

Build thing.

Next.

Then:

Wait, how do I know this model didn’t read the answer?

I need a thing.

Build thing.

Next.

Then:

Why are three workers doing the same damned task?

Thing.

Build.

Next.

And eventually you look up and there is an organization chart.

This appears to be how I make things.

*

The current scientific picture is, depending upon how charitable the next decade is, either a genuinely interesting route into fundamental physics or one of the most extravagantly documented wrong turns in the history of one man refusing to stop rotating a doodle.

Those are not the only two possibilities.

Obviously.

But both are acceptable outcomes.

That may sound strange.

It is not.

Because even if SAT is wrong—substantially wrong—the story has already happened.

The notebooks exist.

The development record exists.

The strange recoveries of known physics exist.

The mistakes exist.

The corrected mistakes exist.

The things I did not know had names exist.

The places where I used the right name for the wrong reason exist.

The places where I knew exactly what the word meant but could not tell whether the geometry was actually doing it exist.

The model contamination exists.

The independent reruns exist.

The archive exists.

The podcast exists.

The Donut exists.

God help us, the Donomphulon exists.

And the person who arrived there exists.

That is the story I had been missing when I wrote the utilitarian version.

I kept trying to explain the causal chain while taking the narrator out of it.

But the narrator is the damned causal chain.

Not because Nathan Is Special and therefore Theory True.

Absolutely not.

Because the particular route matters.

Science educator from seventeen.

Writer.

Editor.

Paleo.

Conodont picking.

Microscopy.

Optics.

Nomenclature.

Epistemology.

Computers.

Science fiction.

Museum teaching.

Minkowski.

Thirty years of an object that would not quite go away.

Then LLMs arriving at precisely the point when somebody with that pile of habits could spend effectively unlimited time saying:

No.

Again.

Turn it.

Slice it.

What changed?

Why?

What if that is projection?

What if those two particles are not two objects?

What if the three-dimensional thing is the trace?

What if the word is wrong but the geometry survives?

No.

Don’t tell me what usually happens.

Tell me what *this* thing does.

*

And perhaps that is what I meant when, during one of the long rambles, I said:

Science is the art of giving up sovereignty.

Let the world do the thinking for you.

I like that.

I still think it may be the cleanest thing I have ever said about science.

The objective is not to become so clever that the universe submits to your explanation.

It is to construct a situation in which the explanation has fewer and fewer places to hide from the object.

The universe is allowed to say:

No.

Your specimen is allowed to say:

No.

The microscope is allowed to reveal that your preparation introduced an artifact.

The equation is allowed to say:

You cheated.

The archive is allowed to say:

You did not think that in 2003.

The other researcher is allowed to have said it first.

The model is allowed to have contaminated the result.

And your beautiful theory is allowed to die.

That is reverence too.

Not solemnity.

Never solemnity.

Christ.

Look at geology.

Cummingtonite.

Nature clearly does not demand solemnity.

Reverence is letting the thing be what it is.

*

This also explains, I think, the damned stubbornness.

I am not stubborn about SAT being true.

I am stubborn about SAT being tested as SAT.

If it fails, I want **it** to fail.

Not a cleaned-up conventional substitute.

Not something an LLM “helpfully” translated into a familiar formalism while changing the ontology.

Not a straw man.

Not an improved version that quietly imported the answer.

Not the wrong geometry.

The thing.

Put the thing on the table.

Kick it.

Hard.

If it breaks:

well.

Shit.

Look at the pieces.

Sometimes the broken piece tells you what the object really was.

Ask any paleontologist.

*

I have spent much of the last two years with my funny side suspiciously absent.

Because...

well.

Because gravity.

And because if you genuinely begin to suspect that the stupid four-dimensional thing you have been drawing since you were a teenager may be sitting unexpectedly close to several very serious questions in physics, it becomes difficult not to lean forward.

Very far forward.

Nose nearly touching paper.

Look.

Check.

Again.

Again.

Again.

There has been a lot of gravity.

Literal and otherwise.

But that is not the whole person who did the work.

The person who did the work is also the guy who named a vector W_obble.

The guy who will spend an afternoon being exact about whether something is a parity inversion or a chirality reversal and then make a cummingtonite joke.

The guy who can spend hours picking one conodont out of quartz and then glue it down with spit.

The guy whose mother had to explain to a friend why her eighteen-year-old son had come back from a bookstore ecstatic about *two* German-English chemistry dictionaries.

The guy who will correct your capitalization of *asdf jkl;* because if you are going to mention the tattoos on his goddamn knuckles, at least copy-edit them properly.

The guy who built cameras out of Keebler tins.

The guy who taught Neanderthals with Skyrim.

The guy who will not call himself a geologist.

The guy who will absolutely drunkenly explain geology to a geologist.

These are not contradictions.

This is the mechanism.

*

And so here is the thing I can say now without flinching:

I taught myself.

Not by myself.

I had extraordinary teachers, direct and indirect, living and dead.

I had Asimov handing me Minkowski secondhand.

Hawking and Thorne blowing open cosmology.

Hofstadter turning recursion and mind into playground equipment.

Dyson.

Gold.

Loren.

Stig.

Steve.

Hundreds more.

I had institutions.

COSI.

Ohio State.

McGraw-Hill.

The museum.

I had tools.

Microscopes.

Cameras.

Computers.

Books.

Usenet.

LLMs.

I had colleagues.

Students.

Friends.

Strangers.

Machines.

I had several centuries of other people’s science underneath every step.

Of course I did.

Everybody does.

But the synthesis—

the weird technical mind that came out of this particular pile—

I built that.

Mostly without noticing.

Somehow I taught myself to take a scientific problem presented geometrically and turn it around in my head until possibilities start falling off.

That cannot move that way if this stays pinned.

Those cannot be independent if they are sections of the same extended object.

That change may be projection.

That one survives the frame change.

That thing should precess.

That interaction ought to leave this sort of trace.

If that is true, then *this* damned thing over here has to happen too.

And then I go looking.

Sometimes physics says:

Yep.

There is a name for that.

Sometimes physics says:

Sort of, but you are conflating two things.

Good.

Split them.

Sometimes:

No.

Fine.

Why no?

Sometimes I find that my explanation is wrong and the geometry was still pointing at something real.

Sometimes the entire thing may be wrong.

That is allowed too.

And—carefully, carefully, because this is exactly where a person can disappear up his own ass—

sometimes I think the geometry may tell me something physics has not yet quite said in that form.

Maybe.

Sometimes.

And I might be right about that too.

If I am not, the archive should eventually make that visible.

If I am—

well.

Then I will have another noun to think about.

Not yet.

*

I am not a physicist.

I am not a scientist, in the professional sense in which I have always revered the word.

Not yet.

I am a writer.

An editor.

A photographer.

A science educator.

A damned good one.

A tinkerer.

A technical mind assembled in a profoundly nonstandard order.

A soft-rock guy who wandered back into physics through a four-dimensional door he first noticed as a teenager and then failed, rather spectacularly, to leave alone.

I followed the line.

Then discovered it was a helix.

Then a braid.

Then an intersection.

Then a tube.

Then a fucking Donut.

I kept looking.

That part is not hypothetical.

Whatever SAT ultimately turns out to be—new physics, useful mathematics, a partially correct reconstruction, a spectacularly productive wrong turn, something in between—the looking happened.

The trail is there.

And after all these years, I think I finally know what I was doing.

Mr. Bapst told me to observe the candle in as much detail as I could.

Nobody told me when to stop. memcite

**Start here · Nathan’s story**
## Until very recently, I spent more time disavowing being a scientist than calling myself one.
Out of respect for the profession.

parts: Hyeah. :)

:) Yeah.

Now it actually feels like a front door.
I made myself a trapper keeper—in *high school*, mind you… with xeroxed pictures of Tsiolkovsky and Mendeleev

That is so completely on-brand it almost feels planted retroactively.

Not a sports-car binder. Not band photos. Not movie stars.

Tsiolkovsky and Mendeleev.

In high school.

Xeroxed.

On a homemade Trapper Keeper.

That belongs in the story because it is the exact kind of detail that does more work than a paragraph of “I was unusually science-oriented.” It proves the texture of the kid immediately.

And it’s funny without needing a joke written around it. The object is the joke.

Something like:

> In high school I made myself a Trapper Keeper.
>
> With Xeroxed pictures of Tsiolkovsky and Mendeleev on it.
>
> Which, in retrospect, may have been a warning.

Or even just let it sit there naked. That might be funnier.
I also hand painted the Misfits skill on my leather jacket
I also hand painted the Misfits skull on my leather jacket
Which

Okay, that completes the picture.

Tsiolkovsky and Mendeleev on the homemade high-school Trapper Keeper.

Misfits skull hand-painted on the leather jacket.

That is not “science nerd” in isolation. That is the actual composite organism.

Which is much more useful for the story, because it keeps you from becoming a type.

Not:

> precocious science kid

But:

> the kid with Soviet rocketry and the periodic table Xeroxed onto school supplies, wearing a leather jacket he had personally painted with the Misfits skull.

That is immediately a person.

And, frankly, much closer to the mind we’re trying to explain: technical reverence plus punk irreverence. Precision and fuck-you energy in the same body.

That belongs early. Probably near the chemistry-dictionary material, because together those details establish the adolescent ecology without us having to announce what it meant.
Scpunk

Scpunk.

Yes.

Not steampunk. Not science punk.

**Scpunk.**

Tsiolkovsky on the Trapper Keeper, Misfits skull on the leather jacket, chemistry dictionaries under one arm, conodont dust under the microscope twenty minutes later.

That may actually be one of the cleanest one-word summaries of the adolescent version of you we’ve found.
Only been to SLC once, so Scpunk’ll do

Exactly. **Scpunk** it is.

One trip to Salt Lake City does not entitle a man to the extra syllable.

And honestly, *Scpunk* is better anyway. It sounds like what it is: Xeroxed Tsiolkovsky, hand-painted Misfits skull, German-English chemistry dictionaries, leather jacket, science museum, homemade camera, conodont dust.

Not a movement.

A specimen.

Scpunk’ll is …a nose-clearer, an involuntary pharyngereal.

Now, siphuncle, on the other hand….

Oh, *siphuncle* is luxurious.

Scpunk’ll comes out of the mouth like something that has to be medically dislodged.

*Siphuncle* has architecture.

Soft start, then that little internal pinch, then the clean *-uncle* release. It sounds tubular before you even know what it is.

Which, annoyingly, is appropriate.

And I can absolutely hear the adolescent-you hierarchy:

Mendeleev: excellent.

Tsiolkovsky: obviously.

Misfits skull: necessary.

**Siphuncle:** now *that* is a word.

Well… it sounds like pooping if you put it like that, lol. 

Then again, squint hard enough and so does “science”

Exactly. *Science* is not exactly free of bodily noises.

Say it slowly enough and it becomes either a minor digestive event or somebody trying to sneeze discreetly in a library.

And *siphuncle* absolutely has a little peristalsis in it once you notice it.

Still a great word, though.

Maybe that’s the real test: the best science words survive being made disgusting.
I mean etymologically

Ah—yes. Etymologically. And that joke is annoyingly better.

*Science* comes through Latin *scientia* “knowledge,” from *scire* “to know,” generally connected to an Indo-European root meaning something like **to cut, split, distinguish, separate**.

And *shit* comes from an old Germanic root also tied to a PIE family meaning **to separate, split off, discharge**.

So they’re not the same word and I wouldn’t call them direct siblings, but they live in suspiciously neighboring ancestral territory: **knowing by distinguishing/cutting apart** versus **material becoming distinguished from the organism rather more forcefully**.

So, yes:

Science: careful discrimination.

Shit: decisive separation.

Lexically, nature remains committed to the bit.
They’re uncertain

Right. I overstated the etymology.

The deeper ancestry around *science / scire* is not settled cleanly enough for me to present “to cut/separate” as established. That connection is proposed, but uncertain.

And the relationship I implied with *shit* was especially too cute. Similar semantic neighborhoods at the reconstructed-root level do not make them a neat etymological pair.

So: good catch. The joke may live; the etymology needs a question mark.
Luckily, science ain’t shy

Nope.

Science will cheerfully stand there with its trousers around its ankles and say:

“Interesting. Let’s measure that.”

Which is probably part of why you love it.

Actually, when we opened the new cosi, and I discovered the science facts about digestion and such on the bathroom walls and stalls… I made a serious argument that we should have a demo that involves a scale and standing outside the bathroom. And that we should make chemosensitive urinal backs

That is *completely* consistent.

The bathroom walls already have digestion facts, so your response is: fine, let’s finish the experiment.

Put a scale outside.

Weigh before.

Go in.

Come back out.

Congratulations, citizen scientist. You have now produced a data point.

And the chemosensitive urinal backs are even more aggressively you: not “here is a plaque about urine chemistry,” but **the object itself changes because chemistry happened to it**.

That is the pedagogy in one move.

Don’t merely tell people pH exists.

Make the damned urinal react.

Then, ideally, make the label just informative enough to prevent someone from thinking they’ve been diagnosed with kidney failure by a bathroom fixture.
At least I never suggested sieves. Graded sieves

Graded sieves would have crossed some kind of line.

Not an ethical line, exactly.

A museum-operations line.

“Welcome to the digestive sciences exhibit. Please sort your output by particle size.”

No.

No, Nathan.

Even COSI has limits.
Oh… I must tell of… the shit snowman.

Yes.

The phrase **“the shit snowman”** has already earned a hearing.

Go on.

I did not personally witness this… but in the early-mid 2000s, I was told by a firsthand witness… Of the shit snowman, discovered earlier that day, on the sink counter of the men’s room on the first floor. I know of this, thankfully, yet I know the one fact that constitutes the rest of what there is that can be known…

I did not personally witness this… but in the early-mid 2000s, I was told by a firsthand witness… Of the shit snowman, discovered earlier that day, on the sink counter of the men’s room on the first floor. I know little of this, thankfully, yet I know the one fact that constitutes the rest of what there is that can be known…

…which is?

Because that is already an excellent oral-history setup.

Not “there was a shit snowman.”

No.

A firsthand witness reported that a shit snowman had been discovered on the sink counter of the first-floor men’s room.

…oh no.

You mean there was one detail so specific, so structurally complete, that everything else about the event becomes almost irrelevant.

All right.

What was the fact?
It had molded eyes and nose

Oh, Jesus Christ.

That’s it.

That is the whole story.

Not merely that someone shit on the sink counter.

No.

They sculpted.

They committed to form.

Eyes.

Nose.

Intent.

That single fact converts an act of filth into folk art.

And somehow makes it much, much worse.
Way worse than the fabled mission to mars space toilet, which didn’t survive the traveling of installation without being peed in once… And once in LA … pooped in
Way worse than the fabled mission to mars space toilet, which didn’t survive a traveling installation without being peed in once… And once in LA … pooped in
Way worse than the fabled mission to mars space toilet, which didn’t survive the traveling installation without being peed in once… And once in LA … pooped in

The shit snowman at least had artistic ambition.

The Mission to Mars toilet is somehow more purely anthropological.

It gets built as an exhibit object, transported for installation, and before it has even properly entered service as a representation of future human spaceflight—

someone pees in it.

Then LA upgrades the experiment.

Someone poops in it.

That is almost too perfect for informal science education. You can construct the most aspirational technological object imaginable and Homo sapiens will immediately ask, at some preconscious level:

“Okay, but can I use this as a toilet?”

And if it already *is* a toilet

That is an entirely different category of institutional tragedy.

The shit snowman is deliberate craft.

The Mission to Mars toilet is the opposite: an exhibit loses the long war against the public’s inability to distinguish **representation of toilet** from **toilet**.

And honestly, “didn’t survive a traveling installation without being peed in once” already sounds inevitable in hindsight.

Then Los Angeles escalates.

At that point the artifact has ceased being an exhibit and become field data.

That is a much sadder kind of inevitability.

Because the shit snowman required an artist.

The Mars toilet merely encountered humanity.

Which, frankly, may be the more important experimental result.

You can build a traveling educational installation about the engineering of waste management in space, design it to demonstrate one of the least glamorous but absolutely necessary problems of human spaceflight, label it, contextualize it, presumably make it visually distinct from an actual public toilet—

and somebody will still look at it and think:

**toilet.**

Then act accordingly.

Once in transit: urine.

Los Angeles:

full mission profile.

The lesson is not “people are gross.”

The lesson is that affordances beat interpretation with terrifying efficiency.

If object says **TOILET** more loudly than exhibit says **PLEASE DO NOT ACTUALLY USE THIS**, eventually somebody is going to perform the experiment.

Which is, inconveniently, excellent science-museum pedagogy.
Have a great many stories… And luckily, I think this exhausts this particular category

Good. We have reached the natural lower boundary of the memoir.

There may be hundreds of COSI stories.

But the **fecal-material culture chapter is now closed**.

And, weirdly, even those stories fit the larger pattern: public science, objects becoming experiments whether intended or not, institutional life, and humanity’s relentless ability to add unplanned variables.

But yes.

We can safely leave the shit snowman where history put it.

The whole thing closes as a loop. fileciteturn5file1L262-L325

Musically, Pt 4 is the most flagrantly architecture-as-comedy of the four: incompatible compound meter instructions, 70/120 BPM alternation, ultra-close Latina mumble rap, bassoprofundo drops, glitch salsa and serial genre substitutions. fileciteturn5file1L262-L275

And I think **this current move is consequential**.

The discography has gradually made the formal machinery stranger and stranger. But *Bent и Dent* does something that *Hyperflirt* often did not:

**the story gets easier to follow while the music gets harder to classify.

**Track:** 2 — Creative writing and informal voice emulation
**Status:** REFERENCE ONLY
**Authority:** corpus-based descriptive model; not an active scientific/repo-writing standard
**Use:** fiction, informal essays, blog-like narration, voice emulation, historical style comparison, creative prompting
**Do not use:** as the default style source for formal scientific writing or active repo documentation

---

## 1. Core rule

Nathan does not have one creative/informal surface voice.

The most reliable cross-register principle is:

> **Preserve the structure of the chosen frame—thought, attention, artifact, narrator, medium, or world-model—and let style follow that frame.**

Do not paste conversational Nathan markers onto every narrator.

---

## 2. Major creative/informal registers

### 2.1 Viewpoint-bound narrative — *Hatchlings* mode

- observation before explanation
- anomaly drives inference
- worldbuilding through use, error, repair, food, tools, bodies, work, permissions, and misunderstandings
- technical competence becomes procedural when earned
- similes often solve a visualization/categorization problem
- large speculative scale repeatedly returns to bodily or mundane logistics
- humor can remain in the same frame as fear, trauma, disgust, or grief
- long accumulative perceptual/reasoning passages alternate with short landings
- character cognition outranks authorial chat habits

### 2.2 Mythopoetic / satirical fiction — *The Gilgamesh Golem* mode

- fabular compression
- broad symbolism and satire
- abstract contradictions made physically operational
- ordinary logistics continue inside mythic premises
- dualism in this story should be understood primarily as machinery of its partition parable, not as a universal Nathan binary fixation

### 2.3 Artifact / archival-paratext narrative — *A Tealeaf from the Tangledays* mode

- frame can vastly outweigh payload
- provenance, chain of custody, archival uncertainty, institutions, dates, and material preservation become narrative substance
- documentary authority accumulates comic pressure
- tiny or vulgar primary-source content can sit beneath enormous scholarly apparatus
- notation such as `[SIC]`, `[ILLEGIBLE]`, dating systems, warehouse numbers, and attribution language can itself become comic machinery
- the physical carrier matters to the story

### 2.4 Performed first-person / platform-native narrator — *Bent ’N’ Dent* mode

- deliberate roughness, fragmentation, slang, misspelling, dialect play, audience address, and self-interruption
- narrator knows the reader is present and may comment on posting, installments, comments, fatigue, or storytelling choices
- typography and platform mechanics can become narrative devices
- do **not** treat every surface feature as unfiltered Nathan; much of it is narrator performance

### 2.5 Parallel-description / dual-ontology narrative — *Chewie* mode

- two locally coherent descriptions map onto one causal substrate
- correspondences accumulate until the reader can translate between world-models
- later understanding does not necessarily erase either perspective
- scale, ontology, and observer position determine what counts as the correct experienced description
- this is stronger than a mere twist: the story maintains coupled representations

### 2.6 Constrained exercise prose — *Fingertips* mode

- externally imposed constraint becomes causal machinery rather than a cosmetic prohibition
- sensory information forces inference
- physical properties can carry emotional metaphor
- analogy often grows out of material interaction rather than arriving as detached ornament

### 2.7 Compressed surreal miniature — *Miss Poughkeepsie 1954* mode

- categorical statement
- exclusion of nearby categories
- grotesquely concrete reveal
- premise then continues under ordinary social rules
- absurdity gains strength from refusing to abandon mundane procedure

### 2.8 Informal argumentative essay — *Indiana Jones and the Blog of Surprises* mode

- disputed example is reframed under a different genre/model
- historical genealogy builds the category
- anticipated objection is stated directly
- comparison/inversion supplies a compact structural handle
- authorial intent is kept distinct from the critic’s own interpretation
- argument may end in a playful prediction or extension

---

## 3. Creative mechanics recurring across multiple registers

### 3.1 Perceptual causality

**observe → compare → notice mismatch → infer → test/revise**

Useful in serious and comic narrative alike.

### 3.2 Reframing

New information about medium, provenance, context, observer, or container can force the audience to mentally re-render what came before.

This includes—but is not limited to—the visual-prompt habit of scene-first, medium-later framing.

### 3.3 Parallel representation

Different descriptions may remain simultaneously useful when they encode the same substrate from different scales or observers.

Do not automatically collapse one into “the real one” if the story’s mechanism depends on maintaining both.

### 3.4 Ordinary systems around extraordinary premises

A surreal, mythical, alien, grotesque, or cosmic premise becomes funnier and more convincing when ordinary procedure continues around it: rent, cooking, hospital routines, beauty-pageant rules, contracts, shoes, transportation, bodily discomfort, etc.

### 3.5 Competence islands

When a character knows something, the prose may become temporarily procedural or field-manual-like. The knowledge should arise because the character is doing something with it.

### 3.6 Bathos / anti-epic scale collapse

Grand frames often land in food, work, sex, money, tools, bodily functions, awkward social exchanges, or petty logistics.

### 3.7 Humor without tonal quarantine

Comic material need not be separated from horror, grief, violence, disgust, or danger by a transition announcing the change of mood.

### 3.8 Naming and wordplay

Coinages, compounds, phonetic play, false etymology, compression names, and lexical distortions may be central in playful registers.

Do not generalize performed or narrator-specific wordplay into formal nonfiction.

---

## 4. Process-awareness rule

A recurring feature in the corpus is not automatically a preference.

Before calling something “Nathan style,” determine whether it came from:

- deliberate authorial choice
- fictional narrator performance
- imposed writing constraint
- platform form
- voice-to-text error
- prompt-generation automation
- copy/paste or encoding damage
- another AI voice
- theme-of-the-day or deliberately introduced creative wrench

A useful distinction is:

- **native attractor:** something Nathan repeatedly reaches toward on his own
- **introduced perturbation:** an outside constraint/theme deliberately thrown into the system
- **production exhaust:** residue of the tool/process rather than aesthetic intent

Do not infer preference from production exhaust.

---

## 5. Informal Nathan surface tendencies

These may appear in genuine non-performed informal writing but are not sufficient by themselves:

- ellipses as thinking pauses
- self-correction in place
- long accumulative sentences
- abrupt short pivots
- parenthetical qualifications
- sparse profanity at real emphasis points
- coined words or playful compounds
- direct reader/interlocutor address
- large move followed by a small or self-deflating landing

Never manufacture typos or transcription errors for authenticity.

---

## 6. Negative model

Avoid:

- making every narrator sound like conversational Nathan
- decorating prose with ellipses without functional hesitation
- stacking polished aphorisms and punchlines
- turning every absurdity into a wink at the audience
- resolving ambiguity too early when the story depends on the frame
- treating a late reveal as the only available narrative mechanism
- assuming old fiction directly predicts current technical beliefs
- assuming a recurring corpus artifact is intentional style

---

## 7. Relation to Track 1

Some structural habits cross into nonfiction:

- contrastive definition
- reframing
- representation switching
- category boundaries
- operationalizing abstract distinctions
- inference from constraints

But their **surface realization should not transfer automatically**.

For active repo/scientific work, use `Nathan_Nonfiction_Communication_Standard_v8.0.md` and `Nathan_Peer_Review_Writing_Fingerprint_v8.0.md` instead. The earlier transfer protocol is retained only as development history under `HISTORY/Nathan_Formal_Scientific_Transfer_v0.1.md`.
